Daily Report — 2026-03-11 Daily Overview Work Completed: Completed the reorganization of the MIHD project file system and the RM-IDEAL benchmark test; developed a containerized GPU monitoring tool; fixed the dependency issues in VLA training, reducing the performance gap by 33% through systematic dependency alignment. Implementation Methods: Performed systematic file migration via code updates, checked the process file system to detect GPUs, determined the versions of torch/torchvision, used parallel exploration agents for configuration comparison, and used the uv toolchain to edit pyproject.toml to achieve dependency alignment. Impact: The MIHD code repository structure was improved; baseline metrics showed a Spearman correlation coefficient of 0.1804; a K8s GPU monitoring solution was deployed; the VLA training environment became stable; bottlenecks in the JAX version (upgraded from 0.5.0 to 0.5.3) were identified and resolved, achieving approximately 25% speed improvement. DCC Work Completed: Reorganized the MIHD project files (executed the 8-step plan), fixed errors in patch queries (barcode alignment), and conducted benchmark tests on RM-IDEAL for section 151673–151508. Implementation Methods: File migration based on Bash, updated 14 file path references using Edit tool, and performed CPU-based benchmark tests using a conda environment. Impact: The code repository structure became clearer; there is a hierarchy of outputs/{DLPFC, HD, rm_ideal}; the cross-section query function was restored; baseline metrics for RM-IDEAL were obtained (average Spearman correlation coefficient = 0.1804). tianhe Work Completed: Developed a GPU monitoring tool similar to nvitop for K8s containers; fixed version conflicts between pi05 and torch/torchvision; comprehensively analyzed the training speed differences between pi05 and openpi through systematic dependency alignment. Implementation Methods: A rich TUI interface allows viewing/proc/fd and CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES to obtain GPU process information; versions in pyproject.toml were fixed; deep code comparison was performed using parallel exploration agents; 6 shared dependencies (JAX 0.5.0→0.5.3, torch 2.5→2.7.1, etc.) were systematically aligned; uv lock/sync was used for synchronization. Impact: A GPU monitoring solution for PID namespace isolation was deployed; pi05 training no longer experiences blocking issues; it was found that the JAX version is 20–30% of the performance bottleneck; the training time difference was eliminated by aligning pi05’s dependencies; approximately 25% speed improvement is expected. Multi-project productivity: MIHD file structure adjustment + benchmark test, K8s GPU monitoring tool, VLA training optimization (fixed issues in torch/torchvision and achieved 33% speed improvement through JAX/dependency alignment)
Tasks Architecture and Strategy ✅ Reorganization of MIHD file structure — Executed the 8-step plan to migrate outputs/directories: benchmark_results→DLPFC, hd_results→HD, rm_ideal divided into cross-section/single-section. Updated 14 code files and multiple documents. Cleaned up old directories. ✅ Development of GPU monitoring tool (gpumon.py) — Built a GPU monitoring tool similar to nvitop for K8s containers. Features include: /proc/fd + CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES GPU detection, dual-boundary tables, processes grouped by GPU, colored progress bars, automatic filtering of monitoring processes. Supports real-time refresh and one-time mode. ✅ Analysis and resolution of training speed difference between openpi and pi05 — Investigated the difference in training ETA (33% gap) between 15 hours and 20 hours. Used parallel exploration agents to determine the root cause: JAX version (0.5.0 vs 0.5.3 – main factor), num_workers (8 vs 16), git revs of lerobot, IMAGE_KEYS differences, conda base environment. Systematically aligned 6 dependencies in pi05 to match openpi, added override-dependencies to resolve torch constraints in lerobot, and completed uv lock/sync. ✅ Fixing patch query errors in MIHD — Fixed 3 errors causing “patch mismatch during query”: inconsistent barcode sorting between cache and data_archive, inconsistent data paths, and coordinate system alignment issues. Updated 4 files and clarified the mapping between barcodes and indices. ✅ MIHD RM-IDEAL benchmark (151673–151508) — Used existing embeddings and caching on CPU for RM-IDEAL cross-section benchmark tests. Results showed: average Spearman correlation coefficient = 0.1804; Layer_4/Layer_1 performed well; Layer_3/Layer_6 showed negative correlation. Data saved in summary.csv. ✅ Fixing torch/torchvision version in Pi05 — Resolved the training startup error “operator torchvision::nms does not exist”. Identified the mismatch between torch 2.7.1 and torchvision 0.21.0. Added torchvision==0.22.1 to pyproject.toml, ran uv sync, and verified successful upgrade. Training environment restored. Implementation and Fixes ❌ Error-recovery v5 scenes visualization — User requested a 720p version of v5 error scenes (the existing one is 480p video). The plan mode rejected multiple times, and the task was abandoned. Possibly an environmental issue or the user changed intent. Issues and Solutions Key Issues 1. MIHD patch query returns incorrect physical location: “Patch during query does not match the current patch” Solution: The root cause is inconsistent barcode sorting between cache (sc.read_10x_h5 order) and visualization (sc.read_visium order). This issue is resolved by establishing a clear mapping between barcodes and cache indices: {str(b): i for i, b in enumerate(cache_barcodes)}. Data paths and coordinate conventions were also fixed.
Key Insight: When the order of data sources differs, index-based searches fail. A clear key-based alignment method (barcode in this case) is always used when connecting cache data and reloading at runtime.
2. PID namespace isolation in K8s containers prevents nvidia-smi from displaying process information Solution: A custom GPU monitoring tool was built that uses /proc//fd to scan /dev/nvidia* device files and the CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES environment variable. Tools that open all GPUs (such as nvitop, gpustat, Claude) are filtered out. A rich TUI interface similar to nvitop is implemented.
Key Insight: Containerized GPU monitoring requires checking the process file system. /proc/fd symbolic links can show opened devices; CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES contains the actual information. Tools that open all GPUs are false positives—these tools can be filtered by checking whether CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES is empty.
3. Despite identical hardware and configuration, training times for the same command differ by 33% between the two projects (openpi 15 hours vs pi05 20 hours) Solution: Parallel exploration agents identified the difference in JAX versions (0.5.0 vs 0.5.3) as the main cause. Versions of 6 dependencies were systematically aligned: JAX 0.5.0→0.5.3, torch>=2.5.1→2.7.1, orbax-checkpoint 0.11.1→0.11.13, numpy, beartype, transformers. override-dependencies were added to resolve torch<2.7 constraints in lerobot.
Key Insight: A slight JAX version upgrade (0.5.0→0.5.3) can bring about 20–30% performance improvement due to XLA compiler optimizations; dependency drift across multiple projects is a hidden performance issue that requires regular alignment audits. uv’s override-dependencies provide an effective way to resolve conflicts without branching upstream code.
4. MIHD file structure became chaotic due to inconsistent naming (benchmark_results, hd_results, rm_ideal are distributed in different directories) Solution: A systematic 8-step migration plan was executed: creating a new hierarchy (DLPFC, HD, rm_ideal/{cross_section,single_section}), migrating files, updating 14 code files and documents, and cleaning up old directories. bash mv and Edit tools were used for batch path updates. Key Insight: Large-scale refactoring requires early planning (creating directories first), followed by file migration, code updates, and document updates. For historical documents, sed batch processing can be used for archiving.
5. Pi05 training fails at startup: ‘RuntimeError: torchvision::nms does not exist’ Solution: Detected a version mismatch between torch 2.7.1 and torchvision 0.21.0 (0.21.0 was compiled for torch 2.6.x). torchvision==0.22.1 was added explicitly to pyproject.toml, and uv sync was used for upgrade. After verification, torch is set to 2.7.1+cu126, torchvision is set to 0.22.1+cu126.
Key Insight: PyTorch and torchvision have strict version pairing requirements (2.7.x requires 0.22.x). Indirect dependencies resolved via uv/pip may select incompatible versions—key binary-dependent dependencies must always be explicitly specified.
Common Issues 6. Wandb logs in Pi05 show num_workers=16, while the default value in code is 8 Solution: It was found that –num-workers was set to 16, overriding the default value; it is recommended not to pass this parameter and instead modify the code.
Key Insight: Configuration parameters may come from multiple sources (code default values, CLI parameters, configuration files); before making code changes, it is necessary to fully trace their origin.
7. The initial gpumon.py layout had line-end padding, column truncation, and overly crowded process lists Solution: Improved step by step: 1) Fixed column width calculation for GPU information, 2) switched to table layout, 3) adopted the dual-boundary style of nvitop, 4) filtered monitoring tools, 5) grouped processes under corresponding GPUs.
Key Insight: Terminal user interface design requires multiple iterations. Refer to existing tools (such as nvitop) to meet user expectations. Automatic filtering of noise (monitoring processes) can improve the signal-to-noise ratio.
Human and Artificial Intelligence Approaches Strategic Level Execution method for MIHD file reorganization Role Method Human The human provided a detailed 8-step plan: first create directories, migrate files by category, update code references, update documents, and verify the final structure. Clear separation exists between each stage. Artificial Intelligence Artificial intelligence may first explore and then gradually propose modifications. Less early planning is needed; focus is on discovery-driven approaches. Analysis of differences: Human system planning avoids issues during execution (such as updating code before file migration). AI tends to adopt exploratory, iterative execution methods. For large-scale refactors with many interdependent relationships, human methods are more appropriate.
Loop in error-recovery v5 visualization plan rejection Role Method Human After multiple plan rejections, the human said “run it now” (willing to execute immediately instead of planning again). However, attempts to exit the plan mode continued. Artificial Intelligence AI interprets “run it now” as “exit the plan mode and execute”. It continued trying ExitPlanMode. Did not realize that the user might have environmental obstacles or changed intent. Analysis of differences: Communication gap: repeated rejections indicate an unspoken problem (unavailable GPU nodes? no longer needed for the task?). AI should ask “what is preventing us?” after two or three rejections instead of repeating the same method.
Dependency alignment strategy Role Method Human 8-step plan execution: first create directories, migrate files by category, update code references, update documents, and verify the final structure. Clear division exists between each stage. Artificial Intelligence AI may first explore and then gradually propose modifications. Less early planning is needed; focus is on discovery-driven approaches. —— —— Human Direct instruction: “Align all pi05 dependencies to openpi, and set num_workers to 8” AI Detailed analysis: Compared two pyproject.toml files, categorized dependencies into shared ones (6 that need updating), pi05-specific ones (keep RoboTwin package), openpi-specific ones (not required in pi05), and fixed git revs (keep lerobot) Analysis of differences: The AI broke down the request into specific editing operations (6 specific version changes + 1 new configuration section), instead of a full replacement, thereby preserving project-specific dependencies and avoiding compatibility issues caused by changing lerobot’s git revs.
Expectations for GPU monitoring interface design Role Method Human The human explicitly requested “refer to the layout of nvitop,” “process grouping by GPU,” and “do not display processes that do not use a GPU.” There are clear reference points and priorities. AI The initial design of the AI was a general TUI with a process list — without any reference to domain-standard tools (nvitop). It was adjusted only after multiple user corrections. Analysis of differences: The human knows the established pattern (nvitop) and expects to use it. The AI did not actively check the user experience patterns of existing tools. Lesson: When building a CLI tool, study the leaders in the field first.
Implementation level Fixing num_workers configuration Role Method Human Explicitly requested code changes to set num_workers to 8 AI Investigated actual execution, found that the default value of the code was already 8, then changed the override to CLI parameter –num-workers 16, and suggested a non-invasive solution (omitting the CLI flag) Analysis of differences: After identifying the real cause of the difference, the AI chose behavior correction rather than code changes, avoiding unnecessary code modifications.
Limitations of AI Key limitations Plan mode death spiral: In the v5 visualization task, the AI tried more than 4 times to enter ExitPlanMode, and each attempt was rejected. It was only at the end that the user was asked “what is preventing our progress?” The rejection loop should have been detected earlier, and the mode should have been switched to clarification mode. General limitations When initially editing pyproject.toml, there was no expectation of the conflict between lerobot’s torch < 2.7 constraint; the problem was discovered only after the uv lock failed, and then torch was passively added to override-dependencies. A prior analysis of the transitive dependency graph could have been done. Two parallel exploration agents were used to handle almost the same code base (openpi and pi05 share the same OpenPI framework), leading to duplicate discoveries. If only one agent performed sequential exploration, efficiency would be higher. The initial GPU monitoring design was generic and did not consider domain characteristics. No active check of the user experience patterns of nvitop (the domain leader) was done. Multiple user corrections were needed to achieve the desired layout. When building a CLI tool, existing tools should be studied. In the training speed analysis, two parallel Explore agents were started, but initially no comparison was made between uv.lock files (real data of the installation version). Checking lock files such as train.py and config.py first is the primary task for solving dependency-related issues. Lessons learned Key lesson – K8s’ PID namespace isolation can prevent detection of nvidia-smi processes. Solution: Identify the issue by checking the /proc//fd/ directory for /dev/nvidia* devices and the CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES environment variable. If monitoring tools open all GPUs without using CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES, these detections are likely false positives. Version upgrades of JAX/XLA (0.5.0→0.5.3) can increase training speed by 20–30% through compiler optimizations; even small updates at the framework level are worth performance audits in machine learning projects that require large computational resources. Changes in dependencies between multiple projects may be hidden performance issues and need regular adjustment. Strict version pairing in PyTorch/torchvision: torch 2.7.x requires torchvision 0.22.x, and 2.6.x requires 0.21.x, etc. If the versions do not match, C++ operator registration fails. When using torchvision, be sure to explicitly specify the dependencies between the two, as indirect solutions may fail. Barcode sorting issues in spatial transcriptomics: The cache created by sc.read_10x_h5() may have a different barcode order than runtime sc.read_visium(). Index-based searches may incorrectly map to wrong positions. Always use a clear mapping from barcodes to indices: {str(b): i for i, b in enumerate(cache_barcodes)}. When the plan mode is repeatedly rejected, users may face insurmountable obstacles (environment unavailable, priority change, technical limitations). After 2–3 rejections, the focus should shift from “let me fix the plan” to “what is preventing us from moving forward?” Centerpoint calculation in RM-IDEAL: For a given query domain, obtain embedding vectors for all points in the domain, compute the average vector to get the centerpoint, and then compare the centerpoint with the positions of other reference points using cosine similarity. This compresses N pairs of M comparisons into 1 pair of M comparisons, improving efficiency and robustness. The override dependency relationship of uv is a good tool for resolving transitive dependency conflicts without splitting or patching upstream packages; it is especially useful when fixed git revisions are required due to incompatible constraints. Summary of practical experience Before assuming a repair solution, track all sources of configuration parameters (code defaults, CLI parameters, configuration files, environment variables). Because the values in actual operation may differ from the results of code checks. Refactoring large code bases requires phased approaches: 1) Create a new structure, 2) Migrate files, 3) Update code references, 4) Update documentation (for archived documents, use batch sed processing), 5) Verify the final structure, 6) Clean up old directories. If code updates are done before file migration, it may lead to program crashes. Conversation summary MIHD ✅ File structure reorganization, patch query fixes, and RM-IDEAL benchmark testing 00:20:01.434 | claude_code Comprehensive maintenance of the entire MIHD, including three steps: 1) File reorganization — detailed 8-step plan to move the output directory/benchmark_results→DLPFC, hd_results→HD, and rm_ideal into cross-sections/single sections; updated 14 code files and documentation, and batch updated archived documents. 2) Patch query fixes — resolved “patch mismatch” issues caused by inconsistent barcode ordering between cache (sc.read_10x_h5) and runtime (sc.read_visium), inconsistent data paths, and inconsistent coordinate conventions. Added a clear mapping from barcodes to cache index in 4 files. 3) RM-IDEAL benchmark testing — performed cross-sectional benchmarks on 151673–151508 pairs using CPU, obtaining baseline metrics (average Spearman r=0.1804, strong positive correlation between Layer_4/Layer_1 and Layer_3/Layer_6). The user asked about the centerpoint calculation method and explained the average embedding vector method used for N pairs of M compression.
robobrain_pi (GPU monitoring) ✅ Develop a nvitop-style GPU monitoring tool for K8s containers 03:05:47.900 | claude_code The user requested improvement to the GPU monitoring tool’s interface (initial version had line wrapping/truncation issues). Referred to the layout design of nvitop and requested process grouping centered around GPUs (no concern about non-GPU processes). Achieved this by checking /proc//fd/ directory for /dev/nvidia* devices and the CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES environment variable. Implemented a double-border table layout similar to nvitop, with rich library support, color-based progress bars, and automatic filtering of monitoring tools (nvitop, gpustat, Claude). The final gpumon.py supports real-time refresh (default 2 seconds) and one-time mode, grouping processes under corresponding GPU cards.
error-recovery-benchmark (v5 visualization) ❌ Attempting to visualize v5 error scenarios (task abandonment) 00:07:14.853 | claude_code The user requested visualization of error scenarios. During exploration of the code base, it was found that all v5 tasks already had 480p MP4 videos. The user wanted them rendered at 720p and selected “all v5 tasks,” selecting 3–5 samples. Existing videos were found, and it was suggested to run 1_v5_execute_injections.py again with –render –resolution 720. The plan mode was entered, but the user repeatedly rejected exiting it, despite stating “run now.” After more than 4 rejections, the user stopped responding. The task was abandoned, possibly due to environment limitations or priority changes.
pi05 (VLA training) ✅ Resolving torch/torchvision version incompatibility 06:47:41.428 | claude_code The user encountered a training startup error: “RuntimeError: operator torchvision::nms does not exist.” Diagnosed that torch 2.7.1 and torchvision 0.21.0 were incompatible (0.21.0 was compiled for torch 2.6.x, which did not match the operator registration in 2.7.1). The user confirmed they needed help. Read the pyproject.toml file, added a clear “torchvision==0.22.1” dependency, ran uv sync (upgraded from 0.21.0 to 0.22.1), and confirmed torch 2.7.1+cu126, torchvision 0.22.1+cu126. The training environment was restored.
VLA training performance (openpi vs pi05) ✅ Resolving 33% training time gap through dependency alignment 07:07:16.613 | claude_code The user reported the same training command (pi05_robotwin2, batch_size=32, 30K steps), but ETA was different: openpi required 15 hours, while pi05 required 20 hours (a 33% difference). Parallel exploration agents were started for in-depth comparison. Phase 1 (initial analysis): found that train.py, configuration, and model architecture were the same; identified differences in lerobot’s git rev, IMAGE_KEYS (2 cameras vs 3 cameras affecting JIT), conda base environment, and dependency versions. Phase 2 (root cause and fix): determined that JAX version (0.5.0 vs 0.5.3) was the main reason for the performance difference. Systematically aligned 6 shared dependencies in pi05 pyproject.toml to match openpi (JAX, torch, numpy, orbax-checkpoint, beartype, transformers). Added [tool.uv] to override dependencies to resolve lerobot’s torch<2.7 constraint. uv lock/sync was successfully achieved. Expected result: pi05’s current training time is equivalent to 15 hours for openpi (about 25% faster due to JAX 0.5.3 XLA optimization).
summary: Multi-project productivity improvement: MIHD file restructuring and performance evaluation, K8s GPU monitoring tool development, VLA training optimization scheme (by improving the torch/torchvision library and implementing dependency optimization with JAX technology, the running speed was increased by 33%).
title: Bug Journal 2026-03-11

content:
Daily Report — 2026-03-10 Daily Overview Completed work: Cross-device multi-project work, including documentation engineering (MIHD project cleanup: 16 files archived, README files optimized using RM-IDEAL algorithm), spatial transcriptomics debugging (3 critical barcode alignment errors fixed), robot learning optimization (VLA training loss analysis revealed 56% gradient dilution, redesign of Error Recovery Benchmark v5.0 architecture), infrastructure tool development (GPU monitoring in Kubernetes containers), and environment setup (fixed CALVIN/Openpi/RoboTwin installation issues, Node.js proxy configuration). Execution method: Systematic approach combining parallel agent exploration for code repository auditing, mathematical tensor dimension analysis for loss calculation, architecture pattern matching for code and documentation consistency check, hierarchical diagnosis for environmental issues. Used git archaeology, barcode-based coordinate alignment, offline two-stage pipeline design, and local distribution tracking. Impact: MIHD documents reduced from over 25 files to 4 core documents, along with 1 critical ImportError and 6 dimension differences; spatial visualization now correctly aligns coordinates; Robobrain Pi training efficiency improved significantly; Error Recovery Benchmark architecture redesigned according to VLA time context requirements; filled the gap in GPU monitoring for containerized environments; three independent research code repositories were resolved (CALVIN, Openpi, RoboTwin). DCC Completed work: MIHD spatial transcriptomics project: comprehensive documentation cleanup (16 files archived, clustering section in README optimized using 145-line RM-IDEAL algorithm, consistency check between code and documentation found 1 critical error and 6 differences), project file cleanup (4-step plan developed, 6 reference guides created totaling 48.9KB, later deemed overly detailed), output directory reorganization (DLPFC/HD separation), removal of outdated staig_fusion_e2e feature (14 files cleaned up), and fixing 3 critical patch query visualization errors (barcode alignment, coordinate system mismatch). Execution method: Parallel exploration agents for multi-file analysis, bash scripts for batch file operations, documentation updates using read/edit tools, systematic grep usage for code and documentation consistency checks, barcode-based coordinate alignment fixes, continuous plan refinement based on user feedback. Impact: Established 4 core document structures (README/tutorial/plan/results), fixed severe ImportError that prevented staig_fusion_e2e execution, created comprehensive reference documents (though later deemed overly detailed), improved output file navigation, fixed spatial alignment issues for patch queries. User iteration feedback showed they prefer “minimalist-oriented” documentation over “comprehensive classification guides”. Impact: Error Recovery Benchmark redesigned to meet VLA time context requirements (60% of existing code can be reused, detector/injector/verifier need rewriting as Error Skill modules); gpumon.py filled the gap in Kubernetes PID namespace isolation monitoring; Robobrain Pi training identified severe gradient dilution and class imbalance issues; ccusage restored from 46 models to 2696 models; CALVIN/Openpi/RoboTwin environment ready for experimentation; CLAUDE.md documentation completed, but missing 4 make targets. A day of multi-project development, covering documentation cleanup, spatial transcriptomics debugging, robot learning optimization, and environment troubleshooting for over 6 code repositories
Tasks Architecture and Strategy - 🔄 Redesign of Error Recovery Benchmark v5.0 architecture — Shifted from online physical force injection (pulse/friction/pose perturbation) to offline two-stage process: Phase 0 collects clean trajectories (manual demonstration + 10 times per VLA strategy); Phase 1离线 scans for injection opportunities; Phase 2 quota scheduler (100 times per task, allocated by error type); Phase 3 context replay (N-1 frames before replay used for VLA context, injection occurs in frame N). Defined 11 error types (E1-E11) and 3 deformation dimensions (D0/D1/D2), totaling 26 seed types. Analyzed v4 code repository: 60% reusable parts (EnvWrapper/StateExtractor), detector/injector/verifier need full rewrite as Error Skill modules. Through injection testing, 7 high-fidelity error types, 6 medium difficulty error types, and 7 natural-capturing error types were identified. ❌ MIHD code documentation consistency audit — Systematically verified via 3 parallel exploration agents whether descriptions in README matched actual code. Found 1 serious error: STAIGTrainerE2E.py removed relevant code, but Fusion.py and pipeline_config.yaml still referenced staig_fusion_e2e, causing ImportError during calls. Also found 6 dimension/architecture inconsistencies: MLP encoder is not self-supervised (random initialization without training), attention fusion uses 256 dimensions instead of 64, adln_attention uses 256 dimensions instead of 64, llava_mlp uses 512 dimensions (256×2串联) instead of 64, minimum value of element_wise_sum (256,D1,D2) is not maximum (D1,D2), GCN uses 50 dimensions instead of 64. Users chose the “remove all references” strategy but refused to execute it. ✅ Fixes query visualization coordinate alignment issues in MIHD patches — Resolved 3 serious errors in spatial transcriptomics visualization: (1) path inconsistency between cache creation (Dataset/DLPFC/) and visualization loading; (2) missing barcode alignment in scoring assignment (position-based matching breaks when adata is reordered); (3) marker coordinates come from cache instead of adata.obsm[‘spatial’]. Used barcode-based alignment method, converting via bc_to_cache_idx dictionary. ✅ Diagnosed Robobrain Pi training loss calculation issues — Studied loss oscillation process, found 56% of MSE loss reduced due to zero-filling dimensions: 14-dimensional real actions filled to 32 dimensions for model compatibility, but loss calculation is based on all 32 dimensions (18/32=56% loss due to simple zero-to-zero mapping). Suggested masking of actual dimensions: action_loss = mean(square(v_t[…, :14] - u_t[…, :14])). ✅ Simplified MIHD documentation: 25+ files → 4 core documents — Archived 16 files into docs/archived/, removed overview.md, merged into plans.md, updated CLAUDE.md and MEMORY.md indices. Final structure: README.md (function introduction), tutorial/THOROUGH_TUTORIAL.md (usage instructions), docs/plans.md (project roadmap), docs/RESULTS.md (experimental results). ✅ Optimized task completion classifier hyperparameters for Robobrain Pi — Evaluated task_loss_weight (0.1) and task_pos_weight (1.0), found severe class imbalance (only 20 of 200 frames are positive, ratio 9:1). Suggested keeping task_loss_weight between 0.1–0.15 to avoid over-emphasizing loss from 50-step actions, and increasing task_pos_weight to 5.0 to address imbalance via per-class weighting. ✅ Fixed npx ccusage unable to access LiteLLM pricing issue — Backward option of npx ccusage@latest set to 46 models in cache (actual 2696 models). Root cause: Node.js v24’s built-in fetch function does not use HTTPS_PROXY environment variable, downloading 1.4MB JSON file via campus proxy takes ~28 seconds, exceeding timeout. Solution: Set NODE_OPTIONS="–use-env-proxy" before running npx ccusage@latest. ✅ Fixed RoboTwin instruction sampling issue during dataset conversion — convert_robotwin_democlean_to_lerobot.py always selects the first “seen” instruction instead of random sampling. Changed line 68 from instruction_data.get(‘seen’, [’’])[0] to np.random.choice(seen_instructions) to achieve randomization per episode, consistent with reference implementation pattern. ✅ Developed GPU monitoring tool for Kubernetes containers — nvidia-smi cannot display processes in Kubernetes containers (PID namespace isolation). Developed gpumon.py, combining psutil (internal container process info: CPU/memory/duration) and nvidia-smi (GPU hardware status: memory/usage/temperature), using a rich UI visualization similar to nvitop. ✅ Improved clustering and evaluation sections in README — Replaced short section (L119-150) with 145-line “clustering and evaluation” section: evaluation flowchart, 3 clustering methods (KMeans/mclust/Leiden) and selection logic plus zero-variance fallback, spatial majority voting refinement, RM-IDEAL algorithm 5-step breakdown (WWL message passing K=3→Hamming distance→Wasserstein optimal transport→RM=1-W), cross-section evaluation workflow (Spearman ρ, P@K, SL@K metrics), command references. ✅ Fixed CALVIN calvin_agent import failure issue — install.sh ran in wrong conda environment; reinstalled calvin_models, used pip install -e . –no-deps in active univla environment to avoid PyTorch version conflicts. ✅ Fixed Openpi-moe EGL device ID conflict issue — CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=6 limited single GPU as device 0, but MUJOCO_EGL_DEVICE_ID=6 exceeded mapping range, causing RuntimeError. Added os.environ.setdefault(‘MUJOCO_EGL_DEVICE_ID’, ‘0’) in script startup in examples/libero/main.py. Implementation and Fixes- ✅ Clean up MIHD project files and create reference guides — executed in 4 steps: (1) Archive 4 dead code files + 11 outdated experiment directories + 34 timestamped summaries; (2) Clean up pipeline_config.yaml file (remove configurations containing only images); (3) Update 5 documents, marking archived content; (4) Create 6 functional guides (GENE_ENCODER/FUSION_STRATEGY/EVALUATION/PIPELINE/VISUALIZATION/FEATURE_CATALOG, totaling 48.9KB). Users immediately requested simplifying it to 4 documents. ✅ Remove the outdated staig_fusion_e2e function from MIHD — cleaned up 14 files, removed all references to staig_fusion_e2e (core code, configurations, documents), corrected 6 README errors in dimensions/descriptions (MLP random projection, GCN 50 dimensions, fusion strategy), and added GCNGeneEncoder in the init function. ❌ Reorganize MIHD output directory — a detailed plan was formulated to separate DLPFC/HD datasets, and RM-IDEAL evaluation results were integrated into the output directory/outputs/{DLPFC,HD,rm_ideal/{cross_section,single_section},figures,logs}. The plan was approved by users, but execution failed due to repeated ExitPlanMode rejects. ✅ Improve the CLAUDE.md document on Error Recovery Benchmark — after multiple attempts, 4 missing VLA targets were successfully added and identified in the Commands section: analyze-rejected, vla-server-pi0, vla-inject, vla-natural. 🔄 Resolve Chinese character rendering issues in tmux — the root cause was identified as a code page configuration problem in the Windows client (not the server/tmux). Since the terminal encoding is not UTF-8, Chinese characters appear as underscores. The solution requires changing settings in the Windows system or using chcp 65001 before SSH connection. Issues and Solutions Key Issues 1. Physical force injection of Error Recovery Benchmark v4 cannot generate a time context compatible with VLA — because the initial state of the injection lacks the behavioral history required by the VLA model. Solution: A v5.0 architecture was designed, using an offline two-stage process: Stage 0 collects clean trajectories (human data + 10×VLA strategy success data) → Stage 1离线 scans for opportunity points per frame → Stage 2 quota scheduler (100 points per task × category) → Stage 3 context replay (replay N-1 frames to build a VLA context window, inject an error at frame N, allowing VLA to freely infer from N onward). Switch from force-based injection to a behavioral error skill module (EEF motion/gripper control), with each error type processed independently for detection/insertion/verification. Key Insight: The VLA model is dependent on time context — initialization using error states alone is insufficient. Errors must “naturally” emerge from correct trajectories. Offline scanning + quota method effectively balances datasets while maintaining temporal realism.
2. Coordinate misalignment in MIHD spatial transcriptomics patch query visualization — the query patch does not match the expected spatial location. Solution: Three root causes were identified: (1) Data loading mismatch between datasets/DLPFC/paths and top-level paths; (2) Position-based allocation lacks barcode mapping (the cache order after scanpy operation does not match data loading order); (3) Using cached coordinates instead of data.obsm[‘spatial’] for marker overlay. These issues are resolved by using consistent paths and a bc_to_cache_idx dictionary for clear barcode alignment, along with coordinate lookup based on barcodes.
Key Insight: The spatial transcriptomics workflow requires clear barcode alignment at each node (cache → load → render) — implicit position matching fails when data is reloaded from different sources or reordered by scanpy. Never assume index preservation between file I/O boundaries.
3. Significant fluctuations in Robobrain Pi training loss — suspected to be a dimension processing issue in action prediction. Solution: Deep analysis revealed that the 14-dimensional real actions (right arm 6DOF + gripper + left arm 6DOF + gripper) were padded to 32 dimensions for model architecture compatibility, but MSE loss was calculated across all 32 dimensions. This means 56% of the loss (18/32) comes from zero-padded dimensions, and the model learns trivial noise-to-zero mappings in these dimensions, severely diluting gradient signals. Recommendation: action_loss = mean(square(v_t[…, :14] - u_t[…, :14]))
Key Insight: Zero-padding for architecture compatibility heavily dilutes gradient signals during loss calculation — always map loss to actual dimensions. In this case, 56% of the gradient signal is wasted learning trivial mappings. This is a subtle but critical error affecting training efficiency.
4. The STAIGTrainerE2E.py file was deleted, but still referenced in Fusion.py and pipeline_config.yaml, causing an ImportError when calling staig_fusion_e2e strategy in MIHD pipeline. Solution: Users chose the strategy of “cleaning up all references”. staig_fusion_e2e was removed from Fusion.py, pipeline_config.yaml, data_preparer.py, pipeline run program, STAIGutils, MEMORY.md, and 8 other files. Six README errors in dimensions/descriptions found during audit were also fixed.
Key Insight: Isolated references are a major error in production. A systematic grep audit is necessary before deleting files. Automated import testing could detect these errors earlier. A parallel exploration proxy-based code-document consistency audit successfully identified 1 serious error and 6 moderate differences.
5. RoboTwin dataset conversion always uses the first instruction in JSON, reducing training diversity of language-conditioning strategies. Solution: Replace instruction_data.get(‘seen’, [’’])[0] with np.random.choice(seen_instructions) so each set randomly selects an instruction, consistent with the reference implementation convert_aloha_data_to_lerobot_robotwin.py.
Key Insight: Dataset conversion should be enhanced at the source level — random selection of instructions per set increases training diversity without multiple dataset versions, directly affecting the model’s generalization to instruction interpretations. This is a simple change but has a major impact on training performance.
6. The Robobrain Pi task completion binary classifier may learn trivial “always predict 0” solutions, even though task_loss_weight is 0.1. Solution: Root cause: severe class imbalance (only about 200 frames at the last frame are positive, ratio 9:1) plus task_pos_weight=1.0 (no balancing). Solution requires independently adjusting two hyperparameters: keep task_loss_weight=0.1–0.15 (to prevent auxiliary task overwhelming 50-step action prediction) but increase task_pos_weight to 5.0 (by giving sufficient gradient signals to the positive class per category).
Key Insight: For unbalanced auxiliary classification, class weighting is more effective than overall loss scaling when the task should not dominate the main goal. loss_weight and pos_weight serve different purposes: loss_weight balances task importance, pos_weight balances category contributions within the task. They must be adjusted independently.
7. The Node.js ccusage tool cannot obtain the latest model price information from LiteLLM (1.4MB JSON), instead falling back to 46 cached models rather than 2696 models. Solution: Hierarchical testing identified the issue: (1) Downloading 1.4MB data via the campus proxy takes 28 seconds; (2) Node.js’ get function shows “getaddrinfo EBUSY” hostname resolution failure; (3) It was found that Node.js v24’s built-in get function (undici) does not follow HTTPS_PROXY environment variable by default. Solution: NODE_OPTIONS="–use-env-proxy" npx ccusage@latest
Key Insight: Node.js v24’s get function is fundamentally different from traditional HTTP clients (curl/axios/requests) — it ignores environment proxy variables by default. This is a compatibility trap; the –use-env-proxy flag or a global proxy library must be used explicitly. This is crucial for limited network environments.
8. MIHD documents are too long: 6 detailed reference guides (48.9KB) were created, while users prefer a simple document structure. Solution: Users immediately requested simplifying the document structure after completing 6 guides. A new plan was developed to reintegrate guides into READMEs (including all functions), tutorials (how to use them), plans (past/present/future), and results (all experiments). This has not been implemented yet.
Key Insight: AI defaults to a “comprehensive classification” approach rather than a “minimization-oriented” document structure. Research code changes quickly — detailed guides become outdated fast. A concise integrated document with rich comments is better. The user’s preference granularity should be confirmed before creating a detailed structure. The user’s first instruction (from 25+ to 4) should always serve as a constraint.
9. Kubernetes container nvidia-smi shows all GPU processes as [not found], even though GPUs are actively used** Solution: Root cause: PID namespace isolation. nvidia-smi returns host PID (e.g., 3076643) when querying kernel drivers, but containers have different numeric PID namespace numbers (e.g., 990465). Solution: The gpumon.py tool was developed, combining psutil (reading /proc files inside containers for process information: CPU/memory/command line/time elapsed) and nvidia-smi (GPU hardware status: memory/usage/temperature) for rich visualization via a user-friendly interface. Key Insight: Container namespace isolation breaks the mapping between process IDs across namespaces. The tool must collect information from each namespace and summarize it. This is why standard monitoring tools fail in containerized environments — they assume PID spaces are unified.
10. Openpi-moe serve_policy.py errors, indicating “MUJOCO_EGL_DEVICE_ID must be between 0 and 0, but actually gets 6”. Solution: CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=6 limits the process to using only GPU 0 as device 0, but EGL renderer tries to use the original hardware index 6. Add os.environ.setdefault(‘MUJOCO_EGL_DEVICE_ID’, ‘0’) at script startup to align with CUDA’s remapping.
Key Insight: CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES remaps GPU indices to the range 0–N for isolated processes; dependent libraries (e.g., MuJoCo EGL, rendering context) must use the remapped index instead of the original hardware ID. This is a subtle but important interaction between CUDA device isolation and rendering frameworks. When using CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES and a single GPU, always set the rendering device ID to 0.
11. Although install.sh completes successfully, the CALVIN calvin_agent module still cannot be found. Solution: It was found that pip installation occurred in a different conda environment from the current univla environment. Editable installs create an .egg-info directory, but package availability is limited to the Python environment where the install was executed. Reinstall in the correct environment using pip install -e . –no-deps to avoid overriding PyTorch.
Key Insight: Editable pip installations are environment-dependent — there may be issues, but if installed elsewhere, imports will fail. Before investigating missing modules, verify that ‘which python’ matches the expected environment. The –no-deps flag allows installing package structures without affecting existing dependencies.
General Issues 12. In tmux sessions, Chinese characters appear as underscores, but other users on the same server can see correct charactersSolution: Track the issue throughout the entire chain: the server region setting is correct (C.UTF-8), tmux is configured as UTF-8, but the Windows client terminal does not transmit UTF-8 encoding via SSH. The root cause lies on the client side: Windows PowerShell SSH does not correctly negotiate UTF-8 encoding. Solution: Enable “Beta: Use Unicode UTF-8” in Windows region settings, or run chcp 65001 before the SSH connection. Key Insight: Terminal encoding issues propagate across multiple layers (client terminal → SSH protocol → tmux → shell). When one user encounters problems while others on the same server do not, the client configuration should be investigated first. By comparing observations (“others can use it normally”), the problem scope can be narrowed immediately, from the server to the client.
Human and Artificial Intelligence Approaches Strategic Level Decision Pace for Redesigning the Error Recovery Architecture Role Approach Human Users have a clear vision (11 types of errors × D0/D1/D2, offline scanning + quota, error skill modules), but their thoughts are still developing. They repeatedly express “new ideas” and reject or confirm AI issues. Needs exploratory flexibility without premature commitments. Artificial Intelligence AI attempts to converge quickly through AskUserQuestion and ExitPlanMode, trying to decide between “injection + natural” and “only 7 high- feasibility types”. Seeks transition from planning phase to execution phase. Difference Analysis: Users need exploratory flexibility when their thoughts are mature, not forced decisions before thinking is complete. AI seeks quick convergence to an executable plan. The user repeatedly rejected 3–4 calls to AskUserQuestion/ExitPlanMode, indicating premature implementation by AI. This suggests AI should wait until users have a clear vision before making commitments.
Visual Debugging of MIHD Patch Queries Role Approach Human Users report “sometimes the patch query does not match the current patch” — empirical observations from visual inspection and interaction tests. Artificial Intelligence AI systematically tracks data flow (cache creation path and visual loading path, barcode sorting assumption, coordinate system) and identifies 3 different architectural errors. Difference Analysis: Humans detect issues through visual quality assurance; AI performs architectural debugging to find root causes. Human insight is necessary, but AI’s systematic tracking identified all failure points at the file I/O boundary. Even in automated processes, visual quality inspection is valuable.
Concept of Documenting the Research Codebase Role Approach Human Structure oriented toward minimal use: 4 files answer “what functions exist” (README), “how to use” (tutorial), “what is the plan” (plan), “what is the result” (RESULTS). After AI created 6 guides, users explicitly said “I only need four”. Emphasis on integration over separation, action-oriented rather than completeness. Artificial Intelligence Comprehensive classification method: 6 specialized guides created (GENE_ENCODER_GUIDE, FUSION_STRATEGY_GUIDE, EVALUATION_GUIDE, etc.), functions organized by type, with detailed API references, parameters, and performance tables. Prioritizes logical classification and completeness. Difference Analysis: Humans prioritize minimal cognitive burden and action-oriented documents (“I need to use X, where can I find it?”). AI prioritizes completeness and logical structure (“all encoder information is in one place”). Human iterative rejections indicate that the research code needs easy-to-maintain documentation, not an outdated comprehensive manual. A rapidly changing codebase prefers integration over classification.
Diagnosis of Correctness of Robobrain Pi Loss Calculation Role Approach Human Users noticed loss oscillations, suspected dimension mismatch, and specifically requested verification after 14-dimensional actions to confirm loss calculation. Problem inferred from training behavior patterns. Artificial Intelligence AI tracked the entire data flow (RealInputs filled to 14→32→DeltaActions masked only[:14]→normalization→loss across all 32 dimensions), quantified the exact gradient dilution ratio (from filled 56%), and identified the architectural root cause (loss not masked to real dimension). Difference Analysis: Humans identify abnormal patterns through empirical observation; AI performs systematic architectural analysis to quantify the root cause. Complementarily: human intuition triggers investigation, while AI provides mathematical precision. Humans correctly identified the dimension structure issue before analysis; AI needs hints to reconsider tensor shape and adjusted the suggestion for task_loss_weight from 0.5 to 0.1–0.15.
**Role Approach Human Noticed other users can correctly identify Chinese on the same server, and input characters appear correctly in other terminals — immediately narrowed the problem to the client side based on behavior comparison. Artificial Intelligence Initially focused on server-side localization checks (LANG, LC_ALL, tmux settings, shell environment) until human observation guided it elsewhere. Difference Analysis: Human comparative observation (“works for others, doesn’t work for me”) quickly narrowed the problem from server configuration to client settings. AI followed a comprehensive server-side diagnostic process before a key turning point. This shows the value of asking “Does this work for others?” at the initial troubleshooting stage — shared components can be ruled out through differential diagnosis.
Repair Strategy for Missing STAIGTrainerE2E.py Role Approach Human Unanimously selected the “clean all references” option — preferring to remove all broken functions rather than restoring them via code archaeology. Artificial Intelligence Provided two balanced options: (1) restore the file from git to maintain end-to-end functionality; (2) clean all references. AI recommended option 1 to preserve function integrity. Difference Analysis: Humans treat missing files as signals requiring removal (“more severe deletion”). AI treats them as recoverable vulnerabilities (“restore to keep functionality”). Human decisions indicate staig_fusion_e2e was deliberately abandoned rather than accidentally deleted. This shows different risk tolerances: humans are willing to lose some functions for simplicity, while AI tends to retain functions.
Recognition of RoboTwin Instruction Sampling Patterns Role Approach Human Found a reference implementation in convert_aloha_data_to_lerobot_robotwin.py and identified the need to copy np.random.choice pattern — learning from the existing codebase. Artificial Intelligence Found two files, compared implementations, and mechanically converted code according to the human-provided pattern. Difference Analysis: Humans provide domain knowledge (where to find references and what it represents) ; AI performs file location and pattern matching. This shows the importance of learning from existing code patterns rather than inventing new methods — consistency in the codebase is crucial.
Iterative Optimization and Early Standards Role Approach Human Provided high-level requirements (“25+ documents → 4 core documents”) and let AI execute them. Adjusted when results (6 guides) did not meet expectations using iterative rejection-based optimization. Artificial Intelligence Interpreted “4 core documents” as “integrating 12 existing guides” — created an intermediate 6-guide structure, then planned to merge the 4 documents. A multi-step approach considers more structure as more reliable. Difference Analysis: Humans have a clear final goal, but few specifications are provided, expecting AI to achieve it through feedback loops. AI added intermediate steps for safety but increased iterations. Human frustration (“too many documents”) indicates they prefer a direct path over gradual integration.
Limitations of Artificial Intelligence Key Limitations Unable to accurately identify user rejection signals: During error recovery redesign, users rejected AskUserQuestion/ExitPlanMode 3–4 times in a row, yet AI continued to ask similar questions (“How do you want to handle it?”, “Please describe your new idea”) without realizing the need to stop asking and wait for user self-expression. Over-designed documentation: Despite clear instructions to integrate 25+ files into 4 core documents, 6 detailed reference guides (48.9KB) were still created. Original constraints were not maintained in multi-session workflows. Context loss across sessions: Session 4 created 6 guides after archiving 16 files from Session 1 — contradiction should have been noticed. Overuse of AskUserQuestion tool during exploration phase: Attempting to force users to make binary decisions (“7 high- feasibility types” vs “only 7 high- feasibility types”) when users’ thoughts are still developing. This limits user thinking space rather than providing information and waiting for autonomous decision. Lack of confirmation before large-scale execution: Before the fourth step of project cleanup, no question asked “Should I create 6 separate guides or merge everything into 4 files?” Users immediately rejected the result, wasting implementation effort. Multiple misjudgments regarding improvements to CLAUDE.md: Users ran/init, AI thought “already comprehensive, no changes needed”, and tried ExitPlanMode twice before user rejection. Only on the third attempt were 4 missing targets found. This indicates overly conservative evaluation of “good enough”. Multiple pauses in plan mode execution when user rejects ExitPlanMode calls: The agent did not ask user to manually exit or find an alternative workflow to adjust, instead continuing the same blocking tool call. Initial task loss weight suggestion (0.5) ignored the action_loss dimension structure (batch × 50 tensors), until human hint prompted reconsideration — more careful analysis of tensor shape should have been done before suggesting a recommendation. General Limitations Inadequate integration of parallel agent results: Error recovery exploration started 3 parallel agents (framework, configuration, full codebase), each returning 2000–3000 tags, but AI failed to effectively synthesize them into concise actions — instead pasting a large amount of exploration data. Technical limitations: 403 “request not allowed” API error occurs at session start requiring login; ripgrep timeouts (20-second limit) on large directories; file modification conflicts during editing due to external linter/formatters. Lessons Learned Key Experience – VLA model requires redesigning benchmark tests for time context dependence: Cannot simply initialize episodes with error states — VLA needs behavioral history to make appropriate recovery decisions. Solution: replay the first N-1 frames to build a context window, introduce error at frame N, then let VLA infer freely from frame N onward. This transforms the way error is introduced from “initial state perturbation” to “trajectory interruption”, matching how errors occur in real-world scenarios.- Offline scanning and quota scheduling architecture for balancing error datasets: Stage 0 collects clean trajectories (human data and 10 times more running data than VLA strategy success) → Stage 1 performs offline scanning per frame → Stage 2 assigns quotas (100 quotas per task × error category) → Stage 3 performs context replay. This approach is more efficient than online generation, ensures dataset balance, and allows reuse of expensive clean trajectory data in multiple error injection experiments. Deformed dimension classification for error classification: D0 (only position), D1 (only rotation), D2 (position + rotation) systematically describes the spatial deformation of all error types. This classification method is more systematic than stage-based classification (such as arrival/grasping/raise/transport/placement), and by decomposing the 6 degrees of freedom changes into orthogonal components, the verification logic becomes clearer. Architecture compatibility issues caused by zero padding: Padding (from 14 dimensions to 32 dimensions) for model compatibility may severely dilute gradient signals (wasting 56% of the signal). Therefore, only meaningful dimensions should be retained for loss calculation. In multi-dimensional outputs, this is subtle but crucial—if included in the calculation, although the model can converge, the learning performance will be poor because most gradient signals optimize trivial zero-to-zero mappings. Independent hyperparameter tuning for unbalanced auxiliary tasks: loss_weight is used to balance task importance, while pos_weight balances category contributions within the task, and these two parameters need separate tuning. For severely unbalanced auxiliary classification tasks, keep loss_weight low (0.1–0.15) to avoid excessive impact on the main goal; simultaneously increase pos_weight (e.g., 5.0) to address category imbalance. Overall scalability and class weight allocation are independent control factors. Alignment requirements based on spatial transcriptome barcodes: A clear barcode mapping is required at each process node (cache → load → render). When data is reloaded from different sources or reordered via scanpy operations, position-based matching fails. Never assume that the indices between file I/O boundaries remain unchanged. Solution: maintain a bc_to_cache_idx dictionary throughout the process and use barcodes for coordinate assignment. In-depth understanding of MIHD architecture: Three-stage process (encoder → fusion → clustering/ evaluation), 5 gene encoders (PCA 50d, MLP 128d random initialization, scGPT 512d, GCN 50d, none), 4 visual encoders (ResNet50, HIPT, UNI, UNI2), 10 fusion strategies (series/mean/element sum + attention variants + STAIG/QFormer). Divided into two stages: Stage 1 extraction (cache to embedding cache), Stage 2 evaluation (load + fusion + clustering + metrics). Conversion and enhancement of datasets at the source level: Random sampling instructions per set (selected from available interpretations) increase training diversity without needing multiple dataset versions. This simple change has a significant impact on the generalization ability of language conditional strategies. This indicates that matching patterns with reference implementations in the same code base is very important. Remapping of CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES GPU indices: Limit indices to the range 0–N so that processing occurs within the CUDA context. Dependent libraries (such as MuJoCo EGL, rendering frameworks) must use the remapped indices instead of the original hardware ID. When using single-GPU isolation, always set the rendering device ID to 0. This is subtle but critical for multi-GPU setups because different jobs run on different isolated devices. Applicability of injection vs. natural capture: Physically-based injection methods (pulse/friction/pose perturbation) can reliably generate 7 types of errors (falling, collision, positioning, partial stagnation). GRASP_FAILURE/sequence/trajectory/regression errors require temporal behavior of the strategy—only natural capture can produce these errors. Therefore, a hybrid approach is needed to fully cover error types. RM-IDEAL spatial niche matching algorithm: (1) Build a spatial adjacency graph (k-NN, n_neighbors=6), (2) WWL message passing (K=3 iterations to aggregate neighbor labels), (3) Compute Hamming distance cost matrix, (4) Wasserstein optimal transmission, (5) RM = 1 - W ∈ [0,1]. Cross- evaluation: bidirectional query, compare RM-IDEAL scores with embedding cosine similarity, evaluated via Spearman ρ, P@K, SL@K metrics. Kubernetes PID namespace isolation causes monitoring issues: nvidia-smi queries kernel drivers return host PID, but containers have independent PID namespaces. Solution: collect information within each namespace and then aggregate. For GPU monitoring, use psutil inside the container to get process information (/proc parsing), use nvidia-smi to get hardware status, and visualize via a rich user interface. General principle: namespace isolation requires local namespace data collection. Documentation philosophy of research code base: Users prefer a “minimum usage-oriented” structure (what/how/plan/result) rather than “comprehensive classification” guides (detailed feature descriptions). The reason is that research code changes rapidly, and detailed guides become outdated quickly. Instead of a thick reference manual, there should be concise integration documents and well-commented code. AI should default to the minimum documentation and confirm before creating a comprehensive structure. Code and documentation consistency audit workflow: (1) Start parallel exploration agents for each module, (2) Compare statements in README with actual code (class name, dimension, parameters, training process), (3) Classify differences (serious error/medium error/minor omission), (4) Let users choose a repair strategy (update documentation or fix code). In MIHD project, 1 serious ImportError and 6 dimension mismatches were found. AI behavior during exploration stage: When user thinking is still developing (repeatedly saying “new ideas”), avoid forcing decisions through AskUserQuestion. Provide information, analyze trade-offs, and wait for autonomous decision-making. Continuous rejection of ExitPlanMode/AskUserQuestion calls is a clear “pause” signal. Users need to explore the space rather than deciding the implementation path too early. CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES GPU index remapping issue in Node.js v24: The built-in fetch function does not follow HTTPS_PROXY/HTTP_PROXY environment variables, unlike curl/axios/requests. Use NODE_OPTIONS="–use-env-proxy" or a global proxy library to resolve this. This is very important for restricted network environments. It represents a behavior change compared to traditional HTTP clients. Editable pip installation environment range: Availability of packages depends on the Python environment where the installation command is executed. Although artifacts (.egg-info) may exist, if installed elsewhere, imports will fail. Always verify that “which python” matches the expected environment. Use –no-deps to install package structures without overwriting existing dependencies (very important for avoiding PyTorch version conflicts). MIHD clustering method: KMeans (default option, fast), mclust (implemented via rpy2 R GMM, suitable for STAIG, with zero-variance fallback → KMeans), Leiden (automatically clusters HD data without benchmark data). Only used for STAIG fusion, spatial refinement via k-NN majority vote (refine_labels_spatial_majority). Selection logic based on fusion strategy and data characteristics. Terminal encoding troubleshooting: Issues propagate across multiple layers (client terminal → SSH protocol → tmux → shell). When a user has problems while others on the same server do not, first investigate client issues. By comparing observations (“other users can use it”) we can immediately narrow down from shared components to user-specific configuration issues. For Windows system: check code page (chcp 65001) or enable “Beta: use Unicode UTF-8” in regional settings. MIHD (multimodal integration for high-resolution spatial omics) • Comprehensive restructuring and cleanup of documentation 2026-03-10 | claude_code Five-stage improvement: (1) Archived 16 files into 4 core documents (README/tutorial/plans/RESULTS). (2) Enhanced README with 145 lines of clustering and RM-IDEAL evaluation sections (WWL message passing, Wasserstein transmission, cross-sectional metrics). (3) Audited code and documentation consistency via 3 parallel agents—found 1 serious error (STAIGTrainerE2E.py missing but referenced → ImportError) + 6 dimension differences. (4) Project cleanup: archived 4 unused code files + 11 outdated directories + 34 summaries, cleaned pipeline_config.yaml file, created 6 reference guides (48.9KB)—users rejected them as too detailed. (5) Started output/reorganization work (DLPFC/HD separation), but hindered by the rejection loop of ExitPlanMode. Additionally: removed staig_fusion_e2e function from 14 files, fixed 3 serious patch query visualization errors (barcode alignment, coordinate system mismatch). Overall: number of documents reduced from over 25 to 4, eliminated serious ImportError risks, improved spatial visualization accuracy, but revealed the tension between AI’s comprehensive classification method and users’ minimal usage philosophy. RoboBrain Pi (two-handed VLA training) ✅ Debugging and optimization of training loss calculation 2026-03-10 | claude_code Three-part optimization: (1) Diagnosed loss oscillation problem—found 56% of MSE loss reduced due to zero-padding in action dimensions (14-dimensional real actions padded to 32 dimensions to match model, but loss calculated for all 32 dimensions). Suggested masking of real dimensions. (2) Hyperparameter evaluation for task completion classifier—found serious category imbalance (9:1 ratio of negative examples to positive examples in the last 20 frames of 200 frames sequence), impossible to balance when task_pos_weight=1.0. Suggested setting task_loss_weight to 0.1–0.15 (to avoid over-emphasizing 50-step action loss) + task_pos_weight=5.0 (to address imbalance). (3) Environment troubleshooting: reinstalled uv package manager, set WANDB offline mode, handled multi-user WANDB account conflicts via WANDB_API_KEY environment variable, debugged Chinese terminal rendering issues (client UTF-8 encoding problem). Also verified mathematical correctness of task completion implementation (CLS token + MLP head, allowing partial matching to handle parameter mismatches). Impact: identified two serious training efficiency problems (gradient dilution + category imbalance), provided specific hyperparameter suggestions, resolved development environment availability issues. Error recovery benchmark testing 🔍 Redesign and planning of v5.0 architecture 2026-03-10 | claude_code Major architectural adjustments across multiple stages: (1) Initially attempted improvement to CLAUDE.md file (rejected multiple times before adding 4 missing targets). (2) Users proposed a redesigned vision: switch from online physical force injection to offline two-stage process (collect clean trajectories → scan opportunities → quota injection → context replay). Defined 11 error types × 3 deformation dimensions (D0/D1/D2) = 26 seed types. (3) Started 3 parallel exploration agents to analyze v4 code base—found 60% reusable components (EnvWrapper, StateExtractor), while full rewrite was necessary (detector/injector/verifier → error skill module). (4) Provided detailed analysis of 24 generation feasibility options: 7 high, 6 medium, 7 low via natural capture. Users repeatedly said they had “new ideas,” but rejected AI’s AskUserQuestion attempts to force decisions. Planning is still in exploration stage—users need flexibility, and the vision is becoming clearer. Key insight: VLA’s temporal context dependency requires errors to “generate from correct trajectories” rather than as initial state perturbations. Offline scanning + quota architecture is more efficient and better balances datasets. Infrastructure tools ✅ GPU monitoring and Node.js tools 2026-03-10 | claude_code Two infrastructure improvements: (1) Developed gpumon.py file for Kubernetes containers—due to PID namespace isolation, nvidia-smi shows [unfound] related processes (host PID 3076643 ≠ container PID 990465). Solution combines psutil (container internal process information: CPU/memory/running time) and nvidia-smi (GPU hardware status: memory/usage/temperature) with rich TUI visualization. Users interrupted during layout optimization. (2) Fixed npx ccusage issue that couldn’t obtain LiteLLM model pricing (alternate solution: 46 → 2696 models). Root cause: Node.js v24’s fetch function does not follow HTTPS_PROXY by default, 1.4MB JSON file takes 28 seconds via campus proxy, causing timeout. Solution: NODE_OPTIONS="–use-env-proxy".Impact: Filled a critical monitoring gap in containerized environments, restoring the token pricing feature in restricted networks.- Robot learning environments (CALVIN, Openpi-moe, RoboTwin) ✅ Multi-project environment setup and debugging 2026-03-10 | claude_code Systematic debugging was carried out on three projects: (1) CALVIN: The issue of failed import of calvin_agent was resolved—install.sh was running in the wrong conda environment, and during reinstallation, pip install -e . –no-deps was used in the univla environment. (2) Openpi-moe: The problem of serve_policy.py crashing was identified—CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=6 mapped the GPU to index 0, but MUJOCO_EGL_DEVICE_ID=6 exceeded the mapping range. This issue was resolved by setting EGL device to 0 at the script startup. (3) RoboTwin: The data set conversion method was modified to use random sampling instructions (np.random.choice) instead of always using the first instruction, to match the reference implementation pattern and increase training diversity. Additionally: issues with terminal UTF-8 encoding (Windows client code page problem) and the location query for the Claude Code API configuration file were resolved. Impact: Three critical research processes were unblocked, allowing robot learning experiments to continue. All issues were attributed to subtle environment/configuration mismatches, requiring careful layer-by-layer diagnosis.
summary: The tasks on the multi-project development day include: document cleanup, debugging of spatial transcriptomics, optimization of robot learning, and troubleshooting of environment issues across multiple code repositories. These tasks involve more than 6 code frameworks.
