Daily Report — 2026-02-23 Daily Overview Completed work: Two major research tasks were executed in parallel: (1) Optimization of MIHD spatial transcriptomics workflow and generalization of visual encoders; (2) Fixing infrastructure issues for error recovery benchmarks and restarting Phoenix model training. Execution methods: Systematic optimization methods were applied to both projects: code analysis to identify bottlenecks, targeted vectorization/batch processing to improve performance, architectural refactoring to increase flexibility, comprehensive ablation studies, and a reliable error handling mechanism for long-running batch processes. Impact: In MIHD: major training bottlenecks were eliminated (initialization speed increased 100–500 times, QFormer accelerated 20–50 times), architectural flexibility was unlocked for modern visual encoders, and empirical evidence was provided for fusion method selection criteria. For error recovery: the entire M14 evaluation workflow returned to normal (649 scenarios × 4 strategies), Pi0.5 training increased from 3K steps to 100K steps with stable monitoring, and the reliability of M13 classification was quantified. DCC Completed work: Four MIHD tasks: (1) Optimization of CPU bottlenecks in fusion training; (2) Generalization of STAIG encoders; (3) Ablation experiments for visual refinement; (4) Deployment of large-scale STAIG across all DLPFC regions and compatibility fixes. Execution methods: Vectorization of NumPy/scipy in edge weight computation, transfer of dropout operations to GPU, addition of batch processing capabilities to QFormer; refactoring of workflow orchestration using encoder family detection; comprehensive experiments comparing the effects of 8 fusion methods and scan_cluster refinement with baseline methods; resolution of UNI2 patch size incompatibility and NaN handling edge cases. Impact: Training bottlenecks were eliminated (QFormer training time reduced from 3.5 hours to 5% GPU utilization), STAIG can support any visual encoder, refinement benefits weak fusion methods (+0.05–0.09 ARI) but harms strong fusion methods (-0.05 ARI), and complete STAIG evaluations were completed in 10/11 regions (average ARI = 0.546). tianhe Completed work: Six critical errors were fixed, 7 parallel GPU processes were initiated (m14_cpu/pi0/pi05 evaluation + Pi0.5 training), and M13 analysis was completed (kappa = -0.02, discrimination report). Execution methods: Iterative repair validation cycles were performed on collector.py (error handling), train_pi05.sh (monitoring), evaluate_mimicgen.py (seed generation), and discrimination scripts (type conversion). Slurm jobs 45628 (an49, 4 evaluations) and 46553 (an46, training) were used. Impact: M14 evaluation can now handle fingerprint mismatches (130 natural scenarios), training results can be observed in real time (no buffered logs), Pi0.5 training stabilizes at 2.0 seconds/step, and it is progressing toward 100K steps; the reliability of M13 classification was also quantified (low kappa value, requiring VLA data). Through vectorization and GPU batch processing, the MIHD fusion workflow was systematically optimized, with speed increased 100–500 times, STAIG extended to support any visual encoder, comprehensive visual refinement experiments were conducted on 11 slices, the error recovery benchmark evaluation crash issue was fixed, and Pi0.5 Phoenix training was restarted, along with improved monitoring mechanisms.
Tasks Architecture and Strategy ✅ Batch QFormer forward pass — The forward_batched() method was implemented, supporting pre-built padding neighbor tensors and key_padding_mask to replace sequential point connections. ✅ Fixing fingerprint mismatch crash in evaluation workflow — collector.py was modified, scene-level try-except blocks were added around _run_episode(), allowing the evaluation to skip 130 incompatible natural capture scenarios instead of crashing at scenario 122. ✅ Vectorization of STAIG edge weight computation — In STAIGTrainer.py and STAIGTrainerE2E.py, O(n²) Python nested loops were replaced with scipy.cdist and NumPy vectorization to compute edge weights during initialization. ✅ Ablation experiments for visual refinement — On 151673 slices, the effects of 8 fusion methods (series, mean, element-wise sum, attention, basic contrast, adln_attention, llava_mlp, qformer) were compared, including scenarios with and without scan_cluster refinement. 🔄 Restarting Pi0.5 LoRA training and adding monitoring — train_pi05.sh was updated with PYTHONUNBUFFERED, stdbuf, error capture, and GPU monitoring; job 46553 was submitted, restarting from step 3000 with a step length of 2.0 seconds/step and a loss of 0.068. ✅ Fixing errors in evaluation scripts (environment seeds, state validation, quaternions) — env.seed() was added in evaluate_mimicgen.py to ensure reproducibility, state dimension verification (8D check) was performed, and quaternions were safely converted using np.clip instead of in-place mutation. 🔄 Restarting m14 evaluation on GPU (cpu/pi0/pi05) — 3 evaluation processes (job 45628) were restarted on an49 using –resume: m14_cpu on 1547 episodes, m14_pi0 on 400 episodes, m14_pi05 on 407 episodes, all proceeding smoothly under new error handling. ✅ Extending STAIG fusion to any visual encoder — Hardcoded UNI encoder requirements were removed from the workflow orchestration layer, STAIG_UNI_FAMILY was introduced, and staig_strict preprocessing was applied only when appropriate. ✅ Completing M13 classifier reliability analysis — 7_classifier_reliability.py was run, producing kappa_matrix.csv and reliability_report.md; Fleiss’ kappa value was -0.02 (poor), 2 non-redundancy violations were found (drop↔grasp_slip kappa = 0.71). ✅ Completing M13 error type discrimination analysis — errors related to int(‘False’) and degradation of scipy.stats.kruskal were fixed, discriminability_report.md was generated showing all SR=0 cases, and Kruskal-Wallis test was not significant. ✅ Generating m14_cpu baseline analysis report — 4_analyze_results.py was run on 726 episodes, producing report.md and summary.json; Random SR=0% RP=2.3%, BC-RNN SR=0% RP=0.6%, Bootstrap 95% CI, and Fisher’s exact test were reported. Implementation and Fixes ✅ Deploying STAIG fusion across all DLPFC regions — STAIG fusion was applied across all 11 slices, pca and non-genetic encoders were used simultaneously, and UNI2 patch size incompatibility and NaN handling issues were fixed. ✅ Moving adaptive dropoutAdj to GPU — By directly generating random numbers on edge_attr devices, data transfer between GPU↔CPU was avoided, eliminating the data transfer between GPU↔CPU. ✅ Updating project documentation to v4.11.1 and v4.12 — The project panorama summary.md was updated, the number of scenarios increased from 454 to 649, training status (job 46553) and milestone progress (M13 analysis completed, M14 in progress) were updated, and version history was added. Issues and Solutions Key Issues 1. QFormer training is very slow (about 3.5 hours), using only 5% GPU utilization, because the Python loop processes 2700 points sequentially. Solution: Batch forward pass was implemented: padding neighbor index tensors were precomputed at the start of training, batch context was built using index_select, key_padding_mask was added in the transformer, and all points were processed in a single GPU parallel forward call. Key insight: During the Python loop, GPU utilization is extremely low—even though the batch semantics refer to “spatial position” rather than “samples,” batch processing is essential for Transformer models.
2. All 3 GPU evaluation nodes (m14_cpu/pi0/pi05) crashed at scenario 122/649 because the xml hash fingerprints of 130 natural capture scenarios were inconsistent, causing EnvironmentMismatchError. Solution: The EnvironmentMismatchError import statement was added to collector.py, and scene-level try-except wrappers were added around _run_episode() to log warnings and skip incompatible scenarios instead of terminating the program.
Key insight: The database contains two sets of fingerprint data (519 pulses/enhancement scenarios and 130 natural VLA generation scenarios); robust error handling at iteration boundaries prevents cascading failures, while –resume preserves completed work.
3. STAIG edge weight computation uses O(n²) nested Python loops, which takes 2–5 seconds for 2700 points, blocking the training process. Solution: scipy.spatial.distance.cdist was used for distance matrix calculation, scipy.special.softmax(axis=1) was applied for row normalization, and NumPy’s advanced indexing function was used to access edge probabilities instead of list comprehensions.
Key insight: Nested loops containing mathematical operations should always be vectorized—using basic functions from scipy/NumPy can achieve 100–500 times acceleration; the key is identifying the O(n²) pattern and finding appropriate library functions to handle paired distances.
4. It is currently unclear whether visual embedding improvements (scan_cluster: 1536d→256d) help improve multimodal fusion performance. Solution: Systematic ablation experiments were conducted: all 8 fusion methods were run with and without the improvement on section 151673, showing that the improvement helps weaker methods (average improvement 0.056, attention mechanism improvement 0.086 ARI), but harms stronger methods (qformer decreases by 0.054, concat decreases by 0.074 ARI)—the dimensionality reduction process requires balancing noise reduction and information retention.
Key insight: The value of dimensionality reduction depends on the capacity of downstream models: simple aggregation methods (e.g., mean, attention mechanism) can benefit from noise removal and avoid the dimensionality crisis, while complex learnable models (e.g., qformer/llava_mlp) can leverage rich information in high-dimensional embeddings—there is no universal answer.
5. Pi0.5 training task (job 46551) abruptly exited after approximately 580 steps because stdout buffering prevented monitoring, and the exit reason was unclear (code 0). Solution: PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 + stdbuf -Ol was added for real-time log output, -eo pipefail + ERR trap was used for error reporting, health checks on the background GPU were performed every 30 minutes, and –resume was used to continue training from step 3000’s checkpoint.
Key insight: Python/JAX stdout buffering may hide training failures; no-buffer output, clear error capture, and regular health checks are essential for 50+ hour training tasks on shared clusters.
6. During STAIG fusion, the pipeline hardcodes vision_encoder=‘uni,’ limiting the possibility of trying other encoders (e.g., HIPT, ResNet50, etc.). Solution: The orchestration layer was refactored: STAIG_UNI_FAMILY was introduced to identify encoders that require staig_strict preprocessing (256×256 patches, no ImageNet normalization, frequency filtering), run_benchmark.py was updated to remove forced encoder coverage, and extract_planner and evaluation_planner were updated to conditionally apply different variants based on encoder family membership.
Key insight: Responsibility separation: The model layer (STAIGTrainer) already handles data of any size via PCA, but the orchestration layer imposes artificial constraints—good architecture makes this generality simple once determined.#### 7. evaluate_mimicgen.py lacks environment initialization, resulting in non-reproducible evaluation results across different runs.Solution: An env.seed(args.seed) call was added before each task’s episode loop to match the reference implementation in LIBERO/Phoenix main.py.
Key Insight: Reproducibility requires explicit initialization of the RNG and environment RNG; comparison with the reference implementation reveals missing initialization steps.
General Issues 8. adaptiveDropoutAdj transfers edgeAttr to the CPU, generates random numbers on the CPU, and then returns them to the GPU—this incurs synchronization overhead per cycle (about 1–2 seconds over 1100 cycles in total). Solution: Directly use torch.rand(..., device=edgeAttr.device, dtype=edgeAttr.dtype) to generate random numbers on edgeAttr_device—eliminating all CPU transfers.
Key Insight: Transfers between small GPUs and the CPU accumulate a large amount of data after repeated operations; random numbers should always be generated on the same device as the operation tensor; CUDA synchronization overhead is significant.
9. UNI2 (ViT-H/14, patch_size=14) fails on STAIG’s 256×256 input, resulting in the error “256 is not divisible by 14”. Solution: When the strict mode of STAIG is detected, automatically adjust the size in UNI2VisionEncoder.extract() to 224×224 (divisible by 14), and then pass the patch to the model.
Key Insight: The visual transformer has strict input size requirements; when adjusting based on patch size, attention should be paid to divisibility constraints; for most ViTs, 224×224 is a safe default size.
10. The discriminability script encounters a ValueError when parsing the success field in JSONL: Invalid decimal base: ‘False’. Solution: Add conversion from string to boolean: success_raw = row.get('success', False); success = success_raw if isinstance(success_raw, bool) else success_raw.lower() == 'true'.
Key Insight: Consistent issues in JSONL serialization—the success field is stored as the string ‘False’, not as a boolean value; defensive type checking can prevent parsing errors, especially when assumptions about the pattern fail.
11. m14_cpu crashes under AssertionError: MUJOCO_EGL_DEVICE_ID(0) must be in CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES(5). Solution: Change MUJOCO_EGL_DEVICE_ID from 0 to 5 to match CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=5, thereby satisfying the assertion about the device ID string in binding_utils.py.
Key Insight: binding_utils.py of Robosuite requires MUJOCO_EGL_DEVICE_ID to be a substring of CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES; when using a single GPU, both must match exactly.
12. Section 151676 causes NaN losses and zero embeddings in STAIG training, causing KMeans to fail on NaN-padded data. Solution: Add np.nan_to_num() in the KMeans fallback path; replace NaN with 0 before clustering, and replace infinity with a larger finite number.
Key Insight: Model crashes (NaN losses) are known failure modes that require graceful degradation handling; input should always be cleaned before passing it to external libraries that may not handle NaN robustly (such as sklearn); record known failure cases.
13. The discriminability script crashes under scipy.stats.kruskal ValueError, because all success rates are the same (all SR=0 cases). Solution: Wrap H, p = scipy.stats.kruskal(*groups) in a try-except ValueError block, returning H=0.0, p=1.0, significant=False, note='all values identical' in case of an exception. Key Insight: Statistical tests fail on degenerate distributions; explicit handling of edge cases and informative messages can prevent silent failures and help interpret results.
Differences in Approaches between Humans and Artificial Intelligence Strategic Level Strategic optimization planning and tactical execution Role Approach Human The user pre-analyzed the MIHD code library and provided a detailed three-part optimization plan, including specific code locations, expected performance improvements, and implementation steps—essentially writing specifications for Claude’s execution Artificial Intelligence Claude strictly follows the provided plan, implementing vectorization using scipy.cdist, random number generation based on GPU devices, and batch processing using padded tensors—focusing on execution rather than strategic planning Analysis of differences: Humans are responsible for strategic analysis and design phases (identifying bottlenecks, selecting algorithms, estimating performance improvements), while artificial intelligence acts as an exact execution agent—this is a clear delegation of implementation after humans complete complex thinking.
Debugging strategies for multi-component process failures Role Approach Human For error recovery crashes, humans provide detailed context information (649 scenarios, fingerprint groups, scenario 122 where the crash occurred), and specify exact repair locations (lines 299–325 of collector.py), using a try-except pattern Artificial Intelligence Artificial intelligence systematically follows the plan, but initially focuses too much on exploring the code structure; under human-targeted guidance, artificial intelligence directly implements repairs and validates through test runs Analysis of differences: Human domain knowledge enables precise identification of root causes (e.g., EnvironmentMismatchError; no scenario-level handling); the advantage of artificial intelligence lies in verification work (e.g., import checks, parallel restarts, progress monitoring), but a clear quick solution plan is required.
Interpretation of experimental results Role Approach Human The user requested a comprehensive comparison of visual refinement effects, but no conclusions were specified—an open analysis request Artificial Intelligence Claude conducted experiments and then summarized key insights: the value of refinement depends on the capacity of downstream models; it helps simplify methods and reduce noise/dimensions, but also has negative impacts on complex methods—not just data presentation, but also causal explanations Analysis of differences: The user requested data, and artificial intelligence provides an explanation framework—Claude identified capacity-related trade-off patterns, rather than just reporting metrics, showing deeper analytical thinking.
Generalization range of the visual encoder Role Approach Human The user simply asked “any visual encoder can be used, not just UNI”—a high-level request, but no specific implementation details were provided Artificial Intelligence Claude analyzed the system architecture and found that the model layer is already flexible, but the coordination layer imposes constraints; then introduced the concept of a “encoder family,” including conditional preprocessing variants—this architectural insight goes beyond a simple request. Analysis of differences: The user specified content (supporting any encoder), and artificial intelligence designed the approach (based on conditional preprocessing within the family)—artificial intelligence provided valuable structural insights on how to meet UNI-specific preprocessing requirements during generalization.
Training monitoring and observability requirements Role Approach Human Based on previous failure analysis, humans specified specific monitoring improvements (PYTHONUNBUFFERED, stdbuf, error catching, GPU memory logging) Artificial Intelligence Artificial intelligence implemented all specified improvements, but initially did not realize the importance of un buffered output; after seeing the note “PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 is active,” artificial intelligence understood this pattern. Analysis of differences: Humans predicted the observability requirements from past failure patterns; artificial intelligence learned this pattern through execution feedback, rather than through active design.
When to stop exploring and start execution Role Approach Human When artificial intelligence was about to start exploring sub-agents, humans interrupted the use of agent tools twice, preferring direct handling of known tasks Artificial Intelligence Artificial intelligence defaults to using agent tools for broad queries like “what was removed from blocking?” even when the task list is clearly stated in the document; it attempts parallel exploration processes. Analysis of differences: Humans recognize when there is sufficient direct execution information; artificial intelligence relies too much on thorough exploration when decision-making is more valuable.
Implementation Level When to use agents, when to use tools directly Role Approach Human The user asked Claude to decide when to start exploring using agents—no micro-management or investigation methods Artificial Intelligence Claude initiated multiple exploration agents to understand the data loading process and fusion training loop, before formulating an optimization plan—actively using agents to explore the open code library. Analysis of differences: Artificial intelligence correctly applies the pattern of using agents for discovery/research tasks and directly using tools for known operations; humans trust this judgment without intervention.
Limitations of Artificial Intelligence Key Limitations Before running geneEncoder=pca and geneEncoder=None, no active verification was done to ensure they produce the same results in STAIG fusion—computing resources were wasted on invalid experiments that provided no new information. Before designing the training restart plan, no active verification of checkpoint status was performed—the fake plan includes “checkpoint 1000,” without checking the current file system status (which is step 3000). This led humans to manually use ls commands to find the 3000 checkpoints later. It was not until humans explicitly stated it that artificial intelligence realized that stdout buffering is a critical failure mode in long-term training. The previously silent exit code 0 should have raised doubts about log reliability. General Limitations – In visual optimization experiments, the best result (0.4832) of the qformer baseline was not noticed initially—only after completing all comparisons did it become apparent; this should have been noticed earlier to adjust experiment priorities. In the implementation phase, inconsistency between the planned text (“checkpoint 1000”) and the actual file system status was discovered, indicating that sufficient verification is needed before deciding on an execution path. After multiple rounds of debugging, the incompatibility issue of UNI2 patch size was identified—if the UNI2 architecture (ViT-H/14) and STAIG’s 256×256 requirements were known in advance, this problem could have been anticipated. Over-reliance on sub-agent exploration for simple status checks (e.g., starting a task agent to check the state of M14/M16, instead of directly reading files) increases latency and complexity without providing corresponding value. When multiple sessions reference the same experiment (visual optimization comparison), Claude does not explicitly connect them in chronological order, nor indicates that these are consecutive experiments—this causes confusion in the narrative flow. Learning Outcomes Key Learning Points- Batch processing is crucial for GPU efficiency: Continuous calls to small GPU operations in Python loops (even 2700 calls) lead to significant resource waste (QFormer uses 5% of GPU resources) — always look for opportunities to merge operations into a single GPU kernel launch to improve efficiency through batch processing. The value of dimensionality reduction depends on the capacity of downstream models: It helps simplify aggregation methods (such as mean or attention mechanisms), reducing the impact of noise and dimension collapse (+0.05–0.09 ARI), but for advanced learning models that can utilize high-dimensional information (such as qformer and llava_mlp), it has a negative effect (-0.05 ARI) — there is no universal solution; preprocessing methods must be adjusted according to model complexity. Robust error handling at the iteration boundary (scene-level try-except) can prevent cascading failures during long-running batch processing, while retaining some results through a recovery mechanism. Vectorization techniques can significantly improve the speed of array operations: Replacing nested Python loops with native functions in scipy/NumPy is almost always worth it — the key is identifying O(n²) patterns and knowing the correct library functions. For long-term machine learning training tasks on remote clusters, unbuffered output (PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 + stdbuf -oL) is essential — buffering may hide hours of failures, making debugging impossible. In RL/robotics evaluations, clear initialization of the RNG for policy and environment must be done — comparing with reference implementations reveals potential missing initialization steps in the documentation. Flexibility of the architecture is achieved through family-based conditional logic: When extending from hard-coded assumptions (only UNI), introduce semantic grouping (encoder families) and adopt conditional behavior instead of eliminating all constraints — this preserves optimization for special cases while providing flexibility. Practical Learning Points In large-scale applications, eliminating data transfer between GPU and CPU is important: Small data transfers seem insignificant, but they accumulate over multiple iterations (1100 cycles × multiple dropout calls), totaling 1–2 seconds — generate and operate on local device data as much as possible. Input requirements for visual transformers are very strict: ViTs require input sizes to be integer multiples of the patch size (UNI2: H%14=0, W%14=0) — when applying preprocessing methods designed for one architecture to another, size constraints need to be validated in advance; for most ViTs, 224×224 is a safe default value. Statistical tests (such as scipy.stats.kruskal) fail on degenerate distributions; always add edge-case handling with informative error messages instead of letting library exceptions propagate. Defensive type checking (isinstance() guard) can prevent parsing errors when serialization format assumptions are wrong; JSONL fields may have inconsistent types across different data sources. Model crashes (NaN losses) require a graceful fallback path: When known failure patterns exist, add cleanup steps (np.nan_to_num) in the fallback path and log the issue — producing a fallback output (ARI=0 and clean data) is better than causing system crashes. When debugging multi-GPU Slurm jobs, MUJOCO_EGL_DEVICE_ID and CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES must match exactly — substrings in binding_utils.py check both for compliance. Dialogue Summary MIHD Spatial Transcriptomics ✅ CPU Bottleneck Optimization and Architecture Generalization 05:38:48.477 | claude_code Comprehensive optimization was applied to the MIHD fusion training process, solving three bottlenecks: (1) Vectorized computation of STAIG edge weights using scipy.cdist replaced O(n²) loops, improving speed by 100–500 times; (2) Moving adaptive dropoutAdj to GPU reduced data transfer time by about 1–2 seconds; (3) The forward_batched() method was added to QFormer, enabling batch processing and increasing speed by 20–50 times. By introducing encoder family detection (STAIG_UNI_FAMILY) and conditional preprocessing, STAIG can support any visual encoder. Comprehensive visual optimization experiments were conducted on 8 fusion methods, showing that optimization helps weaker methods (+0.05–0.09 ARI) but has a negative effect on stronger methods (-0.05 ARI). STAIG fusion was deployed in all 11 DLPFC segments, and through UNI2 compatibility fixes, an average ARI of 0.546 was achieved for 10 valid segments.
Error Recovery Benchmarking ✅ Evaluation Process Fixes and Training Restart 07:06:24.474 | claude_code By adding scene-level try-except error handling in collector.py, the critical evaluation process crash in scenario 122/649 was fixed, allowing skipping 130 fingerprint-mismatch natural capture scenarios. M13 analysis was completed: a baseline report (random SR=0% RP=2.3%, BC-RNN SR=0% RP=0.6%) was generated, reliability analysis (Fleiss’ kappa=-0.02), and discrimination report (all SR=0) were produced. Pi0.5 Phoenix training was restarted with improved monitoring mechanisms (PYTHONUNBUFFERED, stdbuf, error capture, GPU logs), stable operation starting from step 3000 with a step size of 2.0 seconds. Errors in the evaluation script were fixed (environment initialization, state verification, quaternion conversion). Three GPU evaluations (m14_cpu/pi0/pi05) were restarted with recovery capabilities, progressing gradually to 649 scenarios × 4 strategies. The project documentation was updated from v4.11 to v4.12.
Token Usage Total usage: $69.06 — 106.9 million tokens
summary: Through vectorization processing and GPU batch processing techniques, we successfully optimized the MIHD fusion process, resulting in a 100 to 500-fold improvement in execution speed. Additionally, we improved the STAIG algorithm so that it can support various visual encoding methods. Comprehensive visual optimization experiments were conducted on 11 slides, while the crash issues in the error recovery benchmark tests were fixed, and the training process of Pi0.5 Phoenix was restarted, along with enhanced system monitoring capabilities.

Weekly Report — 2026-W08 (2026-02-16 ~ 2026-02-22) This week, with the MIHD spatial transcriptomics project as the main focus, we completed a systematic investigation of H&E Image-Only clustering (establishing the ARI literature baseline of 0.11–0.16), implemented three self-supervised enhancement schemes (SCAN increased ARI from 0.251 to 0.303, +20.6%), and built a two-stage fusion framework for Vision Refinement; simultaneously, on the tianhe cluster, we advanced the Error Recovery Benchmark (verification of M14 evaluation infrastructure, full assessment start for 649 scenarios) and the Phoenix pi0.5 reproduction data pipeline (18.4GB MimicGen dataset uploaded, training configuration in place). Throughout the week, we resolved multiple engineering bottlenecks such as STEGO NaN, double normalization bug, lerobot version conflicts, and HuggingFace proxy issues, while two bottlenecks related to Pi0.5 OOM and visualize_scene.py video validation were postponed to next week.
Weekly Overview Metric Value Date Range 2026-02-16 ~ 2026-02-22 Active Days 3 / 7 Total Conversation Count 9 Projects Involved 4 Tasks Completed 11 Ongoing Tasks 5 Total Tokens 28,509,501 Total Cost $14.13 Average Daily Cost $4.71 Project Progress MIHD (Spatial Transcriptomics Clustering) (3 active days) — 🔄 active Completed:
Completed four core technical documents: RM-IDEAL bilingual guide, visual encoder usage manual, pathological PFM literature review, and UNI/UNI2 original paper evaluation analysis. Conducted a systematic investigation of H&E Image-Only methods, established the DLPFC ARI literature baseline (SpaConTDS=0.16, stLearn=0.11), and analyzed the five root causes of Foundation Model failure. Implemented and verified three self-supervised enhancement schemes: STEGO/BYOL+GAT/SCAN. SCAN achieved the best result with ARI=0.303 (baseline 0.251, +20.6%), and its integration with gene feature fusion was validated as complementary (mean fusion +0.065 ARI). Identified and fixed the STAIG double normalization bug in eval_scan_fusion.py, deciding to use the correct path in run_benchmark.py. Integrated a CacheManager embedding cache in run_benchmark.py (loaded in seconds, supports custom cache names for scan_uni2). Implemented the Vision Refinement two-stage fusion framework (–vision_refine parameter, ~60 lines minimal intrusion), and started batch experiments with 7 fusion strategies in the background. Re-generated all 11 sections visually in batches (using .npz cache, no re-inference required), and added an H&E original image panel. Bottlenecks:
⚠️ The coordinate dimension bug in eval_scan_fusion.py caused incomplete debugging of the SCAN fusion joint evaluation script. ⚠️ The first experiment of Vision Refinement (scan_cluster + concat, ARI=0.313) was lower than direct concat (0.387), and the issue of feature diversity in self-supervised compression losses needs further analysis. ⚠️ The implementation of ImageEncoder enhancement for the large goal 7 in ENHANCEMENT_PLAN_CN.md has not started. Error Recovery Benchmark & Phoenix pi0.5 Reproduction (1 active day) — 🔄 active Completed:
Developed a complete Phase II execution plan with 7 steps, covering large goals G1–G7 and milestones M12–M15, with a key path of approximately 16 days. Verified the M14 baseline evaluation infrastructure for 10 scenarios (sanity check passed), and started full CPU assessment for 649 scenarios (exceeded expectations by 454, +43%). Completed the full data pipeline for Phoenix pi0.5 reproduction: convert_mimicgen_to_lerobot.py, evaluate_mimicgen.py, OpenPI training configuration (100K steps, 4-GPU), and download/format conversion of the 18.4GB MimicGen dataset (7–8/9 tasks completed). Diagnosed the Pi0.5 OOM bottleneck, and standardized GPU access to srun –overlap. Resolved the incompatibility issue between lerobot 0.1.0 and datasets>=4.0 (downgraded to 3.6.0). Established hf-mirror.com as the standard solution for cluster HuggingFace data retrieval. Bottlenecks:
⚠️ Pi0.5 OOM remains unresolved (GPU memory insufficient at 150MB), and the baseline assessment is still blocked. ⚠️ The extension of force parameters in visualize_scene.py is complete, but video validation is blocked due to SLURM node permissions issues. ⚠️ Port conflict on Pi0 VLA Server (port 5555 occupied) caused session interruption. Key Tasks ✅ Systematic Investigation of H&E Image-Only Clustering Methods (2026-02-19) — Collected a comprehensive overview of methods such as MILWRM/F-SEG/Deep Contrastive Clustering, verified the image-only DLPFC ARI values (SpaConTDS=0.16, stLearn=0.11) through ablation experiments, and deeply investigated the applications of BYOL/STEGO/SCAN in pathology, along with a four-level domain gap resolution framework in the CV community. ✅ Establishment of MIHD Technical Documentation System (2026-02-19) — Created four core technical documents: RM-IDEAL bilingual structure document, visual encoder usage guide (12 chapters), pathological PFM literature review, and UNI/UNI2 original paper evaluation analysis (34 clinical tasks). ✅ Analysis of Root Causes of Foundation Model Failure in Spatial Domain (2026-02-19) — Conducted a systematic analysis from five dimensions: domain mismatch in training data, pre-training task mismatch, minimal morphological differences between brain tissue layers, feature redundancy, and lack of spatial context. Supported by cases involving the brown repeated patches in UNI2. ✅ Implementation of Image-Only Clustering Enhancement Schemes (STEGO/BYOL+GAT/SCAN) (2026-02-19) — Created four model files: STEGOHead/BYOLAdapter/SpatialGATRefiner/SCANHead. Completed comparative tests on 151673 sections, with SCAN achieving the best result with ARI=0.303 (+20.6%). ✅ Investigation and Architecture Decision for STAIG Fusion Double Normalization Bug (2026-02-20) — Confirmed that the missing staig_alignment_config in eval_scan_fusion.py caused internal StandardScaler in STAIGTrainer; decided to use the correct path in run_benchmark.py instead of fixing a separate script. ✅ Integration of Embedding Cache Mechanism in run_benchmark.py (2026-02-20) — Introduced CacheManager, checking the cache before gene/vision encoding, and skipping encoder instantiation if hit (loaded in seconds). Supports custom cache names for scan_uni2, with three variants for vision cache: standard, freq, staig_strict. 🔄 Verification of M14 Baseline Evaluation Infrastructure and Full Assessment Start (2026-02-22) — Sanity check (60 episodes, ~7 minutes, SR=0% as expected), followed by start of full CPU assessment for 649 scenarios × 2 strategies × 3 seeds (≈ 3894 episodes), running in the background. 🔄 Construction of Full Data Pipeline for Phoenix pi0.5 Reproduction (2026-02-22) — Written convert_mimicgen_to_lerobot.py and evaluate_mimicgen.py, configured pi05_base_mimicgen_phoenix training parameters, downloaded the 18.4GB MimicGen dataset via hf-mirror.com (9 tasks, 9000 demos), and completed format conversion (7–8/9 tasks). 🔄 Joint Evaluation of SCAN Embedding and Multimodal Fusion (2026-02-19) — Written eval_scan_fusion.py, comparing the optimized 256-dimensional visual embedding of SCAN with PCA gene features across all fusion methods; mean fusion achieved ARI +0.065, partially resolved the coords dimension bug, and script debugging in progress. 🔄 Implementation and Batch Experiments of MIHD Vision Refinement Two-Stage Fusion Framework (2026-02-22) — Added –vision_refine parameter (scan_cluster/stego_refine/byol_spatial), with ~60 lines of code minimal intrusion, first experiment showed ARI=0.313 lower than baseline concat 0.387; 7 fusion strategies running in the background. ✅ Completion of Full Phase II Execution Plan for Error Recovery Benchmark (2026-02-22) — Analyzed the dependencies between large goals G1–G7 and milestones M12–M15, developed a 7-step execution plan, and clarified the GPU allocation strategy (srun –overlap, ≥50% free memory), with a key path of approximately 16 days. ✅ Diagnosis of Error Recovery Benchmark Baseline and Update of GPU Access Specification (2026-02-22) — Resolved Pi0.5 OOM (150MB memory shortage), BC-RNN obs key issue, and 649 scenario readiness; standardized GPU access in CLAUDE.md and MEMORY.md to srun –overlap. 🚫 Extension of force parameters in visualize_scene.py (2026-02-22) — Completed addition of force_override/duration_override/settle_steps parameters and Phase 3 neutral action logic; video validation blocked due to SLURM node permissions issues. ✅ Special Comparative Experiment for STAIG Fusion (151673) (2026-02-20) — Tested staig_fusion × {UNI2_raw, SCAN(UNI2)} separately, ARI values were 0.3929/0.3880, almost equal; verified that STAIG internal StandardScaler+PCA offset the effects of SCAN optimization. ✅ Addition of H&E Panel and Batch Update of UNI2 Visualization (2026-02-19) — Changed to a 1×3 layout (H&E + GT + prediction), re-generated all 11 sections visually using .npz cache, 151510 fixed via hires→lowres symlink. Issues and Solutions 1. STEGO Training loss is NaN throughout, 3639×3639 dense similarity matrix overflows in float32 operations at temperature=0.07 [MIHD] (2026-02-19) Solution: Two-step fix: perform L2 normalization on the input image_emb;Change InfoNCE to the numerical stability version (subtract the maximum value of rows before computing logsumexp, and increase temperature to 0.1).
2. MILWRM was incorrectly classified as an Image-Only method; the initial AI summary will mix multimodal methods with image-only results. The initial research conclusion needs significant revision [MIHD] (2026-02-19)Solution: Use WebFetch to read the full PMC text and confirm that MILWRM is actually based on gene expression, specifically mining only image-only data points from ablation experiments on articles like SpaConTDS. 3. There is a double normalization bug in staig_fusion in eval_scan_fusion.py (STAIGTrainer internally applies StandardScaler again) [MIHD] (2026-02-20) Solution: Abandon fixing the standalone script and directly use run_benchmark.py that correctly passes staig_alignment_config, reusing the verified path.
4. run_benchmark.py instantiates the encoder each time to extract embeddings, lacking pipeline-level cache support [MIHD] (2026-02-20) Solution: Integrate CacheManager from pipeline/cache_manager.py, load from cache before encoding, and write back to cache after extraction; skip encoder instantiation when a cache hit occurs.
5. Lerobot 0.1.0 is incompatible with datasets >=4.0 (torch.stack reports TypeError: Column object replaces list) [Error Recovery Benchmark / Phoenix pi0.5] (2026-02-22) Solution: Downgrade datasets from 4.4.1 to 3.6.0 (<4.0); datasets 4.0 changes the return value of dataset[‘column’] from a list to a Column object, and Lerobot expects a list/tuple of tensors.
6. The official HuggingFace download fails due to proxy (Squid 503), and the Python download script cannot connect [Error Recovery Benchmark / Phoenix pi0.5] (2026-02-22) Solution: Use hf-mirror.com + wget; URL format: https://hf-mirror.com/datasets/{repo_id}/resolve/main/{file_path}，通过集群 HTTP proxy reaches 40–200MB/s.
7. Unstable access to SLurm GPU nodes: srun lacks –overlap, causing command hangs; direct SSH connection is unreliable, and multi-partition submissions are rejected [Error Recovery Benchmark / Phoenix pi0.5] (2026-02-22) Solution: Standardize the workflow: source set-XY-I.sh → squeue → srun –jobid= –overlap; avoid direct SSH to GPU nodes.
8. Abnormal spatial coordinate dimension in eval_scan_fusion.py (turns into (1,2)), causing errors in multiple fusion methods [MIHD] (2026-02-19) Solution: Abandon calling load_spatial_coordinates() (barcode matching fails), and directly read coordinates from adata.obsm[‘spatial’]; fix the unpacking error in load_dlpfc_data return value.
Learning Gains Domain Knowledge (domain) Pure image-only achieves only 0.11–0.16 ARI in DLPFC fine-grained stratification tasks (multimodal reaches 0.45–0.64), which is a combination of extremely small morphological differences between brain layers and mismatch in the Foundation Model training domain; ablation experiments of multimodal methods almost never test image-only separately—this is a noteworthy research gap. Five main reasons for failure in space domain recognition by Foundation Models: ① Training mainly on cancer tissue (domain gap); ② Pre-training task mismatch with inter-layer gradient recognition; ③ Extremely small morphological differences between cerebral cortex layers; ④ High redundancy between image features and gene expression; ⑤ Lack of spatial context in independent encoding of a single patch. STAIG uses BYOL for unsupervised domain adaptation on target dataset H&E patches (keep encoder after training, discard projector/predictor)—this is a direct precedent for introducing unsupervised domain adaptation into spatial transcriptomics; the design of BYOL without negative samples is naturally suitable for small batch ST scenarios (thousands of patches per section). The CV community has a four-stage framework for handling “domain gap + fine-grained task + unlabeled data”: Level 1: direct pre-trained feature clustering → Level 2: STEGO/SCAN feature refinement → Level 3: domain-specific SSL re-training (BYOL/MAE) → Level 4: dedicated Foundation Model; GPFM/CHIEF are the optimal PFM for space domain recognition ARI, and UNI2 are the optimal spot retrieval. Architecture (architecture) SCAN is the optimal ARI (0.303, +20.6%) in image-only spatial transcriptomics scenarios. Its core advantage is that offline feature k-NN mining decouples embedding learning and clustering; its 256-dimensional optimized embeddings complement gene features (mean fusion +0.065 ARI). Two-stage fusion is not necessarily better than single-stage: after scanning_cluster compresses visual embeddings from 1536d to 256d, multimodal fusion ARI (0.313) is lower than direct concat (0.387), indicating that self-supervised compression loses the original feature diversity required for fusion tasks, and the optimization objectives of self-supervised clustering conflict with downstream fusion tasks. Internal StandardScaler+PCA preprocessing in STAIG fusion absorbs the external embedding optimization effect (the ARI difference between SCAN and UNI2_raw is only 0.005); embedding cache should store raw embeddings before normalization, and post-encoder normalization should be performed after loading to ensure consistent results across different call paths. VLA baseline evaluation must explicitly state the checkpoint source: using non-target task fine-tuning models (pi0_libero, pi05_base) to evaluate zero-sample cross-domain recovery capacity—the paper must actively declare this experimental setup, and subsequent comparative experiments after fine-tuning are needed to fully demonstrate the usefulness of the dataset. In complex experimental systems, prefer using existing, verified tool paths (such as run_benchmark.py); standalone scripts easily introduce hidden bugs such as inconsistent preprocessing; before calling internal project functions, read the source code in real time to verify the function signature, rather than relying on memory. Debugging (debugging) When computing large-scale dense similarity matrix (n>3000) and InfoNCE contrast loss, use numerically stable log-sum-exp (subtracting row maximum), otherwise exponential operations with temperature=0.07 at float32 precision will overflow and produce NaN; this is a key engineering constraint for large-scale contrast learning implementation. Tools (tools) Lerobot 0.1.0 has strict constraints on datasets versions; it must be pinned to <4.0 (recommended 3.x); datasets 4.0 change the return value of dataset[‘column’] to a Column object, causing torch.stack to report TypeError; MimicGen is fully compatible with LIBERO obs/action format (84×84 images, 8D state, 7D action)—OpenPI’s LeRobotLiberoDataConfig can be directly reused. The standard solution for accessing HuggingFace on Chinese mainland HPC clusters is hf-mirror.com; URL format: https://hf-mirror.com/datasets/{repo_id}/resolve/main/{file_path}，通过 wget + HTTP proxy reaches 40–200MB/s—this should be used as the default solution. OpenPI’s JAX training naturally supports multi-GPU data parallelism; just specify the GPU list in CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES, and JAX automatically builds a 2D mesh parallel—no changes to TrainConfig are needed; Slurm –overlap is a key parameter for running new commands on existing interactive jobs—it is a core technique for calling cluster GPUs in Claude Code environment. AI Usage Notes Effective Modes:
✓ Parallel sub-tasks explore the project structure and formulate cleanup plans (MIHD organizes tasks), reducing serial exploration time. ✓ Parallel background execution on GPU with three schemes (STEGO/BYOL/SCAN) for comparison and validation, significantly reducing total experimental time. ✓ Use .npz caching to generate visualizations in bulk, completely decoupling inference and visualization—11/11 sections succeed. ✓ Independent temporary script (_test_staig_scan.py) isolates testing a single fusion method, shortening a 2-hour task to 30 seconds. ✓ Independent exploration of JAX multi-GPU mechanisms (no config changes) and the hf-mirror.com alternative download method—no user intervention required. ✓ Minimal invasive code change (about 60 lines): insert a Vision Refinement stage in run_benchmark.py, maintaining architecture stability. Limitations:
✗ Inadequate accuracy in literature classification: MILWRM is incorrectly classified as image-only method; initial research aggregation mixes with multimodal results—requires two user interventions to converge on the correct research boundary. ✗ Lack of awareness to actively expose key experimental assumptions: No explicit mention of the impact of using LIBERO fine-tuning checkpoint in VLA evaluation on experiment effectiveness—needs user inquiry to discuss further. ✗ API usage tends to rely on memory rather than real-time verification: Multiple function signature/return value unpacking errors occur in eval_scan_fusion.py—source code should be read before calling. ✗ Slurm permission issues tend to involve listing multiple partitions (5+ times)—no quick query to the user about correct account/partition information. ✗ Insufficient status judgment for background tasks: Data conversion is still running when LeRobot dataset validation triggers, leading to false timestamp violation errors; frequent sleep polling is interrupted multiple times. ✗ Using CPU by default for model validation in HPC environments hides real performance issues, causing additional interaction overhead. Next Week’s Plan Next week will focus on three parallel lines: ①MIHD: fix the coordinate bug in eval_scan_fusion.py, complete joint evaluation of SCAN embedding and full fusion strategies, analyze batch results of 7 fusion strategies and diagnose the root cause of Vision Refinement compression losses, and consider adjusting refinement hidden_dim or switching to stego_refine/byol_spatial; ②Error Recovery Benchmark: organize full CPU evaluation results for M14 649 scenario, solve Pi0.5 OOM problem (apply larger memory GPU or reduce batch size), start Phoenix pi0.5 100K steps 4-GPU training; ③Engineering blocking removal: resolve SLURM node permission issues and complete visualize_scene.py video validation, resolve Pi0 VLA Server port conflict (detect with lsof -i:5555 + backup port mechanism), and advance implementation of ImageEncoder enhancement for goal 7 in ENHANCEMENT_PLAN_CN.md.

Daily Report — 2026-02-22 Daily Summary Completed Work: Progressed on three major projects: implemented the visual optimization architecture for MIHD and conducted tests; updated tool documentation and generated a 3-week historical report; transitioned the error recovery benchmark test from Phase 1 infrastructure to Phase 2 experiments through M14 baseline evaluation and Pi0.5 fine-tuning preparation. Execution Methods: Organized projects using a systematic multi-agent exploration method; made 10 code modifications in 150 lines of code to achieve visual optimization; performed parallel GPU evaluations on 7 fusion methods; executed M14 sanity checks via Slurm cluster and used EGL rendering; designed a 7-step Phase 2 execution plan with dependency topology; set up a MimicGen dataset conversion process for Pi0.5 fine-tuning. Impact: MIHD gained a new experimental dimension (two-phase fusion) and a clearer project structure; the tool achieved complete documentation coverage and comprehensive work history archiving; the error recovery benchmark test resolved all Phase 2 issues, established a Slurm-based GPU access mode, and initiated the VLA fine-tuning process for 9 Phoenix tasks. DCC Completed Work: Completed the implementation of MIHD visual optimization, preliminary testing, and comprehensive file organization (removed 3 redundant scripts, reorganized documentation, and created a unified plans.md file). Execution Methods: Modified run_benchmark.py file, added –vision_refine parameter, and configured scan_cluster/stego_refine/byol_spatial options; performed PCA+UNI2+scan_cluster optimization on 151673 slices, initiated fusion scanning of 7 methods; used Explore agent to generate cleanup plans, then executed file deletion, log migration, and documentation refactoring. Impact: Implemented a two-phase fusion experiment (optimization + multi-modal fusion); although preliminary results show optimization is not universally better than direct connection; significantly improved project maintainability, reduced the root directory to only 2 core files, and formed a clear three-layer documentation structure. 3. Solution: Continue testing the remaining 6 fusion methods (attention mechanism, adln_attention, llava_mlp, qformer, etc.) to determine whether certain strategies can better utilize the improved 256-dimensional embeddings; consider adjusting the hidden dimension or trying other optimization methods (such as stego_refine, byol_spatial).
Key Insight: The self-supervised clustering method optimizes the separability of clustering, but this may not align with the goal of information complementarity for multimodal fusion. Dimensionality reduction can filter out features valuable for gene-visual complementarity, even if these features are not relevant to image-based clustering.
4. The GPU allocation strategy is unclear: initially assumed only GPU 0 was available, but in fact there are 8 A800 GPUs on the Slurm node. Solution: Manually confirmed the status of all GPUs, used the nvidia-smi tool to check memory usage, and selected GPUs with a memory utilization exceeding 50% for use. The updated plan is to dynamically check memory usage and accordingly allocate CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES to achieve parallel task execution.
Key Insight: In a shared HPC environment, resource availability does not equal idle status. Memory-based thresholds (such as a 50% threshold) should be used instead of simple idle detection. If memory allows, multiple tasks can share a node, maximizing cluster utilization.
5. The SSH connection to the GPU node is unstable and often disconnects, causing interruptions in long-running experiments. Solution: Switch to the workflow recorded in CLAUDE.md: use squeue to find running tasks, then use srun –jobid= to connect to the allocated node. This avoids direct SSH usage and utilizes Slurm task management functions.
Key Insight: Using srun –jobid for task connection is more stable than direct SSH, as Slurm is designed for HPC workloads and follows cluster resource management. Task IDs can be retained across different sessions, enabling reconnection.
Common Issues 6. The MIHD project has accumulated redundant scripts (3 backup versions total, 111KB), scattered log files (5 files, ~5MB), 16 temporary summary fragments, and documents distributed in the root and docs/ directories. Solution: Perform systematic cleanup through parallel task agents: delete redundant scripts (their functions are replaced by run_benchmark.py/run_pipeline.py), create centralized storage for output/log files, delete summary fragments (key data is stored in experiment_comparison.csv), organize documents into a three-layer structure (research/experiments/archived), merge the ENHANCEMENT_PLAN file into unified plans.md, and update all references.
Key Insight: Extra documents naturally accumulate during project iterations; a “cleanup day” is needed regularly: delete outdated backup files, relocate temporary output files, integrate duplicate documents, and update references. The root directory should contain only core document files.
7. When starting the Pi0 VLA server, port 5555 was occupied, causing failure to start. Solution: This issue was discovered via srun output. Several solutions were provided: terminate existing processes, use a different port, or check if the existing server can be reused. The user decides how to resolve the conflict.
Key Insight: Resource conflicts are common in long-running cluster jobs (such as ports, GPUs, file locking). It is necessary to check resource availability before allocation and develop alternative plans.
8. Both CLAUDE.md and README.md for the gadget project lack documentation about the website/tools (the third tool in the project), making the project overview incomplete. Key Insight: Systematic review of the /init command can easily detect long-standing missing documents easily overlooked during incremental development, especially in multiple-tool projects where each tool is independently recorded.
9. QFormer training shows high memory usage (19.4GB), but very low GPU utilization (4%, 55W), leading to slow training progress. Solution: This is characteristic of the QFormer architecture: models and data are stored in VRAM, but cross-attention computation is relatively simple, with most time spent on CPU-intensive k-NN graph construction and loss calculation. This is expected behavior and requires patience.
Key Insight: High memory usage does not mean high GPU load. The learnable query mechanism limits the training process to CPU preprocessing, while the GPU core is mostly idle, and VRAM is used mainly for storage rather than computation.
10. Version 4.4.1 of the dataset library is incompatible with the conversion process, causing import failure. Solution: Downgrade to version 3.6.0 to restore compatibility with the MimicGen-to-LeRobot conversion script.

Lessons Learned Key Lesson – Two-stage fusion (self-supervised refinement → multimodal integration) created new experimental dimensions, connecting image-based and multimodal methods; however, preliminary tests show that under different fusion strategies, refined embeddings are not generally superior to original embeddings—consistency of optimization goals is crucial. Accessing GPUs in an HPC cluster via Slurm job attachment (srun –jobid) is more stable than direct SSH, as the cluster resource management system can be utilized, and it is suitable for long-running scientific workloads. The completion rate of M1-M11 error recovery benchmarks (649 scenarios) provides a solid foundation for M14 baseline evaluation, although currently it is hindered by insufficient Pi0.5 memory. In an HPC cluster, GPU availability should be judged by the free memory space (at least maintaining more than 50% free space), not just its idle state. If memory allows, multiple jobs can coexist on the same node, enabling parallel task execution and maximizing cluster utilization. The dependency topology diagram should appear before the execution plan. Clearly visualizing M14 as a critical path blocker helps adjust resource allocation decisions and timeline estimates, leading to a more strategic scheduling. The collector resumes function makes long-running evaluations fault-tolerant. The合理性 check of M14 confirms that interrupted evaluations can restart from the last checkpoint, which is important for 6-hour full-time runs. The “cleanup day” mode for project maintenance is very effective: using 3 parallel exploration agents for a comprehensive project survey, followed by systematic cleanup (removing redundant files, moving logs, reorganizing documents, updating references/memory), simplifies the root directory and makes the document hierarchy clear and traceable. Systematic documentation audit via /init skills is very effective in detecting long-term gaps accumulated during iterative development, especially for multiple tool projects independently recorded for each tool. The error detection process (20 classifiers, PolicyErrorMonitor) works reliably at scale. In the合理性 check, 37–74 errors were detected per set, proving that the classification method can be put into production use. The conversion process from MimicGen to LeRobot requires careful handling of flat and nested HDF5 layouts. JAX can automatically detect all visible GPUs for multi-GPU training when the batch size is divisible by the number of GPUs. When batch_size equals 64, setting CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0,1,3,4 enables efficient 4-GPU parallel processing without explicit configuration. Exploration agents perform well in organizing tasks of large projects: they can recursively traverse directories, read file headers to quickly identify content, calculate code lines, and compare redundant parts in documents—their efficiency is several orders of magnitude higher than manual exploration. During cleanup work in large projects, if users have clear goals and are willing to take responsibility for plan quality, user-controlled planning (bypassing the approval of ExitPlanMode) may be more efficient. In this case, the AI role becomes an executor rather than a designer. Practical Experience When a project accumulates a large amount of work history, batch generation of historical reports is valuable for establishing searchable archives, even though these reports are mainly meta-work rather than main development content. The gadget project now has a comprehensive report covering more than 3 weeks of project activities. QFormer and other fusion methods based on learnable queries exhibit the characteristic of “high VRAM + low GPU utilization” during training: parameters and intermediate results consume memory, but actual computation (cross-attention mechanism) is lightweight, with most time spent on CPU-intensive k-NN graph construction and loss calculation. SSH to GPU nodes (an49, an16, etc.) blocked by pam_slurm_adopt requiring active jobs, and an49 not present in any SLURM partition despite user’s history showing prior direct access Solution: Verified an49 is completely absent from sinfo output; recommended admin intervention while scripts remain ready to execute

2. All SLURM job submissions fail with ‘User’s group not permitted to use this partition’ across xy-a800, ai, lava, and all other partitions Solution: Created alternative tmux-based launcher (launch_eval_tmux.sh) that works with direct SSH or srun once access is restored; documented the blocker for admin escalation

General Issues 3. SLURM sbatch failed with ‘Invalid generic resource (gres) specification’ when using –gres=gpu:1 and –gres=gpu:2 Solution: Discovered cluster has no GRES configuration (sinfo shows null for all nodes) - removed –gres flags and requested GPUs via node allocation only

Issues and Solutions Key Issues 1. run_benchmark.py re-instantiates encoders and extracts embeddings every time it runs, wasting time spent on UNI2/SCAN features that have already been calculated. Solution: Integrate CacheManager into the has/load/save_*_embedding() methods; add cache checks before encoder instantiation to support variant types (standard/frequent/strict); pass coverage flags to both calling points.

Fixed the _to_robosuite_obs() function to map ‘object-state’ to ‘object’ and use raw robosuite obs from environment._env._get_observations(), instead of using StateExtractor.

Additionally, no baseline of 151673 staig_fusion exists for comparison.
