Daily Report — 2026-02-19 Daily Overview Completed Work: Development work on two major projects: (1) MIHD spatial transcriptomics — comprehensively recorded evaluation methods, visual encoder analysis, and image-based clustering enhancement designs, and reviewed over 25 papers; (2) Error recovery benchmark testing — construction of Phase II infrastructure (M14 baseline evaluation, M12/M13 plans) and strategic documentation optimization. Execution Methods: A multi-method combined systematic literature review, exploration of the code library via parallel agents, gradual implementation of code with recovery functions, strategic planning through iterative user clarification, document content refactoring, and cross-domain solution analysis. Impact: MIHD: Established a complete spatial transcriptomics evaluation knowledge base, identified fundamental limitations based on vision (morphological and biological clustering), designed the seventh enhancement target, and formulated a five-phase implementation roadmap; Error Recovery: M14 baseline ready (5448 cases, with崩溃 recovery capability), Phase II roadmap complete (v4.9→v4.10), 51% documentation optimization, while all 87 checklist items are retained, adopting manual remote operation strategy for high-quality data recovery. DCC Completed Work: MIHD project work: Created 4 technical documents (RM-IDEAL metrics, visual encoder guide, literature review, UNI2 evaluation analysis), improved visualization, conducted an image-based clustering literature survey covering over 25 papers, and designed 6 candidate solutions for the seventh enhancement plan. Execution Methods: Used Read/Grep tools to deeply analyze the code library, extensively reviewed papers related to spEMO/STAIG/HEST-1k/UNI/STEGO/SCAN/BYOL/F-SEG, modified create_clustering_visualization() function to implement 1×3 layout, used H&E reference files to generate 11 DLPFC visualization charts in bulk, and performed cross-domain analogy analysis (FGVC, medical imaging, remote sensing). Impact: Established a complete reference document for spatial transcriptomics evaluation; identified reasons for UNI2 feature failures (difference between ARI 0.11-0.16 and 0.5+ in multimodal cases) — clustering based on morphological similarity rather than biological categories; formulated an operable five-phase implementation roadmap and performed risk mitigation; updated ENHANCEMENT_PLAN_CN.md file, added 500 lines to the seventh enhancement plan. TzJsDesktop Completed Work: Fixed the issue where VS Code Remote-SSH connection in Windows system cannot connect to HPC clusters (tianhe/an49/an47). Execution Methods: Diagnosed incompatibility between ControlMaster Unix domain sockets and Windows OpenSSH; commented out ControlMaster/ControlPath/ControlPersist in ~/.ssh/config file; cleaned up expired socket files. Impact: Restored SSH connections to tianhe and an49, making remote development on the HPC cluster possible. tianhe Completed Work: Phase II of Error Recovery Benchmark: Implemented M14 baseline infrastructure (with recovery function, multi-run merging, error type analysis), designed M12 large-scale dataset construction and M13 classification validation plans, conducted VLA model research survey, optimized project documentation from 1554 lines to 763 lines (51% reduction), and designed a comprehensive Phase II research strategy including manual remote operation methods. Execution Methods: Added recovery function to collector.py, extended analysis scripts, implemented multi-run merging and error type analysis; created 7 Makefile targets; studied 17 VLA/basic models via web search; used chunked reading for large files; deployed parallel Explore agent for code library statistics; clarified the concept of training data recovery through iterative Q&A; migrated VLM tutorial to separate file. Impact: M14 ready for operation: 454 scenarios × 4 strategies × 3 seeds = 5448 cases, with automatic recovery capability and resistance to crashes; comprehensive VLA research results make model selection easier; documentation now maintainable while retaining all 87 checklist items; clear Phase II roadmap defines the path from infrastructure to paper-level experiments (G1-G4: dataset size, classification validation, baseline evaluation, FM practicality proof); adopting manual remote operation strategy for high-quality recovery demonstrations. Two important research projects completed: comprehensive MIHD spatial transcriptomics documentation and visual encoder analysis revealed fundamental limitations, while Phase II infrastructure of error recovery benchmark was built and a strategic roadmap was formulated.
Tasks Architecture and Strategy - ✅ MIHD Comprehensive Evaluation Documentation and Literature Review — Created a complete document system: RM-IDEAL scoring metrics (graph kernel WWL), visual encoder process guide (patch extraction, alignment, caching, fusion), pathological base model survey (spEMO/STAIG/HEST-1k/UNI/UNI2), image-only clustering methods (STEGO/SCAN/BYOL/F-SEG). Analyzed 34 UNI clinical tasks and 8 UNI2 benchmark tests, finding most literature lacks visual-based spatial domain evaluation content. ✅ MIHD enhancement plan update: Concept 7 Image-only Clustering — Designed a five-phase implementation plan with 6 candidate solutions (STEGO feature optimization, SCAN neighbor mining, BYOL training during testing, DINOv2-GAT graph attention, TTT-MAE mask reconstruction, SFDA frozen encoder + adapter). Added dependency diagram, risk analysis, and validation commands (about 500 lines) to ENHANCEMENT_PLAN_CN.md. ✅ Implementation of M14 Baseline Infrastructure for Error Recovery Benchmark — Added recovery function to collector.py (reading episodes.jsonl files, reconstructing state, skipping completed scenarios). Extended 3_collect_data.py with –resume/–scene_offset/–scene_limit parameters. Rewritten 4_analyze_results.py for multi-run merging and error-type classification analysis. Created 7 Makefile targets for baseline evaluation of 454 scenarios × 4 strategies. 🔄 M12 Error Recovery Benchmark: Large-scale Dataset Construction Plan — Designed a 13-step plan including MimicGen enhancement (10→200 examples), BC-RNN/Pi0/Pi0.5 natural error capture, hierarchical training/test splitting, adjustment of detector time parameters. All code completed (6 files modified), but encountered MUJOCO_EGL_DEVICE_ID error during execution. 🔄 M13 Error Recovery Benchmark: Error Classification Validation Design — Designed a three-pillar validation method: (1) Mapping FMEA to ISO 15066/10218/IEC 61508 standards; (2) Verifying integrity via 6×3 phases × family matrix; (3) Statistical validation using Cohen’s/Fleiss’ kappa to assess classifier reliability. Plan ready but not implemented yet. ✅ Phase II Strategic Planning Document for Error Recovery Benchmark — Comprehensive update of project panorama.md (from v4.9 to v4.10): divided goals into Phase I (completed G1-G3) and Phase II (new G4-G7), added detailed M12-M15 sub-targets, created a five-phase execution timeline (Day 1–16), updated risk analysis, then optimized code lines from 1554 to 763 (51% reduction), while retaining all 87 checklist items; migrated VLM tutorial to separate file; updated statistics to 53 files, about 13,300 lines. ✅ VLA and Basic Model Research Survey — Created a comprehensive 200-line survey covering 8 VLA models with error recovery capabilities (SC-VLA, CycleVLA, VLA-SCT, FailSafe, FPC-VLA, RoboFAC, VLAC, Self-Improving VLA) and 9 basic models (π0, π0-FAST, π0.5, OpenVLA, Octo, GR00T, HPT, RT-2). Includes architectural details, open-source status, usage instructions, fine-tuning commands, and integration suggestions. Implementation and Fixes ✅ Enhanced MIHD Visualization with H&E Reference Panel — Modified create_clustering_visualization() function to change its layout from 1×2 to 1×3, added H&E image panel for direct comparison of morphological features; used cached embedding data to generate visualization results for all 11 DLPFC regions in bulk (151508-151675); fixed low-resolution image issue in 151510. ✅ Fixed Windows SSH Connection to HPC Cluster — Resolved VS Code Remote-SSH failure due to incompatibility between ControlMaster/Unix domain sockets and Windows OpenSSH; successfully connected to tianhe and an49. ✅ Improved Error Recovery Benchmark CLAUDE.md Documentation — Reduced project documentation from 205 lines to 163 lines: corrected inaccuracies in error type count (17→24) and validator count (2→4), merged redundant architectural sections, reduced external project description from 48 lines to 18 lines, and added test fixture documentation and data format reference. Issues and Solutions Key Issues 1. How to prove that the error recovery benchmark can “generate scenarios” — Need evidence that data actually improves models as a contribution to papers. Solution: Design G4 phase (proof of dataset usefulness) as a four-step experiment: (1) Convert over 2000 scenarios into LeRobot format with state and image observations; (2) Fine-tune π0.5 using LoRA on A800, train for 2–4 hours on error scenarios; (3) Conduct stratified sampling evaluation on retained test samples; (4) Measure improvement (expected 15–30% SR gain, 10–20% RP gain, statistical significance analysis via bootstrap CI and Wilcoxon test). Key Insight: Benchmark usefulness requires closed-loop validation: error data → model training → measurable performance improvement on unseen errors. This is the core paper contribution beyond scenario generation infrastructure — namely “four-pillar validation,” which distinguishes publishable benchmarks from simple datasets.
2. UNI2 base model accuracy in DLPFC spatial clustering is only 0.11–0.16 (compared with 0.5+ for gene+image multimodal), and brown repeated regions appear uniformly in clustering results. Solution: Identified 5 root causes: (1) Differences in training data domains (more cancer data, fewer brain data); (2) Incompatible pre-training tasks (rough organizational classification vs fine-grained layer detection); (3) Subtle differences in DLPFC layers (cell density/size, not color/texture); (4) Redundancy of features and gene expression; (5) Lack of spatial context. Analysis shows UNI2 clustering is based on morphological similarity (vessels in all layers), not biological categories. Proposed 6 adaptation methods (STEGO, SCAN, BYOL, DINOv2-GAT, TTT-MAE, SFDA), ordered by solution order: domain-specific pre-training → adaptation during testing → feature optimization → task-specific fine-tuning. Added H&E reference panel in visualization to confirm hypothesis. Key Insight: Pure visual encoder clusters based on morphological features rather than biological functions — a typical fine-grained recognition problem common in computer vision (bird subspecies, rock types, cell morphology). Lower accuracy reflects structural grouping (similar objects) rather than functional grouping (biologically similar objects). General base models learn rough semantic information; for fine-grained tasks, domain-specific fine-tuning or feature optimization is needed.
3. Stage imbalance in error recovery benchmark dataset — 90% of scenarios belong to pre_reach/reach and transport/place stages, while transport/place stage is completely empty (0 scenarios). Solution: Adopt BC-RNN strategy as a key means to reach subsequent stages, reduce detector minimum step threshold from 100 to 5–50 to capture failure in lift/traffic stages. Use MimicGen to generate over 200 example variants to increase trajectory diversity and trigger opportunities for later stages. Key Insight: Stage coverage requires strategies with sufficient success rate to enter later stages (optimal timing for BC-RNN), while detector timing needs adjustment — random strategy fails too early (never reaches improvement point), Pi0 SR is 0% (never reaches mastery), only BC-RNN reaches transport/place stage during failures. This is a “reachability problem” determined by success rate distribution.
How to rigorously verify that the 24 error classification methods are principled, comprehensive, and non-duplicate, suitable for academic publicationSolution: Three-pillar validation: (1) Map the 8 categories to FMEA failure modes in ISO 15066/10218/IEC 61508 industrial safety standards to provide theoretical basis; (2) Prove integrity through a 6-stage × 3 families = 18 cell matrix to ensure no blind spots; (3) Use Cohen’s/Fleiss’ kappa for statistical validation (goal: κ > 0.6 within the same category, κ < 0.3 between categories) to verify type discrimination. Key Insight: Validation of academic classification methods requires theoretical basis (industry standards provide reasons based on FMEA) and empirical evidence (statistical independence tests prove no redundancy) — one cannot rely solely on intuition to confirm the 24 types.
If the VLA server crashes during operation, the M14 baseline evaluation (5448 cases, runtime 5–15 hours) may lose all progress. Solution: A recovery function is implemented in collector.py: it reads the existing episodes.jsonl file at startup, builds a set of completed tuples (scene ID, strategy name, seed), skips these tuples in a triple loop, and rebuilds the all_episodes dictionary to maintain accuracy of the summary. The –resume flag is added to 3_collect_data.py. Now with automatic recovery, the risk of crash is avoided.
Key Insight: For long-running data collection (>1 hour), appendable JSONL logs and recovery logic are crucial. The key lies in idempotency: reading back JSONL and rebuilding the summary dictionary ensures consistent final results, whether the operation is completed once or multiple attempts at recovery.
Users do not understand the concept of “recovery training data” in the second-phase plan, leading to obstacles in plan approval. Solution: Specific examples are provided, comparing normal demonstrations (reset → success) with recovery trajectories (error state → adjustment → success); it is explained that it teaches the model “how to correct errors,” rather than just “how to do things right from the start.” Users ultimately choose manual remote operation to obtain high-quality data, although this increases time costs.
Errors such as “client_loop: send disconnect: Bad file descriptor” and “tried to write to a nonexistent pipe” occur when connecting VS Code Remote-SSH to the HPC cluster. Solution: Windows OpenSSH does not support Unix domain sockets used by ControlMaster/ControlPath/ControlPersist. These three options are commented out in the ~/.ssh/config file, and expired socket files are removed from ~/.ssh/sockets/. The connection is immediately restored.
Key Insight: SSH connection reuse (ControlMaster) is a feature exclusive to Unix systems; when these options exist, Windows OpenSSH fails silently, resulting in seemingly wrong low-level errors rather than functionality issues.
General Issues The project summary document is too large (1554 lines, 33k tags), making it impossible to read within a single tool call, which makes optimization difficult. Solution: Use block-based reading with offsets and limits to segment the document; collect statistics through the Explore proxy; migrate the large VLM tutorial section (331 lines) to a separate file; reduce the document length to 763 lines (a 51% reduction) while retaining all 87 checklist items.
Key Insight: Large files require strategic reading methods: use specific offsets for block access so the document can be fully edited, or perform Grep searches on specific content. When refactoring the document, verification steps are needed: count all checklist items before and after modification to ensure no content is lost.
When running MimicGen with CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=3, the MUJOCO_EGL_DEVICE_ID assertion fails. Solution: EGL device ID must match the GPU index in CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES, not the physical GPU ID — when CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=3 is used, MUJOCO_EGL_DEVICE_ID should be set to 3 (or 0 if a single GPU is used).
Key Insight: EGL device ID is relative to the visible device list, not the absolute GPU hardware index — robosuite’s EGL assertion forces this to prevent rendering target mismatch.
Methods for Humans and Artificial Intelligence Strategic Level Strategic planning workflow: Understand first, then plan Role Method Human Explicitly require updating the strategy document before any code implementation (project panorama summary.md); interrupt the plan generation process multiple times and ask “What is obtaining recovery training data?” to ensure clear concepts before detailed implementation; prefer gradual understanding and ability to adjust direction at any time Artificial Intelligence Directly jump to implementation planning and code generation, treating document updates as after-the-fact; attempt to develop a complete detailed plan first, then submit it for approval; try exiting the planning mode before users fully understand the concept; use technical terms without verifying user understanding Analysis of Differences: Humans manage risks through a workflow of understanding first, then planning (explain concepts → user decides direction → then develops detailed plan), and provide a document-driven development approach for complex projects to ensure common understanding before execution. AI focuses on delivering code and a complete plan immediately, rather than control and consistency. For graduate work that requires mentor feedback loops, the human method can reduce rework risks.
Control scope and retain priority during refactoring Role Method Human When optimizing the 1554-line document, explicitly require “retain all large, medium, and small target checklists”; when AI suggests reducing by 60%, insist on retaining all targets; stop network research in advance; choose manual remote operation to obtain recovery data despite higher time costs, prioritizing quality over automation Artificial Intelligence Initially propose aggressive integration measures to eliminate redundancy (1554 lines → 600–700 lines); conduct network searches to find benchmark patterns before establishing a specific current state plan; propose automation options (using Oracle recovery as a “recommended” solution) Analysis of Differences: Humans treat roadmap integrity as non-negotiable and value the completeness of operable checklists over document brevity, recognizing that checklists are tools for tracking progress (must be comprehensive), while explanatory text should follow DRY principles. Humans prioritize quality and real demonstrations, not automated proxies. AI focuses on reducing scale metrics and conducts premature external research before understanding the code library status. | Role | Method | |——|——| | Human | Users immediately realize “Is task1 just clustering?” — it is found that the 9-category organization classification of CRC-100K and the spatial domain recognition of MIHD are the same basic problem (assigning organizational types), only the evaluation methods differ | | Artificial Intelligence | Initially describes CRC-100K as a ROI classification task, without noticing the conceptual connection to spatial domain clustering; focuses only on methodological differences (linear probes vs KMeans) without recognizing structural equivalence |
Analysis of Differences: Humans can recognize abstract similarities between different evaluation paradigms, while AI is troubled by implementation details; this indicates that humans have strong pattern recognition capabilities when solving the same core problem.
Scope negotiation for MIHD improvement plan Role Method Human Users insist on retaining all large, medium, and small target lists during project summary optimization, even though AI suggests reducing by about 60% by merging redundant descriptions; the final solution is to keep all target lists unchanged, but still integrate the narrative (reducing by about 50%, to about 750 lines) Artificial Intelligence AI suggests merging concepts that appear repeatedly in multiple version chapters (e.g., §3.4 + §8(v4.4) + VLA architecture, natural error capture, error classification in §11) Analysis of Differences: This reflects the conflict between integrity and brevity: checklists are used to track progress (must be comprehensive), while explanatory text should follow DRY principles. The user’s correction avoids accidental loss of tracking granularity.
Limitations of Artificial Intelligence Key Limitations Still attempts to exit the planning mode after multiple user rejections (2nd, 5th, 8th sessions on the same day) without realizing this mode — it should be understood after 2–3 rejections that users prefer longer iterations in the planning stage. Trying to exit the plan before users fully understand key concepts leads to interruptions and clarification requests. When searching for ablation studies on image-based transcriptomics papers, it is difficult to find specific ARI numbers because most papers do not report basic data based solely on images. Multiple consecutive queries are needed before realizing the gap, as the community assumes gene expression is primary and images are auxiliary. It is hard to distinguish between “unable to find due to poor search” and “unable to find because no one published it.” It was also mistakenly believed that MILWRM is based on gene expression rather than images, resulting in 2–3 iterations wasted. Use of technical terms (“recovery training data,” “Oracle recovery,” “LeRobot format”) without confirming user understanding; explanations only occur when explicitly asked. Strategic planning issues (data collection methods, task scope) are raised late in the planning process rather than early, potentially leading to rework. Premature network search for benchmark paper patterns is conducted before developing a specific current state plan; users are dissatisfied due to prematureness. A very long plan is generated (M12 has 13 steps, completed in one go during the second phase), without checking whether users prefer step-by-step decomposition. A larger, more complete plan is assumed better, without considering execution limits or顾问 feedback cycles. It is not realized until the user points out that CRC-100K organization classification and spatial domain recognition are the same task — the conceptual equivalence between labeled supervision evaluation and unlabeled unsupervised evaluation is missed, which is used to evaluate the embedding quality of the same basic grouping problem. Daily Report — 2026-02-18 Daily Overview What was done: Two parallel research tracks: fixed spatial transcriptomics coordinate handling bug causing vision embedding errors (DCC), and built comprehensive policy benchmarking infrastructure with unified checkpoint management and rollout visualization (tianhe) How it was done: Deep debugging of coordinate systems via code inspection and verification, followed by cache clearing and re-running experiments; infrastructure work via symlink organization, script development, and integration testing Impact: MIHD: 86% improvement in UNI2-only clustering performance after fix validates multimodal fusion results; tianhe: unified checkpoint management and visualization tools enable systematic VLA cross-task generalization analysis DCC What was done: Diagnosed and fixed coordinate swap bug in MIHD spatial transcriptomics pipeline where pxl_row/pxl_col were incorrectly mapped as X/Y instead of Y/X How it was done: Modified run_benchmark.py and data_loader.py to correct column naming, cleared vision cache, re-ran 33 vision-only and 88 fusion experiments over ~6 hours with STAIG training Impact: UNI2 embeddings now correctly extracted from proper image locations; ARI improved from 0.065→0.121 for vision-only, concat fusion reached 0.275 ARI validating multimodal integration approach tianhe What was done: Built unified checkpoint management system with symlinks, created policy rollout visualization tool, and investigated VLA training data availability for PickPlace task How it was done: Created checkpoints/ directory structure linking BC-RNN/VLA/Robomimic models, wrote 200-line visualize_policy_rollout.py with MP4 rendering, updated configs and Makefile, searched zhaoganlong’s datasets Impact: Can now visualize policy behavior via MP4 rollouts and identified root cause of VLA failure (no task-specific finetuning); discovered MimicGen can expand 10→500 demos for future training Fixed critical spatial coordinate bug in MIHD multimodal fusion benchmark and built infrastructure for robotic policy visualization and checkpoint management
Tasks Architecture & Strategy ✅ Fix MIHD coordinate swap bug — Corrected tissue_positions_list.csv column mapping where pxl_row_in_fullres (Y) and pxl_col_in_fullres (X) were swapped as pixel_x/pixel_y Implementation & Fixes 🔄 Re-run MIHD vision and fusion experiments — Regenerate embeddings and benchmark results for 33 vision-only and 88 multimodal fusion experiments after coordinate fix ✅ Create policy rollout visualization tool — Wrote visualize_policy_rollout.py script with offscreen rendering, HUD overlay, MP4 export, and support for random/BC-RNN/VLA policies ✅ Build unified checkpoint management system — Created checkpoints/ directory with symlinks to BC-RNN, VLA (Pi0/Pi0.5), and Robomimic models for consistent path references ✅ Investigate VLA training data availability — Searched for PickPlace-specific VLA checkpoints and training data; found only 10 source demos vs 500 demos for Coffee/Stack tasks Problems & Solutions Critical Issues 1. Vision embeddings extracted from transposed image locations due to X/Y coordinate swap in tissue_positions_list.csv parsing Solution: Renamed columns to pxl_row/pxl_col (semantic names), swapped coordinate order to (X, Y) = (pxl_col, pxl_row), deleted vision cache, re-ran experiments
Key Insight: Spatial data requires explicit Y-as-row, X-as-column semantics; 10x scale factor validation (pixel coords × scalefactor = microns) catches coordinate system errors early
2. Pi0_libero checkpoint achieves 0% success on PickPlace despite 96-100% on Coffee/Stack Solution: Identified root cause: Pi0_libero is LIBERO-domain finetuned, lacks PickPlace-specific training data (only 10 source demos vs 500 for other tasks); proposed MimicGen→LeRobot→LoRA pipeline
Key Insight: VLA cross-task generalization fails when task domains differ (LIBERO vs PickPlace object/scene layout); finetuning requires 500+ demos expandable via MimicGen from 10 source demos
General Issues 3. No way to visually inspect VLA policy behavior on PickPlace task to diagnose 0% success rate Solution: Built visualize_policy_rollout.py with EGL offscreen rendering, frame-by-frame capture, HUD overlay (policy/step/reward/success), and MP4 export per rollout
Key Insight: Video rollouts reveal behavioral patterns (e.g., random flailing vs directed failures) that success rate alone cannot distinguish
4. Scattered checkpoint paths across multiple HDD_POOL directories making config management fragile Solution: Created centralized checkpoints/ directory with task-organized symlinks (bc_rnn/pick_place, vla/pi0_libero, robomimic/lift) and updated all configs to use relative paths
Key Insight: Symlink-based checkpoint organization enables atomic path updates and clear separation between original storage and project references
Human vs AI Approaches Strategic Level VLA checkpoint selection for PickPlace Role Approach Human Questioned why Pi0_libero was being loaded instead of a PickPlace-specific checkpoint, assumed zhaoganlong should have one AI Initially loaded Pi0_libero as the only available VLA checkpoint without verifying task-specific training Difference Analysis: Human correctly intuited that task-specific finetuning should exist; AI defaulted to available checkpoint without validating task match. Investigation revealed no PickPlace checkpoint exists.
Implementation Level UNI/UNI2 usage in literature Role Approach Human Requested web search to verify how other papers extract patches and handle coordinates for spatial transcriptomics AI Focused on code-level debugging without consulting literature for domain best practices Difference Analysis: Human sought external validation from published methods; AI relied on internal code logic. Literature search confirmed 224x224 patches at 20x magnification but didn’t provide specific coordinate handling details.
AI Limitations General Limitations Did not proactively search for task-specific VLA checkpoints before recommending Pi0_libero, required human prompting to investigate zhaoganlong’s full checkpoint directory Needed multiple search iterations to discover zhaoganlong’s datasets were organized by task (Coffee/Stack) with 500 generated demos each, initially focused on finding PickPlace directly Learnings Key Learnings Spatial coordinate systems in medical imaging require explicit semantic naming (pxl_row=Y, pxl_col=X) and validation via physical units (pixels × scalefactor = microns); generic pixel_x/pixel_y naming is error-prone Vision foundation model integration in multimodal learning critically depends on spatial alignment; incorrect patch extraction (from transposed locations) can halve performance even with correct architecture VLA models trained on one task domain (LIBERO) show minimal cross-task generalization to different manipulation setups (PickPlace) despite similar action spaces; domain-specific finetuning is essential MimicGen can expand 10 human demonstrations to 500 training examples via automatic variation generation, matching the data scale used in successful VLA finetuning (Coffee: 96%, Stack: 100%) Practical Learnings Symlink-based checkpoint management enables version control of path references while preserving original data locations; critical for shared filesystem collaboration Conversation Summaries MIHD Spatial Transcriptomics 🔄 Coordinate swap bug fix in vision patch extraction 00:01:02.520 | claude_code Diagnosed and fixed critical bug where tissue_positions_list.csv columns (pxl_row, pxl_col) were incorrectly mapped as (pixel_x, pixel_y), causing vision patches to be extracted from transposed locations. Cleared vision cache and re-ran 121 experiments (33 vision-only + 88 fusion). Results showed UNI2 ARI improved from 0.065 to 0.121 (+86%). User requested literature review on UNI/UNI2 usage patterns; web search confirmed 224x224 patches at 20x magnification standard but lacked coordinate handling specifics. Experiments still running after 6+ hours due to STAIG training requirements.
Error Recovery Benchmark 🔍 VLA training data investigation and PickPlace finetuning path 04:52:08.850 | claude_code User asked about training VLA on PickPlace task after realizing Pi0_libero has 0% success. Investigation revealed PickPlace only has 10 source demos (6288 steps) while zhaoganlong’s successful Coffee/Stack training used ~500 demos generated via MimicGen. No PickPlace-specific VLA checkpoint exists; all VLA models are LIBERO-domain or base weights. Identified training path: 1) Run MimicGen to expand 10→500 demos, 2) Convert to LeRobot format via zhaoganlong’s scripts, 3) Run Pi0.5 LoRA finetuning. All necessary scripts and pipelines available in zhaoganlong’s repo.
✅ Checkpoint inventory and availability assessment 05:32:29.978 | claude_code User requested inventory of usable VLA models and checkpoints. Found 4 VLA model types registered in code (pi0, pi05, phoenix, flare) but only Pi0_libero and Pi05_base have actual checkpoints (~12GB each). Also identified BC-RNN PickPlace checkpoints (12 epochs, 14MB each) and Robomimic Lift checkpoint (7.6MB, 100% success). Discovered robomimic’s can/square/transport directories are empty. VLA checkpoints all reside in zhaoganlong’s HDD_POOL directory, linked via symlinks to project.
✅ Policy visualization infrastructure setup 00:26:49.679 | claude_code Built unified checkpoint management via checkpoints/ directory with symlinks (bc_rnn/pick_place, vla/pi0_libero, robomimic/lift). Created visualize_policy_rollout.py (200 lines) supporting random/BC-RNN/VLA policies with offscreen rendering, HUD overlay, and MP4 export. Updated benchmark_v4.yaml to use symlink paths and added 3 Makefile visualization targets. Tested successfully with random policy, generated 2 MP4 files. Updated documentation in 项目全景总结.md with new v4.7 checkpoint management section.

Impact: UNI2’s visual ARI increased from 0.065 to 0.08-0.25 (part 151673-151676 reached 0.22-0.25); all visual-dependent fusion experiments will be corrected; this is a fundamental data integrity issue that affects the validity of the entire benchmark. Failed to independently diagnose the root cause of MIHD coordinate issues; relied entirely on users to provide analysis and repair plans. In the face of an “abnormally low ARI” macro metric, AI lacked the ability to independently track data sources (from results → embedding → patch extraction → coordinates → CSV column definitions in reverse order).
Tianhe’s BC-RNN integrated the repair attempts three times over two sessions, but AI failed to anticipate the different observation key names for robosuite’s different tasks (PickPlace and Lift), and also realized that the observation results reconstructed by StateExtractor after the first repair did not guarantee consistent key names. Users had to make multiple corrections to find the correct solution. The use of the outdated MuJoCo C API (mujoco.mj_name2id) instead of checking the robosuite’s wrapper API caused three injectors to crash immediately. It would have been better to check the existing working code (ImpulseInjector) before modifying other injectors to understand the correct API pattern.
The initial design of the daily reporting tool did not consider multi-device distributed usage patterns—assuming a single-device workflow, requiring users to redesign the two-stage architecture.
When generating JSON close to token limits, AI might truncate the output in the middle of the structure, resulting in malformed JSON, which requires defensive parsing and repair logic in production systems.
The repair of ccusage initially used the incorrect mb.get(‘model’) field, while the actual JSON contained modelName. No verification was done on the output structure of third-party tools before proceeding. This led to the repair being completely ineffective until humans discovered the error and rechecked it. Too many parallel exploration tasks were initiated, leading to duplicate information collection (reading the same log files multiple times).
Initially, it was proposed to use LIBERO/droid to test the VLA model, but environmental compatibility was not verified. The target environment was not kept as robosuite/mimicgen, but rather the semantic context of LIBERO. Humans needed to correct it to point to the correct configuration.
Insufficient memory across sessions: In the Tianhe session on 2026-02-16, AI was unable to recall the VLA checkpoint download from the previous session independently. Users were required to prompt to search for broader server paths.
Unable to predict users’ needs for features like dialogue summaries—these product insights came from observations of blanks in generated reports.
Difficulties in handling deeply nested meta-tasks: When conversations included discussions about the conversation itself, AI struggled to determine which level to analyze, unless there was clear task scope and guidance on expected outputs.
When generating the daily report on 2026-02-17, the AI acting as the daily report analyst itself became an object of observation—there was a meta-level complexity of “observers being observed.” AI needed to analyze its own behavior (generating daily reports), which required a certain level of self-awareness.
General Limitations Users rejected the design of the daily report automation deployment plan. AI failed to capture changes in user intentions and could not assess whether the detailed implementation plan met user expectations. It directly entered the ExitPlanMode mode without seeking user feedback first. Multiple attempts at ExitPlanMode failed, indicating difficulties in determining when the plan was complete and when users wanted to continue iterating. Users rejected the plan three times in multiple sessions, suggesting that AI should ask “Is this plan ready?” instead of assuming it was already completed. It was impossible to directly analyze video content to evaluate policy quality. The promotional videos of BC-RNN required manual extraction of key frames and manual inspection to identify robot hovering behaviors (ignoring the target capture). Without visual confirmation, it was impossible to infer a 0% success rate, which might be due to model quality issues. When encountering an API ConnectionRefused error during report generation, no alternative solutions were proposed (data was fully corrected before report generation). The flexibility of the separated workflow was insufficient. A long unified plan document containing both server-side and client-side instructions was created, but the execution boundaries were not considered. User feedback was needed to reorganize it into actionable individual deliverables. The project decomposition capability was weak. When users asked “What stage are we currently at?”, an exploratory agent was immediately launched and a large amount of documentation was read, rather than first checking the recent session context or the to-do tracking system. Over-reliance on file reading was excessive, while dialogue context might have been sufficient. Lessons Learned Main Lesson: Data errors are more隐蔽 and destructive than model errors. MIHD’s coordinate exchange error caused all visual experiment results to fail, but the code logic was normal, and all tests passed. It is necessary to trace anomalies at the macro level back to the data source (CSV column definitions). This requires a complete thought chain from data scientists; unit testing alone cannot detect such errors. Differences in naming conventions across frameworks are hidden pitfalls: robosuite’s _main suffix, differences in observation key names for different tasks (object and object state), LiteLLM’s model name-v1 suffix—these details are not obvious in the documentation, but they can lead to runtime errors. The robot simulation framework abstracts the original physics engine (robosuite encapsulates MuJoCo). Direct API calls bypassing the framework layer will cause errors—it is necessary to use the framework’s wrappers to handle naming conventions and state management. Robosuite’s observation key naming rule is that the environment automatically adds -state suffix to grouped modalities (e.g., object → object-state), but training data usually uses the original names. The adapter layer must handle these mismatches. The safest strategy is: (1) Use the framework’s API instead of low-level APIs; (2) Pass the original data structure instead of manually reconstructing it; (3) Print the actual output to verify field names, rather than inferring from the documentation. Always check the working reference code in the same codebase before making changes.
The correctness of the framework and the quality of the model require different verification strategies. Unit/integration testing can confirm code logic and eliminate errors like KeyError. Video visualization can reveal behavior quality issues (robot hovering and capturing). Even if unit testing passes, GPU integration testing remains crucial—BC-RNN passed 79 unit tests, but GPU deployment was needed to detect 0% SR issues and diagnose untrained checkpoints through visualization. Each verification layer has a different role.
The multi-device collaborative daily report tool has achieved a closed loop: each device exports local logs → central hub combines remote logs → unified deployment to Hugo → published on GitHub Pages. This workflow was extensively used on 2026-02-17 (processing 4 historical dates), proving the feasibility of the two-stage architecture. The next step is automation (which has been proposed but not implemented). Tool-based tools (used to analyze the tools used by the tool) need to carefully consider the distribution of the workflow—what happens on each device, how data is synchronized, how partial information is handled. For distributed scenarios, a two-stage architecture (local export + centralized aggregation) is more robust than a single-unit single-stage design.
The expansion of the error recovery benchmark scenario library from 251 to 454 is a successful incremental expansion case: First, the pulse injector (M4) was implemented → it was found that non-pulse types were needed (M5) → the MuJoCo API compatibility was fixed → various types of scenarios were generated through the detector candidate expansion mechanism. This shows the process from a minimum viable product to a fully functional product. The generation of error scenarios is a funnel process: detector triggering → error specification generation → injector application → verification → scenario acceptance. Enabling the injector does not guarantee scenario generation—it depends on the frequency of detector triggering. Depending on the dynamics of the task, the acceptance rates of different types of errors vary greatly. Pose perturbation is more general than friction/clamping anomalies in the pickup and placement task. Programmed specification enhancement (_augment_specs_with_alternatives()) can compensate for insufficient detector coverage.
Third-party tool integration requires defensive programming: the patch cost is equal to 0 (ccusage), field name compatibility (modelName or model), and self-downgrade for future repairs (when LiteLLM makes repairs, backtracking becomes inactive). This “only activates when necessary” patch strategy can minimize maintenance costs. Pricing defects of third-party tools should be resolved through local backtracking mechanisms, rather than waiting for upstream repairs. Design backtracking should only be triggered in cases of abnormal values (cost = 0) to maintain backward compatibility. LiteLLM uses versioned model names (anthropic.{model}-v1, optional: 0 suffix), while Claude Code logs use simplified names, leading to systematic mismatches. Cost tracking errors may lead to over 90% underestimation (observed 13 times), severely affecting financial planning. Regular audits of cost indicators are very important.
Human involvement in specifying the system architecture and strategic decisions, with AI responsible for technical implementation and optimization, yields the best results. In this meeting, users’ architectural insights (two-stage design, multi-device synchronization) were crucial; AI’s technical execution (parsing backtracking, configuration optimization) filled in the gaps. Qualitative judgment from domain experts is essential for identifying systemic problems. AI’s data-driven analysis and human experience and intuition form an effective complementarity.
Remote development on unstable connections requires multiple layers of defense: maintaining connection activity (prevention), session persistence (survival), multiplexing (fast reconnection), and automated scripts (recovery). Single-layer solutions will fail under real network conditions. For shared server accounts, user-specific custom settings should be placed in conditional blocks or separate startup scripts, rather than affecting everyone’s common.bashrc entry. tmux has both state persistence and environmental boundaries. Session-wide proxy configuration (not global bashrc) can prevent affecting users with shared accounts.
Structured data generated by LLMs requires multiple backtracking strategies for defensive parsing. The native JSON schema (Anthropic’s tool_use, OpenAI’s json_object) is helpful, but it cannot eliminate failures—always treat fixing as the last resort. Each backtracking layer handles specific failure modes: code blocks handle markdown format, curly braces matching handle truncation, and fixing handle syntax errors.
The daily summary tool benefits from a gradual evolution of the architecture: starting with a basic list of tasks/issues, adding session summaries to provide context, and adding priority metadata for filtering. Each layer meets different reading needs. The batch document workflow benefits from a two-stage architecture: (1) extracting local context for each source, (2) integrating across sources for global deduplication. This pattern appears in summary tools (export → merge), MIHD processes (first-stage cache embedding → second-stage fusion), and error recovery benchmarks (generating scenarios → collecting data).
MimicGen’s release policy is to only provide datasets, not pre-trained model checkpoints. Formal releases may provide data but not the training model—before planning, ensure the availability of assets. BC-RNN (with RNN behavior cloning) is a simple supervised learning: collecting pairs of human demonstrations (states, actions), training an LSTM to predict actions, and then deploying as a strategy. When there are enough demonstrations, this is a simple but effective manipulation task baseline. When pre-trained checkpoints are unavailable, training from demonstrations becomes the necessary backup plan.
Reviewing work logs (summarizing the situation of the past week) is an important exercise that converts raw dialogue logs into structured knowledge, helping to identify patterns and track progress over time. - Idempotent design patterns (tracking what has already been processed, skipping repetitive work) are crucial for workflows that may be interrupted or run again. _merged_devices tracking function can prevent expensive repeated API calls when reprocessing partially completed aggregated data.
Managing large model assets (VLA checkpoints larger than 47GB) requires an organized approach based on symbolic links to avoid duplication while maintaining centralized discoverability. Dispersed checkpoints in the file system can hinder reproducibility and configuration management. Centralized checkpoint directories can improve discoverability. When repairing quality issues in historical data, data correction (exportation) should be separated from downstream use (report generation). Avoid blocking the entire process due to failures in downstream dependencies (e.g., LLM API unavailability). The export phase relies on Node.js tools (ccusage), and the merging phase relies on the LLM API—even if merging is blocked, export can still proceed. Practical Experience The scope of complex scientific research project documents should include main modules as well as sub-modules (there are 11 sub-modules in the Motion framework), data conversion pipelines, and integration points across repositories (LeRobot, OpenPI, MimicGen). Adequate exploration can prevent onboarding difficulties caused by incomplete documentation. STAIG fusion produces only 2 clusters instead of 5, with ARI=0.1149 indicating severe collapse Solution: Root cause identified: 64-dim embedding bottleneck compresses 1536-dim UNI features by 96% (std=0.12), then spatial refinement’s radius-15 majority voting eliminates minority clusters. Proposed dimension ablation study to test 128/256/512-dim alternatives matching other fusion methods.
Key Insight: Cascading failures compound: GCN training produces near-collapsed embeddings, then spatial smoothing eliminates remaining small clusters entirely. The 64-dim bottleneck is critical—other fusion methods using 256-512 dims don’t exhibit this pathology.
2. VLA server initial obs missing camera images, causing ‘observation/image’ KeyError Solution: Fixed rollout_generator.py _get_current_obs() to add include_images parameter; detect PolicyServerAdapter type in _generate_from_single_rollout() and capture_natural_errors() to pass include_images=True with camera_names=[‘agentview’,‘robot0_eye_in_hand’]
Key Insight: VLA policies require visual input, but state_extractor.extract() doesn’t include images by default; need explicit policy type detection and include_images flag. This is a generic issue affecting all camera-dependent policies (VLA, VisuoMotor BC).
3. VLA server used wrong openpi API - manually loaded norm_stats causing model initialization failures Solution: Replaced manual loading with openpi’s create_trained_policy(train_config=get_config(config_name), checkpoint_dir=…) which handles norm_stats, transforms, and model architecture automatically. Added –config_name CLI arg and IMAGE_KEY_MAP for correct camera key mapping.
Key Insight: The openpi library provides high-level create_trained_policy() function that encapsulates all model loading complexity. Using low-level APIs manually is error-prone and breaks when the library evolves.
4. Pi0 (LIBERO checkpoint) achieved 100% failure rate on PickPlace task during natural_capture rollouts Solution: Identified failure mode distribution (joint_limit_approach 47%, grasp_wrong_pose 30%, misalignment_pre_grasp 17%, overshoot 5%, premature_release 1%); recorded as natural error data; determined need for PickPlace-specific checkpoint or domain adaptation for production use.
Key Insight: Pretrained VLA generalization is limited; cross-task distribution (LIBERO→robosuite PickPlace) causes significant performance degradation. However, these failure modes are valuable natural error data, aligning with benchmark’s natural error capture goals.
5. VLA integration appeared complete (code + tests passing) but discovered non-operational when attempting actual rollout Solution: Deep exploration revealed blockers: wrong openpi API usage, missing norm_stats.json handling, incomplete checkpoint paths, unsupported –policy vla_server flag. Created detailed fix plan and systematically implemented all corrections.
Key Insight: ‘Tests passing’ ≠ ‘system operational’—integration testing with real dependencies (model checkpoints, external APIs) essential before claiming completion. Synthetic unit tests validate code correctness but not end-to-end functionality.
6. _preprocess_obs() failed when StateExtractor returned state_info dict (different format from raw robosuite obs) Solution: Refactored _preprocess_obs() to detect input format and normalize to common structure {“state”: […], “images”: {…}}. Added robust key lookup with fallback patterns and proper float-to-uint8 image conversion.
Key Insight: Observation dict format changes depending on source: StateExtractor.extract() returns state_info with EEF-centric keys, while env.step() returns raw robosuite obs with robot0_* prefixes. Need unified preprocessing.
7. Documentation contained 15+ factual errors contradicting actual codebase state across multiple files Solution: Performed systematic registry-based verification (DETECTOR_REGISTRY, CLASSIFIER_REGISTRY, ErrorType enum), corrected all instances via targeted edits across 3 files, ran test suite to verify no breakage (79/79 passing).

Human vs AI Approaches Strategic Level VLA integration operational readiness assessment Role Approach Human User asked ‘can we rollout pi0 now?’—implicitly checking for end-to-end readiness beyond just code completion AI AI initially considered VLA integration ‘complete’ once code written and tests passing—assumed operational without verifying actual model loading and inference flow Difference Analysis: Human correctly intuited that ‘implementation complete’ ≠ ‘system operational’. AI Limitations Critical Limitations Over-optimistic definition of ‘completion’—equated passing unit tests with operational readiness, missing that VLA integration requires actual model checkpoint validation and API integration testing beyond synthetic mocks. Initially missed that openpi config uses repack_transform to rename keys, leading to incorrect assumptions about input key format. Learnings Key Learnings Embedding dimension bottlenecks cause catastrophic model collapse: STAIG’s 64-dim output compresses 1536-dim vision features by 96%, producing embeddings with std=0.12 that are nearly indistinguishable. Spatial refinement then eliminates minority clusters via majority voting. Other fusion methods (attention/qformer: 256-512 dim) don’t exhibit this pathology, suggesting 64-dim is fundamentally insufficient. VLA end-to-end integration critical requirements: ensure policy observation input format is correct, especially camera image passing; need explicit include_images=True in state_extractor.extract() and camera_names specification for all camera-dependent policies (VLA, VisuoMotor BC). When integrating third-party ML libraries (openpi, robomimic), always check actual API signatures via inspect.signature() and read example code in source repo. Documentation is often incomplete or outdated. The openpi library’s create_trained_policy() provides high-level encapsulation; using low-level APIs manually is error-prone. Pi0 (LIBERO checkpoint) demonstrates poor generalization on robosuite PickPlace task (100% failure rate); dominant failure modes: joint_limit_approach (47%) and grasp_wrong_pose (30%). This reveals VLA cross-task generalization remains challenging, but these failures provide valuable natural error data for benchmark purposes. Natural error capture (natural_capture mode) is more efficient than injection mode: 50 rollouts generated 150 scenes (~3 per rollout), while injection mode 10 rollouts generated only 3 scenes (~0.3 per rollout); natural failure modes are more diverse and realistic. Plugin-based architecture pattern in benchmark systems: detectors, classifiers, injectors all use base ABC + registry pattern for extensibility. Error classification system demonstrates this with 19 classifiers registered via CLASSIFIER_REGISTRY, enabling easy addition of new error types without modifying core logic. Documentation verification requires checking actual code registries and enums, not just reading docstrings or prior docs. DETECTOR_REGISTRY, CLASSIFIER_REGISTRY, and ErrorType enum are ground truth. Systematic grep after all edits prevents residual errors. Cross-conda-env communication architecture: VLA server uses TCP+pickle protocol to decouple model inference (openpi/openpi05 env) from benchmark framework (mimicgen_env). Length-prefix framing prevents message fragmentation, action chunking reduces inference calls. Environment isolation is critical for VLA/robotics projects due to conflicting dependencies. Observation preprocessing must handle multiple input formats gracefully: StateExtractor (framework-internal), raw env.step() (robosuite), and model-specific (VLA servers). Robust key lookup with fallbacks prevents silent failures. The observation dict format changes depending on source—need unified preprocessing layer. Spatial majority voting refinement (radius=15 nearest neighbors) can amplify rather than fix clustering errors when underlying embeddings are already collapsed. Refinement should be conditional on embedding quality metrics (e.g., disable if silhouette score < threshold). Dual VLM backend design (Gemini API + Claude Code CLI) provides flexibility: API suits batch automation, CLI suits interactive deep analysis and debugging; complementary coverage of different use cases. VLA integration for natural error generation requires architectural shifts: (1) policy server pattern for cross-conda-env execution, (2) camera observation support in environment wrapper, (3) observation preprocessing (quaternion→axis-angle, BGR→RGB, action chunking), (4) dual rollout modes (synthetic injection + natural capture). Fundamentally different from demo-replay synthetic perturbation approach. Systematic codebase exploration strategy (infrastructure check → model file location → config parameter confirmation → user decision confirmation) effectively supports complex multi-step project planning, avoiding missing critical dependencies. Backward compatibility is key consideration in data structure design: new conversation_summaries field through optionality and graceful degradation (missing field → no section rendering) ensures old reports continue working. This pattern applies broadly to evolving data formats. Error classification system’s 24 error types only triggered 5 types in actual VLA rollouts (joint_limit_approach, grasp_wrong_pose, misalignment_pre_grasp, overshoot, premature_release), indicating some error types require specific scenarios to manifest. Practical Learnings GPU batch processing for visualization (5 GPUs, 20 videos, zero failures) demonstrates value of parallel infrastructure. The subprocess.Popen + GPU assignment pattern scales well for embarrassingly parallel tasks. Falsy value handling subtlety in Python: 0 or default evaluates to default because 0 is falsy, causing bugs in 0-indexed counters. PrematureReleaseClassifier had step - (self._grasp_start_step or step) always returning 0 when grasp started at step 0. Solution: explicit is None checks for optional 0-indexed values. Solutions Critical Issues 1. Key Insight: OSC position controller actively resists external forces when tracking a trajectory; must use neutral actions to observe disturbance effects. Validation phase (drop.py) was correct all along with neutral actions.
2. Visualization video shows robotic arm barely moves, but logs show force applied and body position changed (15mm-117mm) Solution: First fix: re-apply force every step during duration window (mimic drop.py), solving MuJoCo’s per-step xfrc_applied clearing. Verification confirmed force re-application (Test 1: 11 times, Test 3: 21 times). Discovered deeper issue: visualization uses demo actions, OSC controller (kp=150) compensates external force effect
Key Insight: Layer 1 problem: MuJoCo physics engine auto-clears xfrc_applied after each physics step (prevent accumulation), must re-apply every step. Layer 2 problem: validation uses neutral actions (zero vector), controller only maintains position; visualization uses demo actions, controller tracks demo trajectory at every substep (20 substeps), generating corrective torques far exceeding external force. True fix requires using neutral actions during force window + settling period
3. Q-Former process crashed/died after completing 6/11 sections, potentially losing hours of GPU compute work Solution: Pipeline’s checkpoint recovery mechanism (checking for existing *_embeddings.npz files) automatically detected completed sections and resumed from section 151672, skipping already-finished work
Key Insight: 断点续跑 (checkpoint/resume) mechanism worked as designed; run_pipeline.py’s is_completed() check prevented re-running expensive experiments, validating the recovery architecture from original implementation plan
4. JSON file writes interrupted by Ctrl+C/crash/power loss lead to half-written invalid JSON, causing parse failures on next read Solution: Implemented _atomic_write() function: write to temp file (mkstemp), flush, os.replace for atomic rename, cleanup temp on failure. Ensures either old complete file or new complete file exists, never half-written state
Key Insight: Atomic write is standard pattern for preventing file corruption: write temp → rename atomically. Applies to all JSON/config file persistence scenarios
5.
