content:
Daily Report — 2026-02-14 Daily Summary Completed Work: Major improvements were achieved in four projects: (1) MIHD: Architecture refactoring to eliminate redundant computations; (2) Error Recovery Benchmark: Fixed forced injection and detector trigger vulnerabilities; (3) CalendarPro: Added batch deletion functionality and an interactive confirmation interface, while fixing 403 permission errors; (4) gadget/summarize: Implemented a configuration system, rclone synchronization, and Claude CLI backend. Implementation Methods: Through architectural redesign (two-stage pipeline separation), deep debugging (forced mechanisms, task phase detection), feature development (batch operations with security confirmation), infrastructure improvement (configuration files, cloud synchronization, multi-API support), and code quality enhancement of the system. Impact: MIHD: Reduced embedded computation by 62% (from 286 tasks to 110 non-duplicate tasks), enabling model reuse across different parts. Error Recovery: Successfully generated PreGrasp scenarios and implemented a cooling mechanism for each detector. CalendarPro: Eliminated 403 warnings and implemented multi-event operations based on patterns. Gadget/summarize: Established cross-device workflow and achieved automatic cloud synchronization. DCC Completed Work: In-depth work on MIHD project: Monitoring benchmark, designing and implementing a complete two-stage pipeline refactoring (extracting embedded vectors → evaluating fusion results), analyzing visual encoding bottlenecks, and formulating optimization plans. Implementation Methods: Tracking progress and timeouts of benchmarks, removing inefficient strategies. Implemented 11 pipeline modules and wrote 3 entry scripts. Conducted end-to-end testing. Analyzed code to identify bottlenecks: serial patch extraction, excessive GPU cache clearance, lack of encoder-level caching. Impact: Shifted the architecture from O(encoder × fusion × part) to O(encoder × part + fusion × part). Reduced UNI2 embedded computation from approximately 77 times to 11 times (a reduction of 86%). Specific optimization targets were defined to achieve 2–5 times acceleration. MacBook Completed Work: Quick maintenance of the gadget toolkit: Running/init updates to CLAUDE.md, then cleaning up the documentation after users deleted outdated tools. Implementation Methods: Analyzed the code library structure, rewritten CLAUDE.md to reflect the current state (only keeping summarize and benchmark), and removed references to 6 deleted tool categories. Impact: Synchronized the documentation with the actual code library, ensuring that future Claude instances will have accurate project outlines. tianhe Completed Work: Fixed error recovery benchmark issues: forced injection mechanism vulnerability, PreGrasp detector trigger problems, implementation of a cooling mechanism for each detector, and enhancement of forced visualization effects. Implementation Methods: Conducted root cause analysis (task phase stubs, mismatched main name, global cooling mechanism blockage), code refactoring (get_task_phase, rollout_generator cooling mechanism tracking, visual forced override), and iterative testing via scenario generation and video rendering. Impact: The PreGrasp detector now operates normally (successful scenario generation), the forced injection mechanism works properly (applied correctly to the correct subject), and each detector cooling mechanism prevents interference. The forced visibility issue is still under investigation (30N is insufficient for OSC controllers). TzJsDesktop Completed Work: Developed two major features: (1) CalendarPro improvement (fixed 403 errors with Google Calendar, added batch deletion functionality and an interactive Discord interface, improved code quality); (2) Upgrade of the gadget/summarize tool (configuration system, rclone synchronization, Claude CLI backend, ccusage fix, documentation improvement). Implementation Methods: CalendarPro: Modified API calls (settings and calendarList), expanded the data model for batch operations, created a Discord button confirmation view, and provided fallback logic for LLM failures. Gadget/summarize: Implemented a configuration system, integrated rclone CLI, added a Claude_cli backend via child processes, resolved Windows/nested environment issues, and enhanced JSON parsing robustness. Impact: CalendarPro: Eliminated repeated 403 errors, allowing users to safely delete multiple events at once. Gadget/summarize: Established a complete cross-device workflow (export → sync → merge → deploy), achieved automatic cloud synchronization, and the default Claude CLI backend does not require an API key. Major architectural refactoring of the MIHD benchmark process was completed (two-stage extraction-evaluation architecture), critical error recovery benchmark vulnerabilities were fixed (forced injection mechanism, detector trigger, cooling mechanism for each detector), CalendarPro was improved, batch deletion functionality and Google Calendar permission fixes were added, and the gadget/summarize tool was upgraded with a configuration system, rclone cloud synchronization, and multi-API backend support.
Tasks Architecture and Strategy - ✅ Implementation of MIHD two-stage pipeline architecture — A complete pipeline refactoring was designed and implemented: 11 pipeline modules and 3 entry scripts were created, along with the pipeline_config.yaml file. First stage: Extract and cache all encoder embeddings (deduplication). Second stage: Load cached embeddings, then perform fusion and evaluation operations. Four fusion strategies were successfully tested in section 151508. ✅ Fixed forced injection mechanism in error recovery benchmark — A critical vulnerability was fixed; the issue arose from applying force on the wrong object (changed from bin2 to gripper EEF). The root cause was the absence of ‘gripper0_eef’ in the possible_names list. A persistent forced mechanism was also implemented to address the automatic cleanup issue in MuJoCo xfrc_applied. ✅ Fixed PreGrasp detector not triggering problem — The root cause was that stub _check_phase_condition() always returned ‘unknown’. This issue was resolved by using get_task_completion_stages() for phase detection. Problems related to using demonstration actions, proximity door bypasses, cooling time for each detector, and object naming were also fixed. The detection logic was simplified: checking state changes in N steps instead of continuous approximation. 🔄 Investigate visibility issues in error recovery benchmark — Even when a force of 30N was applied, the robot arm showed no obvious movement in the video. Issues with the force mechanism (such as dominant OSC control cycles, too short force duration, or problems with the injection mechanism) need further investigation. ✅ Implemented batch deletion functionality for CalendarPro — The DeleteData model was extended, adding date_from/date_until/batch fields, updated the LLM prompt, modified search_events to accept custom time ranges, rewritten the handle_delete processor, created a BatchDeleteApprovalView with Discord buttons, and added batch deletion functionality in the semantic router. ✅ Implemented gadget/summarize configuration system — A ~/.config/summarize/config.json configuration file was created, supporting parameters such as device name, log directory, report directory, and rclone_remote. Subcommands –show and –init for the configuration file were implemented. Priority order: CLI flags > environment variables > configuration files > default values. ✅ Implemented rclone cloud synchronization for gadget/summarize — Integrated the rclone CLI tool, enabling automatic cloud upload after export/merge. Serverless scenarios are supported. rclone_path configuration was added for environments that do not require sudo. ✅ Analyzed MIHD visual encoding performance — Visual encoding bottlenecks were analyzed: Serial patch extraction took 10–30 seconds, too many torch.cuda.empty_cache() calls (about 100 times), and lack of encoder-level caching. A detailed three-part optimization plan was developed. ✅ Implemented cooling time for each detector in error recovery benchmark — The global cooling counter was changed to a cooldown_counters dictionary for each detector, ensuring that the cooling of one detector did not interfere with others (proximity distance cooling previously caused pregrasp failures). ✅ Fixed Google Calendar 403 permission issue — get_user_timezone() was changed from calendarList().get() API to settings().get() API, which only requires the calendar_events range, eliminating the 403 error every time a user message appears. ✅ Added backup logic for batch deletion when LLM fails — When the LLM timed out (due to nested Claude environment), passthrough of raw_input and Extract_delete_query() regex extraction were added to parse search keywords, date ranges, and batch flags from user input. ✅ Set Claude CLI as the default API backend for summarize — The summarize_with_claude_cli function was implemented via child processes calling ‘claude –print’. It can be used without an API key. It was set as the default backend, replacing anthropic. ✅ Solved Windows child process and nested Claude code issues — shell=True was added to npx and Claude calls to support Windows .cmd files. The CLAUDECODE environment variable was removed to avoid detection of nested sessions. ✅ Implemented export merging for existing files — Duplication logic based on a (source, project, timestamp) tuple was added. Multiple exports on the same day/device do not lose previous conversation records. 🔄 Improved detailed responses in Discord replies in CalendarPro — The response display for deletion operations was enhanced to show event name and date/time, but responses for other intentions still lack sufficient details (for example, schedule confirmations should explicitly state what activity is arranged). ✅ Fixed ccusage Opus cost calculation error — It was found that the –offline mode displayed the price of Opus 4.6 as $0. The –offline parameter was removed to get the latest online price. The cost display was corrected from $0 to $19.11. ✅ Optimized time and data format for ccusage — fetch_ccusage was moved after AI summary, including token consumption of the summary itself. The original JSON format of ccusage was stored directly. merge_token_usages was rewritten to support detailed information for each device. ✅ Enhanced JSON parsing robustness for summarize — _parse_json_response was rewritten, adding a three-step fallback mechanism: direct parsing → code block extraction → search for {to} substring. This allows handling cases where LLM adds explanatory text before and after JSON. Implementation and Fixes- ✅ MIHD benchmark monitoring and timeout configuration — Monitored the slow training-based fusion method. The timeout was increased from 1 hour to 2 hours. Based on user decision, staig_fusion_e2e was removed from the configuration. ✅ Added force override parameter and updated force range — A --force_override parameter was added to the visualization tool for dynamic force testing. force_norm_range was increased from [3.0, 15.0] to [15.0, 45.0], and force_clip was increased to 60.0. ✅ Fixed Discord bot empty message crash issue — An ‘if response:’ check was added before sending messages to prevent Discord API errors when the processor returns an empty string after sending a message directly through the channel. ✅ Updated gadget/summarize documentation — tutorial.md and README.md were rewritten. Configuration files, cloud synchronization, installation instructions for rclone without sudo, and explanations for three API backends were added. A requirements.txt file was created. ✅ Code quality fixes for CalendarPro — Default responses were added for 4 new intents in dual_verify.py; bare except was changed to except (ValueError, TypeError) in executor.py; the instantiation of Scheduler in periodic_checker.py was moved. ✅ Cleaned up documentation in gadgets project — CLAUDE.md was updated via the /init command, and then the documentation was cleaned up after removing 6 tool categories. README.md and CLAUDE.md were updated to reflect the current state (only containing summarize and benchmark). ✅ Cleaned up invalid rejection tracking code — add_rejected_candidate(), get_rejected_candidates(), and analyze_rejected() were removed from database.py. total_rejected/rejection_stats was removed from DatabaseMeta. All references were updated. Issues and Solutions Critical Issues 1. MIHD Benchmark: Redundant embedding computation — The same gene/visual encoder runs hundreds of times under different fusion strategies (e.g., PCA was calculated 55 times, UNI2 was calculated 77 times) Solution: A two-stage pipeline was designed and implemented: in the first stage, all encoder embeddings are extracted and cached (deduplication, 110 tasks out of 286 experiments, reducing by 62%); in the second stage, the cached embeddings are loaded, and then only fusion + clustering + evaluation are performed. Now the UNI2 model needs to be loaded only once for all 11 parts, instead of 77 times. Key insight: The current cache uses {gene}{vision}{fusion}/{section}_embeddings.npz as the key, including the fusion name, so changing the fusion method causes data re-extraction. Encoder-level caching (gene_cache/{encoder}/{section}.npz, vision_cache/{encoder}/{section}.npz) makes data reuse possible. Reuse of model instances across different parts can further improve efficiency.
2. Error recovery benchmark: Force is applied to bin2 (using bin2 instead of gripper EEF), but no interference with the robot is visible in the video Solution: Detailed logging revealed that the force is applied to bin2. The root cause was the absence of ‘gripper0_eef’ in the possible_names list, and the geometric fallback search matched robot0_screen_collision (containing ’ee’), thus bin2 was selected. This issue was resolved by adding ‘gripper0_eef’, ‘robot0_right_hand’, and ‘gripper0_gripper_base’ to possible names.
Key insight: The EEF body names for different robots are different (Sawyer uses gripper0_eef, not the generic gripper_link), and these names need to be explicitly included in the possible names list. Fallback to geometric search may cause strings containing ’ee’ to match irrelevant geometric shapes.
3. Error recovery benchmark: Despite registration, PreGrasp detector never triggers — get_task_phase() always returns ‘unknown’ Solution: The root cause is that when calling get_task_phase(), it calls a stub _check_phase_condition() that always returns False. All detectors dependent on task_phase (PreGrasp, GraspPrecond) are affected. The complete phase detection logic exists in get_task_completion_stages(). The problem was solved by rewriting get_task_phase() to use sensor-based detection methods. Multiple cascading errors were also fixed: lookahead uses a neutral action instead of a demonstration action, the接近 door prevents the detector from activating before contact, global cooling time prevents simultaneous detection, and MuJoCo body names do not match.
Key insight: There is (get_task_completion_stages) with functional implementation in the code library, and a always-failing stub (_check_phase_condition), indicating the caller used the wrong method. The symptom is that the detector does not trigger, but the root cause is dead code in the infrastructure layer. When logical contradictions are observed (no rejection but no output), infrastructure audits should be prioritized over symptom debugging.
4. Error recovery benchmark: duration_steps configuration parameter does not work — all forces last only 1 step (0.05 seconds) Solution: MuJoCo automatically clears xfrc_applied after each sim.step(). The solution is to modify collect_rollout_stats() to loop call injector.apply() during the first segment of verification rollout, and call injector.clear() after the duration ends.
Key insight: xfrc_applied in MuJoCo is a persistent field, but it is cleared automatically, so the application layer must explicitly re-apPLY the force for each step to maintain continuous force. This is a systemic error that affects all types of errors.
5. Error recovery benchmark: 30 Newtons are not visible in the visualization video of the robot’s arm movement Solution: A --force_override parameter was added to test larger forces without regeneration; the force range in the configuration was updated to 15–45 Newtons. The problem persists at 30 Newtons — further investigation is needed into the force mechanism (possibly the OSC control loop is too strong, the force duration is too short within 1 step, or xfrc_applied is not applied correctly).
Key insight: The force injection mechanism works (xfrc_applied is set or cleared), but 30 Newtons may not be sufficient to counteract the 150 Newtons/m of stiffness of the OSC controller, or the duration of 1 step (about 20 milliseconds) is too short for visible effects. The OSC control loop may suppress external forces within one control cycle.
6. CalendarPro: Users cannot delete multiple calendar events that match a pattern (e.g., “cancel all GB teacher meetings before March 1”) — the robot only says “Please specify the events to delete” Solution: The data model was extended to support date ranges and batch operations, the LLM prompt was updated to extract these fields, the search function was modified to accept custom time windows, and an interactive confirmation interface with Discord buttons was added, showing a preview and explicit approval.
Key insight: For productivity tools, single-item CRUD operations are insufficient — batch operations with safety confirmation (preview and user’s explicit approval) are crucial for user workflows involving patterns.
7. Gadget/summarize: Headless server cannot install cloud driver to achieve automatic synchronization Solution: The rclone CLI tool was studied and integrated, supporting token replication authentication (authorize rclone via browser on the machine, then copy the token to the headless server).
Key insight: rclone supports over 70 cloud service providers, and token replication for headless authentication is the best cross-platform cloud CLI option.
8. Error recovery benchmark: Global cooling time prevents pregrasp detector from activating near trigger Solution: Tracking of each detector’s cooling time was implemented (cooldown_counters dictionary), giving each detector independent cooling time. Detected results were filtered, and detectors still in the cooling period were removed.
Key insight: Global cooling time is not suitable for multi-detector systems because different detectors target different stages/conditions. A multi-detector system requires cooling time tracking for each detector.
9. CalendarPro: Each user message call to Google Calendar API returns a 403 permission error, causing a warning in the console Solution: The calendarList().get() API was switched to settings().get(setting=‘timezone’) API, which only requires the calendar_events scope instead of broader calendar access rights.
10. CalendarPro: When the LLM times out (nested Claude code environment), batch deletion fails because intent.data is empty — the semantic router correctly classifies the intent but does not extract structured data Solution: A穿透 of raw_input was added in the processor, enabling extract_delete_query(). Regular expressions were used to extract search keywords from Chinese/English phrases, and a date extraction pattern was added to identify ranges like “before March 1”.
Key insight: The dual verification system needs independent extraction capabilities in both paths — only SR fallback cannot fully rely on structured data generated by the LLM.
11. Gadget/summarize: ccusage — In offline mode, the cost of Opus 4.6 is shown as $0 Solution: –offline parameter was removed, and online mode was switched to get the latest model pricing.
Key insight: The offline pricing table does not include the latest models (such as Opus 4.6); online access is needed for accurate billing. Although online mode is slightly slower, data accuracy is more important.
12. Error recovery benchmark: The接近 door (max_eef_object_distance=0.05m) prevents pregrasp from operating within 0.05–0.1m Solution: A list of detector names was added to bypass the door check — detectors with their own distance verification (pregrasp, grasp_precond) can skip the door check.
Key insight: The接近 door is designed for contact-based detectors, but it is incorrectly applied to all detectors without considering their operating distance. Specific detector limitations should not be covered by global doors.
13. CalendarPro & gadget/summarize: Nested Claude code sessions prevent Claude CLI subprocess calls, causing LLM classification to always time out during developmentSolution: CalendarPro: Attempted to cancel the CLAUDECODE environment variable when starting the subprocess, but still failed — the final solution is to test in a non-nested environment. Gadget/summarize: Successfully canceled CLAUDECODE and CLAUDE_CODE_ENTRY in the subprocess environment. Key insight: Development environment tools may interfere with the system being tested in an invisible way — AI calls via subprocess are particularly vulnerable to environmental interference. Subprocesses inherit the parent process’s environment variables, so these variables need to be explicitly removed.
14. Gadget/summarize: Windows subprocess cannot find npx (.cmd file) Solution: The shell=True parameter was added in the subprocess.run call.
Key insight: The npm global command in Windows is actually a.pdf file, and Python subprocesses do not parse these files by default; shell execution is required.
15. Gadget/summarize: The JSON returned by the LLM may contain code blocks or explanatory text at the beginning and end Solution: A three-step JSON parsing method was implemented: direct parsing → extraction of ```json code blocks → search for {to} substring.Key Insight: The output format of LLMs is unstable, and multiple fallback layers are required to ensure robustness.
16. Gadget/summarize: Multiple exports on the same day/device will overwrite the existing conversation history. Solution: When existing files are detected, deduplicate them based on a tuple of (source, project, timestamp) and then merge them.
Key Insight: The deduplication key should be the smallest field combination that uniquely identifies the conversation. device_summary and token_usage use the latest values because they are cumulative statistical information.
General Issues 17. CalendarPro: After sending a confirmation via channel.send(), BatchDeleteApprovalView returns an empty string, causing the main loop to attempt calling the Discord API but fail due to an empty message. Solution: Add an ‘if response:’ check before message.channel.send(response) to skip sending when the response is empty.
Key Insight: When the processing program directly sends a message via the channel, an empty string should be returned to indicate “processed” — the main loop needs to follow this signal.
18. MIHD benchmark: The basic_contrastive fusion test timeouts; each part actually takes about 77 minutes. Solution: Increase the timeout to 2 hours (7200 seconds) in run_all_benchmarks.py.
Key Insight: Since the training loop during the training phase requires 300–550 cycles, the time required for a training-based fusion strategy is much longer than that of a simple fusion strategy.
Methods of Humans and Artificial Intelligence Strategic Level MIHD pipeline architecture decision Role Method Human The user immediately identifies the core inefficiency (redundant embedding calculations) and proposes a solution: “For each slide, we first need to obtain the embeddings of each slide… store them in a file, and then fuse the same embeddings.” The user insists on “complete rewriting” instead of incremental improvement. Artificial Intelligence The AI studied the existing code repository in detail, understood the specific implementation methods, then designed a detailed module structure and wrote all the code. The AI focuses on maintaining backward compatibility and reusing existing encoder implementations. Analysis of Differences: Humans have architectural vision and make strategic decisions (two-stage separation, complete rewriting). The AI transforms this into a detailed technical plan, using appropriate abstraction levels, handling edge cases, writing implementation code, and debugging issues. Humans decide “what” and “why”, while the AI handles “how” and has technical depth.
Error Recovery Benchmark: Strategy for tracking the root cause of problems Role Method Human The user asks: “Why are candidates rejected? If there is no rejection, why is there no output? Since this part was not written, please remove dead code.” Artificial Intelligence The AI spends a lot of time debugging at the symptom level (adding logs, adjusting parameters, analyzing trajectories) without directly questioning the correctness of the infrastructure code. Analysis of Differences: Humans quickly find contradictions through logical reasoning (no rejection but no output = infrastructure failure), while the AI tends to assume the existing code is correct and looks for reasons at the parameter/configuration level. The user’s question drives the discovery of the STUB root cause.
CalendarPro: Recognition of the need for batch deletion functionality Role Method Human The user immediately realizes that the current deletion workflow is insufficient. When they say “There are no meetings with GB teacher before March 1st, please cancel these schedules for me”, it fails — they understand that users need to operate on the pattern, not individual projects. Artificial Intelligence The initial implementation of the AI only supports deletion of individual projects and requires explicit specification — it did not anticipate batch operations as a core requirement. Analysis of Differences: Humans realize that real-world usage patterns require batch operations and date ranges; the AI starts from a CRUD-style paradigm for individual projects.
Error Recovery Benchmark: Simplification of PreGrasp detector logic Role Method Human The user points out: If this is a gradual change process, just check whether the current gripper is within 0.0–0.3 range, and if it changes after 10 steps, no complex “approaching” logic (continuous frame distance reduction) is needed. Artificial Intelligence The AI initially implemented a complex_check_approaching() method that requires continuous frame distance reduction and maintains Prev_distance and approaching_count states. Analysis of Differences: The human’s simplified method is more robust: for gradually changing gripper movements, the continuity check fails; directly checking the state change N steps earlier is a more important criterion. The AI tends to over-design, introducing unnecessary state tracking.
CalendarPro: Identification of the root cause of 403 permission errors Role Method Human The user provides exact log lines and immediately identifies this as a mismatch in OAuth scope, pointing out that the calendarList API call is the culprit. Artificial Intelligence The AI initially proposes a fix but does not verify whether the fix truly resolves the specific API call that causes the 403 error. Analysis of Differences: Humans have domain knowledge about Google Calendar API scope requirements and can accurately point out the mismatch at the API endpoint; the AI follows a more general debugging process.
Gadget/summarize: Requirement for cross-device synchronization Role Method Human The user proposes constraints such as “I don’t want it pushed to GitHub, but I want automatic cross-device transmission” and actively asks for a solution using the headless server CLI upload. Artificial Intelligence The AI confirms the device environment (Windows+Mac+Linux) and preference settings (cloud synchronization) through AskUserQuestion, studies rclone and other tools, and provides a complete solution. Analysis of Differences: The user clearly defines the problem and constraints; the AI fills in details through research and technical solution design. The user emphasizes that the headless scenario avoids defects in the solution.
MIHD timeout and fusion strategy selection | Role | Method | |——|——| | Human | The user observes that the training-based fusion process is too slow, so they make a pragmatic decision: increase the timeout to 2 hours, completely skip staig_fusion_e2e, and reduce the iteration count of Q-Former from 200 to 50. The user balances completeness and actual runtime. | | Artificial Intelligence | The AI monitors progress, reports timing statistics, and offers decision suggestions to the user when Q-Former hinders other experiments. The AI provides options but gives decision power to the user. |
Analysis of Differences: The user makes resource allocation decisions based on domain priorities. The AI provides data and options but recognizes that these are research-based judgments, not purely technical issues.
CalendarPro: Need for detailed confirmation information Role Method Human The user requests more details in their Discord reply, especially wanting to know which tasks are performed when — they value transparency and verification. Artificial Intelligence The AI initially provides little success/failure information and no specific explanation. Analysis of Differences: Humans understand that users need detailed feedback to verify system operations; the AI defaults to brief confirmation information.
Gadget/summarize: Diagnosis of ccusage Opus billing issues Role Method Human The user manually runs npx ccusage daily –json, finds that Opus fees display normally but the script output is incorrect, and directly points out that –offline might be the problem. Artificial Intelligence The AI first investigates the code logic, checks the call to ccusage and output processing, then compares the difference between with and without –offline output, and finally identifies the pricing table issue. Analysis of Differences: The user’s empirical intuition quickly identifies the problem; the AI verifies assumptions through systematic comparison. The user’s domain knowledge accelerates the diagnosis.
Gadget/summarize: ccusage data format Role Method Human The user suggests “ccusage can export in JSON format, which would be more convenient”, “wants to see detailed ccusage analysis”, and “when summarizing, all ccusage values for the day should be included”. Artificial Intelligence The AI changes fetch_ccusage to directly store raw JSON, rewrites merge_token_usages to support detailed information per device, and adds cache hit rate and model cost breakdown in Markdown. Analysis of Differences: The user defines requirements from a usage perspective (detailed, complete, readable); the AI transforms these requirements into technical implementations (retaining original data, improving rendering).
Limitations of Artificial Intelligence Key Limitations Despite analyzing the code repository, no proactive suggestion was made for a two-stage architecture to handle MIHD issues. Users must identify inefficiencies and propose solutions themselves. The AI should detect such redundant calculation patterns during the initial exploration. Error recovery benchmark: Initially, get_task_phase() was not identified as a STUB, and a lot of time was spent debugging at the symptom level (adjusting detector parameters, analyzing trajectory data) rather than directly auditing the correctness of infrastructure code. CalendarPro: Initially, it was not realized that deletion of individual projects is insufficient for actual user workflows — the user needed to explicitly point out this limitation with specific examples. Error recovery benchmark: Initially, no issue was found that force applied to the wrong body; first, the size and duration of the force were tried, and only then was the root cause located through debugging logs. Error recovery benchmark: Not realized that 30N force without any movement indicates a fundamental mechanism problem (OSC control cycles dominate, insufficient duration or injection error), rather than just needing greater force. CalendarPro: When implementing the first solution to fix the 403 error, it was not verified whether the solution was effective — the user had to come back and point out remaining issues. CalendarPro: Default use of the simplest confirmation information instead of detailed information — no anticipation that users need comprehensive feedback for verification. Gadget/summarize: No proactive discovery that ccusage should be called after AI summary (until the user pointed it out). Gadget/summarize: Insufficient understanding of Claude CLI in nested environments — only environment variables were removed, and the problem was not fully resolved, nor did any stderr output or other debugging methods be attempted. Gadget/summarize: Initial JSON parsing was not robust enough, and LLM output containing Markdown code blocks or surrounding text was not considered. Gadget/summarize: Configuration file solutions did not consider CLI tools like rclone until the user explicitly mentioned headless needs. General Limitations Error recovery benchmark: Despite multiple corrections, the same SSH command format error occurs repeatedly, more than 40 times — not understood that SSH commands need to use the ‘cd’ command explicitly before running the script. Gadget/summarize: Grep tools often time out, forcing reliance on Bash grep or Read tools as alternatives. Lessons Learned Key Lesson - Two-stage pipeline mode in the experiment matrix: When running M encoder × N fusion × K parts, divide it into a first stage (M×K encoding tasks using a cache mechanism) and a second stage (loading M×N×K evaluation tasks from the cache). Simplify the redundant calculation of O(M×N×K) to O(M×K + M×N×K), while achieving shared encoding. The design of the cache key is very important: encoder-level caching allows different fusion parts to share resources.- MuJoCo xfrc_applied behavior: Although the documentation indicates that xfrc_applied can maintain persistence between calls, mj_step() automatically clears it. To achieve continuous force application, the operation of each step must be explicitly reapplied at the application layer. For true pulse behavior, it must be explicitly cleared via injector.clear() after duration_steps. Code odor exists: When a function contains complete logic and the caller always uses a failed stub, the call relationships should be audited immediately rather than debugging parameters. When logical contradictions (no rejection, no output) are observed, infrastructure audits should be prioritized over symptom-based debugging. Visual balance of force injection: The OSC controller requires ≥25N of force to see visible displacement when kp=150 N/m, but the OSC control cycle may suppress external forces (about 20 milliseconds) within one control period. A careful balance between force magnitude and duration is needed. Productivity tools need batch operations with security mechanisms: (1) pattern matching to find multiple items, (2) previewing which items will be affected, (3) explicit user confirmation before execution. For actual workflows, single CRUD operations are insufficient. rclone is the best cross-platform cloud CLI choice, supporting over 70 providers, and headless authentication can be achieved by copying the token (run rclone authorize on a machine with a browser, then copy the token to the headless server). Model reuse between batches: For visual encoders that handle multiple parts, the model only needs to be loaded once for different parts, rather than reloading each part. This reduces the model initialization cost from O(n) to O(1). This is very important for large transformer models like UNI2. Risk of mismatch in fallback mechanisms: When the main method fails, falling back to a looser matching method (such as geometric name search) may produce incorrect results (“ee” matches the screen rather than the end effector). Additional verification is needed in the fallback path. EEF body names vary across robots (Sawyer uses gripper0_eef instead of the general gripper_link), and these names need to be explicitly included. For state change systems, simplifying detection logic is necessary: For discrete state systems (such as the change from 0 to 1 for a clamper), continuity-based detection is unreliable; one should directly check whether the state change is different (whether it changes after N steps). Multi-detector systems need tracking of each detector’s cooling time—global cooling may prevent simultaneous detection from different sources. Detector-specific constraints (distance thresholds, phase requirements) should not be covered by global rules—let the detector verify them itself. OAuth permission requirements vary greatly between Google Calendar API endpoints—the permissions required to set up the API are lower than those for calendarList API, even if the same information (timezone) is needed. A dual-validation system (semantic router + LLM) needs independent extraction capabilities in both paths—it cannot be assumed that the LLM always successfully generates structured output. The pricing table for ccusage offline mode does not include the latest models (such as Opus 4.6); online data acquisition is needed for accurate billing. Although the online mode is slightly slower, data accuracy is more important. In Windows systems, shell=True must be used when child processes call .cmd files, otherwise the globally installed npm command cannot be found. Bottlenecks in visual encoding: (1) Serial patch extraction loops are CPU-intensive operations (3000–4000 iterations). (2) Calling torch.cuda.empty_cache() after each batch process increases significant overhead. (3) The hard-coded batch_size=32 may not be the optimal choice. Perform performance analysis before optimization. Environment switching based on child processes: When dependencies require different conda environments, use child processes to call scripts in the target environment instead of trying to switch inside Python. User feedback should be detailed and specific—for calendar operations, always include: what action was taken, which events were affected, and when they occurred. The development environment may interfere with the system being tested—nested Claude code sessions can block AI provider calls based on child processes. Child processes inherit parent environment variables and specific variables (such as CLAUDECODE) need to be explicitly removed to avoid nested detection. JSON parsing requires a multi-layer fallback mechanism to handle various formats of LLM output: direct parsing → extracting code blocks → searching for {to} substrings. The LLM output format is unstable, so robustness is required. The priority order of configuration files should be: CLI parameters > environment variables > configuration files > default values, to ensure flexibility and overrideability. The choice of deduplication key should be a minimal field combination that uniquely identifies entities. For dialogue: (source, item, timestamp). 🔄 Benchmark progress monitoring and timeout configuration

content:
Daily Report — 2026-02-13 Daily Overview Completed Work: Progressed on four major projects: MIHD benchmark data repair and architecture planning, refactoring the gadget toolkit and making it open source, completing the robot error recovery framework, and enhancing the production version of CalendarPro with intelligent features. Execution Methods: Through systematic root cause analysis, modular architecture design, a two-stage pipeline model, comprehensive test coverage (over 107 tests per project), appropriate asynchronous lifecycle management, and dual-language documentation writing. Impact: MIHD is ready for 286 experiments and has complete spatial data; gadget supports cross-device workflows and is open source; the error recovery infrastructure is robust, including full replay functionality; CalendarPro is ready for production, featuring automatic learning, personalized energy prediction, and thought organization functions. DCC Completed Work: MIHD spatial transcriptome benchmark: data repair (4 failed sections) and a complete 7-stage enhancement plan design (standardization/Q-Former/LLaVA MLP/specific domains/batch correction/multi-part/configuration refactoring). Execution Methods: Extracted missing spatial coordinates from Dataset.zip, fixed boundary checks for frequency filter, added an alternative mclust→KMeans solution, resolved GPU monitoring thread issues; research code repository (config_manager.py 590 lines, run_benchmark.py 2600 lines) and QueST reference implementation, and wrote independent plans with exact line counts. Impact: All 11 DLPFC sections now work properly and have complete spatial data; a comprehensive blueprint for stages 1–7 provides a detailed roadmap for implementation, including precise integration points and dependencies. MacBook Completed Work: Gadget toolkit: refactored the daily summary tool into a two-stage multi-device architecture (export→merge), integrated ccusage token statistics, initialized Git repository with complete documentation. Execution Methods: Redesigned daily_summary.py, added CLI subcommands, collected device information, designed a recoverable JSON log format, used subprocess to handle token statistics; created .gitignore file, managed test/ as a git submodule, and wrote 7 READMEs containing all tools. Impact: The daily report tool now supports cross-device collaboration workflows and automatically tracks token usage; the gadget repository is open source on GitHub with complete documentation, improving maintainability. tianhe Completed Work: Error recovery benchmark: completed v4.1 infrastructure (4/4 validators, video annotations), diagnosed and fixed critical replay environment mismatches through a three-layer root cause analysis, reduced documentation from 615 lines to 101 lines. Execution Methods: Implemented LargeOffsetValidator and StuckValidator, with 41 tests passed; added frame annotations based on cv2; identified mismatches between PickPlace_D0+controller_configs and bare PickPlace by loading env_args from HDF5 metadata; systematically removed approximately 190 dead code lines. Impact: Scene generation capability increased tenfold (from 3 to 30 scenes), and EEF proximity is more appropriate (5 cm vs 22 cm); trigger steps now occur during replay when the robot approaches objects; documentation became more operable and concise, with size reduced to 1/6 of the original. TzJsDesktop Completed Work: CalendarPro major release: implemented an automatic scheduling system for repetitive tasks, fixed production bugs (double verification mismatch, error swallowing, duplicate event modifications), completed P0 reliability fixes and P1 intelligent upgrades, built an automatic organization function for random thinking, and updated comprehensive documentation. Execution Methods: Created a RecurringTaskStore with JSONL persistence and a PeriodicChecker with asyncio background loop; fixed dual_verify.py to prioritize LLM over semantic router; added CalendarServiceError exception propagation; implemented elastic token parsing, 30-second timeout for AI providers, message queue callback function; added automatic collection of learning data and personalized settings based on energy prediction; built a thought capture system with idle detection and AI organization. Impact: 107 out of 110 tests passed; users now see detailed error messages instead of silent failures; the system can automatically learn user behavior for personalized energy prediction; repetitive tasks are automatically scheduled; brief thoughts are captured during idle time and organized into target hierarchies. This was a comprehensive development day covering multiple projects: repaired MIHD spatial transcriptome data issues and designed a 7-stage enhancement plan; refactored the gadget daily report tool into a two-stage multi-device architecture and established a Git repository; implemented error recovery benchmark validators and fixed critical replay environment mismatches; built CalendarPro’s repetitive task automatic scheduling function, fixed production bugs, completed P0/P1 roadmaps, and added random thinking functionality.
Tasks Architecture & Strategy - ✅ Designed MIHD 7-stage enhancement plan — Studied the code repository and QueST reference documents, designed stages 1–7: configuration refactoring, standardized integration, UNI2+scGPT experiments, Q-Former/LLaVA MLP fusion, niche queries, batch correction, multi-part modes. Wrote complete independent plans with specific line counts, named mutable-riding-eclipse.md. ✅ Fixed replay environment configuration mismatch — Used a three-layer root cause analysis to identify the mismatch between PickPlace_D0+controller_configs and bare PickPlace; loaded environment parameters from HDF5 metadata; restored proximity threshold after fix. ✅ Fixed CalendarPro double verification intent mismatch — Modified dual_verify.py to prioritize LLM intent when mismatches occur, as LLM has a complete conversation context while SR only matches keywords. ✅ Added CalendarPro calendar error reporting function — Refactored calendar_service.py to throw CalendarServiceError instead of silent failure; updated all handlers (discord_bot, scheduler, api_routes) to capture and display detailed error messages. ✅ Fixed MIHD data issues in 4 failed sections — Extracted missing spatial files from Dataset.zip (tissue_positions_list.csv, scalefactors_json.json, images); fixed boundary checks for the frequency filter; added a fallback mechanism from mclust to KMeans. ✅ Refactored gadget daily summary into a two-stage architecture — Redesigned daily_summary.py, added CLI subcommands (export/merge/legacy); added device information collection; designed versioned JSON log format; implemented token usage statistics. ✅ Implemented CalendarPro periodic task system — Created RecurringTaskStore with JSONL persistence and PeriodicChecker using asyncio background loop (15-minute interval); added MANAGE_RECURRING/QUERY_RECURRING intents, semantic routing, Discord integration. 18 tests passed. ✅ Fixed CalendarPro periodic event modification issues — Modified update_event() function to detect periodic instances and delete duplicate recurrence/recurringEventId fields before updating, so Google Calendar only creates an exception for a single instance. ✅ Created CalendarPro PLANNING.md document — Created a comprehensive planning document with over 330 lines, including project positioning, module maturity ratings, target hierarchy, architecture decisions and reasons, P0-P3 roadmaps, known defects, etc. ✅ CalendarPro P0 reliability fix — Implemented a three-stage fallback mechanism, handled AI provider timeouts (asyncio.wait_for + httpx.Timeout), completed message queue callbacks, service layer error handling, and conducted 56 intent classification boundary tests. ✅ CalendarPro P1 intelligent upgrade — Implemented automatic collection of learning data, personalized energy prediction via personalize_rhythm(), integrated learning functionality into IntelligentScheduler, and improved the format of conversation context. ✅ Implemented CalendarPro random thinking function — Built a complete thought collection system: ThoughtStore stored as JSONL, IdleDetector reused by EssentialScheduler, ThoughtOrganizer with background asyncio loop, integrated with Discord, providing 3 processing methods, 25 tests passed. ✅ Wrote comprehensive documentation for gadget — Created independent README documents (summary/video/audio/image/paper/git/test) for 7 tools, a root README containing an overview table of tools, and summarize/tutorial.md quick-start guide. ✅ Fixed MuJoCo speed exchange error — Corrected env_wrapper.py, treating cvel[3:] as linear velocity and cvel[:3] as angular velocity (MuJoCo stores [angular velocity, linear velocity]). ✅ Implemented error recovery validators (LargeOffset, Stuck) — Created large_offset.py and stuck.py validators with configuration sections and 16 unit tests (8 each validator), completing 4/4 validator suite. ✅ Simplified error recovery CLAUDE.md documentation — Reduced documentation from 615 lines to 101 lines by eliminating duplicate content, removing sections irrelevant to the README, merging related parts. ✅ Enhanced visualization with frame annotations — Added annotations based on cv2: colored banners for different stages (green/red/orange), semi-transparent info boxes, detection/injection/verification details, and frame counter. Implementation & Fixes ✅ Initialized gadget’s Git repository — Created .gitignore file, executed git init command, added test/ as a submodule into TzJ2006/test.git, then committed to git@github.com:TzJ2006/gadget.git. ✅ Integrated ccusage token statistics — Called npx ccusage via subprocess to extract ccusage information, parsed JSON output; integrated it into all three entry points; displayed token usage section in markdown reports. ✅ Updated CalendarPro documentation — Updated CLAUDE.md document, added 10 previously unrecorded systems; expanded README with 4 types of usage examples, Discord command references, learning system documentation; also added PowerShell startup script. 🔄 Cleaned up error recovery code — Phase one completed: removed approximately 190 dead code lines (ReplaySystem, ReplayDriftError, duplicate detect() method); commented out the stub of BCPolicy. Phases two to five were interrupted due to reasons. Issues and Solutions Key Issues 1. The error recovery robot never approached objects during replay (minimum distance is 0.22 m, requiring contact for the task) Solution: Thoroughly analyzed robosuite source code, HDF5 metadata, and MuJoCo body mapping relationships; it was found that the replay using PickPlace_D0+controller_configs recorded in PickPlace actually uses pure PickPlace. The same operation produces a completely different trajectory.
Key Insight: Environmental configuration (kp, damping coefficient, ramp_ratio in controller_configs) fundamentally changes the robot’s dynamics. Replaying using environment metadata fully matching the HDF5 dataset—parameter adjustment can hide the root problem.#### 2. There is a conflict between CalendarPro’s semantic router and the LLM, causing the system to always use SR, resulting in incorrect routing (for example, the “leetcode” keyword → using manage_recurring instead of update).Solution: dual_verify.py was modified to prioritize LLM intent when mismatches occur. The LLM possesses a complete conversation context, while SR only matches keywords. The log shows “→Using LLM intent” for monitoring.
Key Insight: The classifier based on keywords fails when handling ambiguous expressions. When semantic routers and LLM opinions disagree, the model supported by context (LLM) should be trusted instead of the faster model (SR). SR filters obvious cases, while LLM acts as an arbiter.
3. Missing data in the 4 parts of MIHD causes pipeline failure (missing spatial files, empty region in frequency filter, STAIG model crash) Solution: Spatial files were extracted from Dataset.zip; boundary checks (min_w/min_h >= 10) were added; a fallback mechanism to mclust for KMeans was introduced, and processing was done using try/except wrappers.
Key Insight: Spatial transcriptomics data requires strong fault tolerance: multi-path candidate search, image processing boundary checks, statistical model fallback strategies to handle distribution anomalies.
4. The original single-step workflow of gadget cannot support multi-device collaboration (log must be manually copied to each device) Solution: Reconstructed into a two-stage process: (1) Export sub-commands to generate local JSON logs containing device information (no API key required); (2) Combine sub-commands, aggregate multiple logs, and call the API to generate the final report; the old mode is retained for backward compatibility. Key Insight: Multi-device workflows require a portable intermediate format (versioned JSON logs) and clear stage division (local parsing and remote merging). Key design includes: device information collection, version support designed for future expansion, optional device summaries to prevent information loss during merging.
5. After adding adjacent gating, all error detectors failed—iterative threshold adjustments (0.05→0.15→0.25→0.30 meters) did not produce any trigger signals Solution: A diagnostic script was written to measure the distances between actual EEF objects, revealing that the issue was environmental mismatch rather than threshold problems. The root cause was the replay configuration problem, not detector sensitivity issues.
Key Insight: When all detectors fail, real conditions should be measured via diagnostic log records before adjusting thresholds. Symptoms without trigger signals often hide fundamental mismatches (e.g., incorrect controller dynamics).
6. CalendarPro calendar API errors (403 permission insufficient, HttpError) are captured via print() and returned as None, causing users to receive a generic “failed” message and causing confusion Solution: A CalendarServiceError exception was created; all calendar_service methods were refactored to provide detailed context information when errors occur; all callers were updated to capture and display user-friendly messages containing technical details.
Key Insight: Silent error handling (print + returning None) violates the contract of error handling. Users cannot fix issues they cannot see. Errors with context should always be passed to the presentation layer and properly formatted.
7. CalendarPro AI provider lacks a timeout mechanism—network pause may cause the entire robot to freeze indefinitely Solution: All API calls were wrapped with asyncio.wait_for(timeout=30.0), and httpx.Timeout(30.0) was added to the client constructor. When the timeout occurs, an AIResponse with error fields is returned.
Key Insight: Timeout protection requires dual layers: asyncio coroutine level (wait_for) and HTTP client level (httpx.Timeout) to capture different failure modes.
8. When AI returns prose, multiple blocks, or truncated JSON before JSON, CalendarPro’s JSON parsing fails—leading to intent classification crashes Solution: The_extract_json() function was implemented to extract the first complete object by balancing bracket counts; a three-stage fallback mechanism (direct parsing → trailing comma correction → general intent) was added; ValueError exceptions for logging and fallback were removed.
Key Insight: Production-grade AI systems need graceful degradation—they must not crash for malformed output, and safe fallback intents should always be provided.
9. The planning document lacks self-containedness—users repeatedly reject ExitPlanMode, demanding “writing every sentence of the plan into the plan file” Solution: The planning document was rewritten to be fully self-contained: user decision records, code snapshots with exact line numbers, QueST reference code details, and complete implementation code were added; each stage had a “inserted after line X” location.
Key Insight: The planning mode document must be fully self-contained so that sessions can be restored later. Users’ rejections indicate insufficient document details—all exploration results (exact positions, line numbers, function signatures, existing code) need to be written into the plan instead of relying on external context.
10. MuJoCo’s speed switching causes false instability triggers (angular velocity is misread as linear) Solution: Array slicing was exchanged: linvel = cvel[3:], angvel = cvel[:3] to match MuJoCo’s [angular velocity(3), linear velocity(3)] layout.
Key Insight: Documentation and code do not match: code comments claim [linear, angular velocity], but MuJoCo stores [angular velocity, linear velocity]. Always verify based on the source document rather than inline comments.
11. The CLAUDE.md file has 615 lines, with many repetitions between sections, and some content belongs to the README file Solution: The documentation was rewritten, focusing on: (1) inconspicuous information (server limits, common pitfalls); (2) integrating commands into a single block; (3) removing easily identifiable content (file tree, method signatures); (4) retaining only architectures that require multi-file reading.
Key Insight: Documentation for AI agents should focus on content that cannot be discovered via tools, rather than a comprehensive reference. Simplicity improves usability—101 lines vs. 615 lines make it clearer.
12. When CalendarPro updates duplicate events, it modifies the entire series instead of individual instances, even though singleEvents=True is used during search Solution: update_event() was modified to detect duplicate instances (with recurringEventId) and remove duplicate/recurringEventId before calling the API. Google Calendar creates a separate exception for such instances.
Key Insight: The implicit behavior of Google Calendar API: singleEvents=True during search provides instance IDs, but updates/removals require explicit removal of relevant fields to avoid modifying the entire series. Duplicate operations should always be tested on a test calendar.
13. CalendarPro’s asyncio.create_task() used for the message queue has no exception handling callback—tasks may terminate silently when the queue is full, and user messages will never be processed Solution: done_callback=_on_queue_task_done was added to all create_task calls; a cleanup handler was implemented to log exceptions and remove dead tasks; a close() method was added for closing.
Key Insight: asyncio background tasks are “forgotten” by default, so done callbacks must always be added for monitoring/cleanup, especially long-term tasks.
General Issues 14. Manually querying token usage is cumbersome—users want automatic daily statistics Solution: ccusage@latest daily –json was called via a sub-process to integrate ccusage, and output was parsed; automatic collection was performed at all three entry points; a total table and model details were displayed in the token usage section; data was merged across devices.
Key Insight: Automate data collection by leveraging existing tools instead of re-implementing. Design considerations include: fault tolerance of sub-processes (silent skip if unavailable), multi-device aggregation strategy (summing tokens/costs, merging model details), and readable presentation (tables > lists).
15. MIHD GPU peak statistics always show zero (ResourceMonitor never calls update_peak_stats()) Solution: ResourceMonitor was refactored: start_monitoring() started a daemon thread that samples every second, stop_monitoring() terminated the thread and sampled the final peak, and threading.Event lifecycle control was added.
Key Insight: Monitoring peak statistics requires continuous sampling during operation, not just start/stop snapshots. Background daemon threads are a standard solution, but proper lifecycle management is needed to avoid resource leaks.
16. The gadget test/catalog is a nested Git repository with its own remote address, causing nested repository conflicts during git add operations Solution: Git submodules were used: the test folder was moved to a backup location, ‘git submodule add git@github.com:TzJ2006/test.git test’ was run for cloning, the backup was removed, and .gitmodules automatically recorded the configuration. Key Insight: Git submodules are suitable for nested repositories with independent remote repositories. Key point: submodules record commit hashes rather than branches; git submodule update --init --recursive is required during cloning; when updating, the directory must be entered in the submodule and git pull must be executed, then the commit hash is modified.
17. CalendarPro’s start.bat cannot detect conda environments (cmd does not support ‘conda activate’ without conda init, CONDA_PREFIX is unavailable in new cmd windows) Solution: A start.ps1 script that supports native PowerShell conda functions was created; PowerShell can directly execute ‘conda activate calendarpro’. start.bat was updated to allow calling PowerShell under -ExecutionPolicy Bypass; PID tracking and stop.ps1 were added.
Key Insight: Windows batch files perform poorly in conda integration. For conda workflows on Windows, PowerShell is a better choice. Always test environment activation in a new shell, rather than using inherited conda sessions.
18. CalendarPro’s simulation patch failed because generate_with_fallback was imported inside the method, not at the module level Solution: The patch target was changed from ‘src.thoughts.thought_organizer.generate_with_fallback’ to ‘src.aiProvider_selector.generate_with_fallback’, so the patch could be applied in the source module.
Key Insight: During simulation, patches should act on the function definition location, not the import location—local imports create new references, thus bypassing the module-level patch.
19. After creating test_thoughts.py, pytest async tests for CalendarPro reported ‘coroutine never awaited’ warnings Solution: The pytest-asyncio package was installed, which can automatically detect async test functions and run them in the event loop.
Key Insight: pytest itself does not support async tests—the pytest-asyncio plugin must be installed in pyproject.toml dependencies.

Daily Report — 2026-02-12 Daily Overview Completed work: Optimized the MIHD’s CLAUDE.md document and designed a multi-phase plan including standardization, Q-Former/LLaVA fusion strategies, and specific queries and batch correction inspired by QueST. Execution method: Simultaneously explored the code repositories of MIHD and QueST, studied the architecture of Q-Former, decomposed 6 user ideas into dependent implementation phases, and defined the scope through user questions. Improved the MIHD documentation and designed a comprehensive 7-phase enhancement plan including standardization, Q-Former fusion, and QueST-inspired functionalities
Tasks Architecture and Strategy ✅ Designed a 7-phase MIHD enhancement plan — Created a full implementation plan covering standardization, Q-Former/LLaVA fusion, QueST specific queries, batch correction, and configuration adjustments, along with a dependency graph. ❌ Implemented phases 1 to 7 of the enhancement plan — Users stopped implementation before proceeding to review the plan; implementation is ready, awaiting user approval. ✅ Studied the architecture of Q-Former and QueST — In-depth research on BLIP-2 Q-Former and LLaVA MLP connector, QueST’s GIN layer, batch correction via adversarial training, and specific queries through k-hop subgraph pooling. Implementation and Fixes ✅ Improved the CLAUDE.md document — Analyzed the existing CLAUDE.md document, removed redundant content, added missing components (GCN encoder, fusion strategy, test commands, utils module), and reduced the document count from 579 lines to 188 lines. Issues and Solutions Key Issues 1. Inconsistent standardization in MIHD — UNI2/scGPT uses L2 norm, while HIPT/ResNet50/MLP/GCN does not, and no post-fusion standardization is applied. Solution: Designed a three-point normalization system (after encoding, before fusion, after fusion) and can configure different methods (L2, standard scaling, none) via the new utils/normalization.py module. Key insight: Inconsistent standardization across different encoders affects downstream clustering performance; the three-point normalization method provides fine-grained control.
2. QueST uses adversarial training for batch correction, but it is unclear whether this works for spatial transcriptomics. Solution: Developed a BatchCorrection plugin module based on QueST’s discriminator/generator pattern and evaluated its effectiveness. **Key insight:**移植 batch correction into the MIHD environment requires empirical validation rather than assuming applicability.
General Issues 3. User idea 3 is not clear enough — “Q-Former similar to LLaVA”, but LLaVA uses a simple MLP, while Q-Former comes from BLIP-2. Solution: Proposed clarifying the issue; users chose to implement both (Q-Former with cross-attention and a 2-layer MLP for LLaVA) to compare lightweight and heavy fusion effects. Key insight: Clarifying architectural ambiguities early avoids wasting implementation resources in the wrong direction.
Human and AI Approaches Implementation Level Scope of QueST idea implementation Role Method Human Explicitly decided to implement QueST-inspired functionalities in MIHD, rather than just understanding QueST. AI Initially assumed the task was research/understanding; later needed clarification. Analysis of differences: Humans clarified the implementation intent from the start; AI initially operated in a exploratory research mode until it was corrected.
Fusion strategy between Q-Former and LLaVA MLP Role Method Human When faced with a choice, users decided to implement both to compare lightweight and heavy fusion effects. AI AI identified the architectural differences and asked users to choose one. Analysis of differences: Humans find comparative evaluation valuable; AI initially sought a single decision.
When to start implementation Role Method Human Users stopped the assistant’s work before implementation began, hoping to review the plan first. AI AI was ready to start implementation immediately after creating the plan. Analysis of differences: Humans prioritize reviewing the plan; AI assumes continuation only after approval.
Limitations of AI General limitations AI did not actively clarify ambiguous scopes (Q-Former and LLaVA MLP, research and implementation) before extensive exploration, wasting human resources on potentially unnecessary research. AI assumed users needed immediate implementation right after creating the plan without confirming user consent, requiring user intervention to stop. Learning Outcomes Key takeaways For complex multi-project plans, clarify scope and architecture choices before deep exploration — ask “both or one?” “understand or implement?” and “partial process or full process” in advance. Dependency analysis is crucial for multi-phase plans — standardization must occur before fusion experiments, configuration basics enable smooth subsequent work, and QueST batch correction requires standardized fused output. Document improvement is important: MIHD’s CLAUDE.md was reduced by 67%, while adding missing content through removal of redundancy, discovery of information, and implementation history. Metrics overlay not appearing on plots despite modifying utils/visualization.py Solution: Discovered duplicate create_clustering_visualization() function at line 1644 in run_benchmark.py that shadowed the utils version - modified both

2. Risk of overwriting existing good results from pca_uni_staig_fusion directory Solution: Used –skip_cached flag instead of –override to preserve cached embeddings for completed sections

General Issues 3. Parallel GPU tasks caused OOM kill (exit code 137) when running 3 STAIG fusion experiments simultaneously Solution: Switched to sequential execution by chaining commands with && in a single Bash call
Key Insight: Deep learning benchmarks with large spatial transcriptomics data require exclusive GPU access - parallelize across CPU-bound tasks only
4. Sections 151510, 151672, 151674 fail with missing spatial coordinates or OpenCV errors Solution: Script continues with remaining sections - identified these as data integrity issues requiring separate investigation
Key Insight: Robust benchmark pipelines should validate data prerequisites (spatial coords, image files) and fail gracefully with clear error messages

The relay layer is a key isolation layer that protects repository write permissions. Semantic consistency between interface names and actual behavior must be strict: the name ‘staig_fusion’ naturally promises the same meaning as STAIG; allowing significant differences in default behavior can cause many hidden errors; global coverage behaviors (e.g., forcing encoder to UNI) must be clearly indicated in logs. Low CPU and GPU utilization simultaneously indicates the program is waiting on single-thread I/O, not CPU; performance bottlenecks in visual feature extraction usually occur in data preprocessing (patch extraction) rather than model forward pass. Errors in R interfaces (e.g., mclust) are not intuitive in Python; sufficient pre-validation should be added at the Python level and clear error messages with shape information provided; when R packages are unavailable, silent degradation must be clearly warned against, and algorithm behavior should not be changed without notice. Domain Knowledge There are five quantifiable key implementation differences between MIHD and original STAIG (prioritized): ① Mixed coordinate scales for full-resolution images (most critical); ② Silent degradation of mclust; ③ Reversed gene preprocessing order; ④ Difference in number of pseudo-label clusters; ⑤ Hyperparameter and image transform differences. ✗ Insufficient thoroughness in fixes: when removing trend charts, only the call was removed initially, and a second fix is needed. ✗ Easy to overlook existing global coverage logic: when adding UNI2 tqdm, not realizing that strict mode will force encoder coverage. ✗ No pre-check of HPC environment modules (e.g., scanpy) before verification, leading to ModuleNotFoundError during validation, increasing debugging rounds. ✗ Multiple options for low GPU utilization issues, but no active suggestion to use profile tools (py-spy, nvprof) to precisely locate the actual bottleneck. SameLabel@K metric returned 0.0 even though embedding clearly retrieved same cell types Solution: Root cause: eval_mask excluded all niche spots via ~niche_mask, leaving zero Layer_3 spots. Fixed by computing SameLabel over all_valid_mask (including niche) while keeping Precision@K on eval_mask (excluding niche to avoid self-match bias)
Key Insight: Different evaluation metrics require different exclusion masks - retrieval rate needs the full valid set, while rank agreement needs to exclude the query region itself

General Issues 3. Node ID collision risk when combining query and reference subgraphs in shared label dict Solution: Applied node ID offset of adata_q.n_obs to all reference node IDs before creating combined label dict, ensuring no key collisions
Key Insight: When merging graphs from separate AnnData objects, node indices overlap - use deterministic offsets rather than relying on disjoint ID spaces
4. Wasserstein distance solver dependency - POT library not installed in quest conda environment Solution: Implemented two-tier solver: try import ot.emd2() first (fast C backend), fallback to scipy.optimize.linprog with HiGHS solver (no extra dependency, sufficient for small subgraphs ~30-100 nodes)
Key Insight: Always provide dependency-free fallbacks for optional performance optimizations - scipy is ubiquitous, POT is not

Captures spatial niche structure independent of learned embeddings. Evaluation metrics for niche query require careful mask design: Precision@K uses eval_mask (~niche to avoid self-match), SameLabel@K uses all_valid_mask (including niche for retrieval rate), Spearman uses eval_mask (rank correlation on non-self spots) Practical Learnings When porting graph algorithms between frameworks: squidpy.gr.spatial_neighbors() → sklearn NearestNeighbors + scipy sparse, torch_geometric.k_hop_subgraph() → networkx BFS. Pattern: translate to dependency-minimal equivalents. Caching strategy for expensive computations: RMIdealEvaluator precomputes all k-hop subgraphs at init (~8min for 4384 spots), saves to .npy cache, subsequent runs load instantly. Cache key should include spatial graph parameters (n_neighbors, k_hop).
